design_detail: Cochrane systematic review (update of a review first published in 2001 from a protocol published in 2000; searches to November 2015) of randomized controlled trials in which an alpha2-adrenergic agonist (clonidine, lofexidine, guanfacine or tizanidine) was the main medicine for the acute phase of managed opioid withdrawal, compared with placebo, reducing doses of methadone, symptomatic medicines, or another alpha2-agonist regimen. Random-effects meta-analysis (RevMan 5) of risk ratios and standardized mean differences, with GRADE summary-of-findings tables for the comparisons with methadone and with placebo. 26 trials, 1728 participants.
can_establish: Whether, in supervised withdrawal from heroin or methadone in trials published between 1979 and 2013, clonidine or lofexidine lowered the chance of severe withdrawal and raised completion compared with placebo, and how they compared with a methadone taper in withdrawal severity, time course, time in treatment, adverse effects and completion, each with the review's own GRADE rating.
cannot_establish: Effects in people withdrawing from illicitly manufactured fentanyl or from prescription opioids (no included trial), in withdrawal managed alone at home (one small home-based trial, clonidine against lofexidine), on relapse, overdose or engagement in further treatment afterwards (almost never reported), which alpha2 agonist works best (direct comparisons too few and too diverse to pool), the size of the effect on peak withdrawal against placebo (not pooled, I2 98%), or whether unpublished trials are missing (publication bias not assessed).

sample.recruitment: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO and Web of Science searched to November 2015 without language limits, plus reference lists, trial registries, conference proceedings and contacts with investigators. The trials came from 12 countries (USA 5, Spain 5, UK 4, Italy 3, China 2, and one each in Australia, India, Switzerland, Taiwan, Germany, Hungary and Iran). Settings: 16 inpatient, 7 outpatient, 1 prison health centre, 1 mandatory treatment centre, and 1 with day-care-like clinic sessions (Results › Included studies; Treatment setting).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized controlled trials giving detailed drug and participant information and data on withdrawal, adverse effects or completion, in people primarily dependent on opioids undergoing managed withdrawal, with an alpha2 agonist as the principal medicine. Excluded: alpha2 agonists combined with opioid antagonists (antagonist-induced withdrawal) and comparisons with buprenorphine, both covered by separate Cochrane reviews.
sample.demographics: In 19 trials all participants were withdrawing from heroin or other short-acting opioids, in 5 from methadone, in 1 from either, and in 1 mostly from opium. Two-thirds to three-quarters of participants were men in most trials, and all were men in five. Average age was 23 to 32 years in 19 of the 20 trials that reported it (39.7 years in a trial on an AIDS ward); no trial included adolescents. Three trials had low levels of injecting (Results › Participant characteristics).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; completion of withdrawal is itself an outcome. The review judged incomplete outcome data at high risk of bias for the withdrawal and adverse-effect outcomes in two of the methadone-comparison trials (Cami 1985; San 1990).
sample.selection_effects: Supervised, mostly inpatient settings; several trials excluded people with polydrug or alcohol dependence; two trials were in compulsory treatment (the review left out completion and duration data from Jiang 1993 for that reason); one trial was in people admitted for AIDS-related illness. No trial involved illicitly manufactured fentanyl, and the newest trial is from 2013. Trials needed to report doses and participant characteristics in detail, which may favour better-reported trials.

exposure.measurement: Randomized allocation to an alpha2-adrenergic agonist (clonidine, lofexidine, guanfacine or tizanidine) as the main medicine during a managed withdrawal episode.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as the review reports them: mostly oral (intravenous clonidine in two Italian trials), two to four doses a day adjusted daily to withdrawal symptoms and blood pressure. Maximum clonidine amounts across trials 0.9 to 1.35 mg a day (the review gives the typical maximum as around 1.0 mg a day in Results › Treatment regimens and around 1.2 mg a day in Implications for practice); lofexidine maximum 1.6 to 2.0 mg a day; clonidine usually started at 0.1 to 0.2 mg a dose and lofexidine at 0.4 to 0.6 mg a dose. Maximal doses for a few days around peak withdrawal (usually two to four days after stopping opioids), then tapered and stopped seven to ten days after stopping opioids. Scheduled treatment lasted one to two weeks in 15 trials, under a week in 4 (shortest three days) and over two weeks in 5 (longest 30 days). Methadone comparison arms used reducing doses, often over about ten days; in the multicentre trial (Kleber 1985; Senay 1983) methadone was reduced from 20 mg a day to zero over 20 days and followed by placebo to day 30, against ten days of active clonidine followed by placebo. Participants withdrawing from methadone started from 40 mg a day or less in four trials.
exposure.polysubstance: Several trials excluded polydrug or alcohol dependence; in one, 37 of 86 participants were also withdrawing from benzodiazepines. Symptomatic and adjunct medicines (benzodiazepines, neuroleptics and others) were allowed in many trials and not standardized. The planned subgroup analysis by polydrug use could not be done.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: outcomes were measured during the withdrawal episode itself.

comparison.controls: Placebo (6 trials: Batey 1987, Benos 1985, Bruno 1979, Gerra 1995, Nazari 2013, Yu 2008), reducing doses of methadone (12 trials), symptomatic medicines (4 trials), or a different alpha2 agonist (5 trials). In San 1990 the clonidine and guanfacine arms were combined against methadone to avoid double counting.
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials. The review notes that in Batey 1987 random allocation was probable but not stated, and that in Gerra 1995 the adequacy of sequence generation was doubtful (high risk).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. Comorbid psychiatric and physical illness, polydrug use and the precipitants of withdrawal were planned subgroup factors but could not be analysed.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison arms came from the same trial populations; other drug use was not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: Withdrawal scales differing between trials (modified Himmelsbach, Objective and Subjective Opiate Withdrawal Scales, trial-specific observer and participant scales); severe withdrawal (leaving treatment for intolerable withdrawal, or a high objective score); days in treatment; adverse effects (hypotension or its symptoms, withheld doses, drop-out for adverse effects); completion (naloxone challenge or urine screening in four trials, completion of the scheduled programme in three, retention at the scheduled end in one, acceptance of naltrexone in one).
outcomes.validity_norms: No common instrument; the authors state that the different ways of assessing and reporting withdrawal made the severity analyses not robust (Discussion › Summary of main results; Potential biases in the review process).
outcomes.operationalization: Adverse effects were defined as clinically significant withdrawal signs (such as vomiting and diarrhoea) plus events not typical of withdrawal. Completion was defined differently in different trials and pooled as one outcome.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The 12 counts the pooled analyses in the Data and analyses tables (3 against placebo, 9 against methadone including the two subgroup analyses).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The review judged blinding for subjective outcomes at low risk in 4 of 6 placebo trials and 9 of 12 methadone trials (high risk in Gerra 2000 and Senay 1983); duration and completion were treated as objective and at low risk in all trials.

analysis.effect_sizes: Against placebo: severe withdrawal RR 0.32 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.57), 3 trials, 148 participants, GRADE moderate (illustrative 589 against 188 per 1000); without the high-risk trial RR 0.28 (0.09 to 0.83), 117 participants. Completion RR 1.95 (1.34 to 2.84), 3 trials, 148 participants, moderate (288 against 561 per 1000); without the high-risk trial RR 2.12 (1.40 to 3.19). Peak withdrawal score not pooled (2 trials, 113 participants, I2 98%). Against reducing doses of methadone: severe withdrawal RR 1.18 (0.81 to 1.73), 5 trials, 340, low; peak withdrawal score SMD 0.22 (-0.02 to 0.46), 2 trials, 263, moderate; overall severity SMD 0.13 (-0.24 to 0.49), 3 trials, 119, moderate; duration of treatment SMD -1.07 (-1.31 to -0.83), 3 trials, 310, low (longer with methadone); hypotensive or other adverse effects RR 1.92 (1.19 to 3.10), 6 trials, 464, low (79 against 151 per 1000), and RR 2.02 (0.62 to 6.64), 203, without three high-risk trials; drop-out for adverse effects RR 3.62 (0.77 to 16.94), 4 trials, 153, low; completion RR 0.85 (0.69 to 1.05), 9 trials, 659, low, with significant heterogeneity (568 against 483 per 1000); by opioid, heroin RR 0.87 (0.61 to 1.25) and methadone RR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18); by setting, inpatient RR 0.87 (0.68 to 1.12), I2 67%, and outpatient RR 1.09 (0.73 to 1.64), I2 0%.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (aggregate trial data; no meta-regression).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol published in Issue 2, 2000; review first published in Issue 1, 2001. The 2016 update reports a changed search (Web of Science added; one MeSH term removed). Of six planned subgroup factors only opioid type and setting could be analysed, for completion against methadone.
analysis.selective_reporting: Engagement in further treatment, a planned secondary outcome, could not be assessed. The placebo peak-withdrawal analysis is not pooled and appears in no summary table, although the plain-language summary describes the placebo evidence as very low to moderate quality. Sensitivity analyses were limited to outcomes with at least three trials, two of them at low or unclear risk.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The placebo comparison rests on 148 participants; drop-out for adverse effects rests on few events with none in the methadone arms; the authors state that the small numbers limited their ability to judge the effect of trial quality and publication bias.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In three small placebo-controlled trials (148 participants) clonidine or lofexidine roughly halved the chance of severe withdrawal and doubled completion, with consistent sensitivity analyses. Against a methadone taper, severity was similar overall, withdrawal came and went earlier, treatment was shorter, adverse effects (mainly low blood pressure, dizziness, drowsiness and dry mouth) were about twice as common, and completion did not differ detectably (RR 0.85, 0.69 to 1.05). Lofexidine lowered blood pressure less than clonidine in three small direct comparisons that could not be pooled. Neither approach fully relieved aches and pains, poor sleep, low energy, chills or anxiety.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that clonidine and lofexidine are more effective than placebo, that they do not differ significantly in efficacy from a methadone taper, that methadone has fewer adverse effects than clonidine, and that lofexidine has a better safety profile than clonidine. Gaps: (1) ‘no significant difference’ from methadone is read as similar efficacy, although the low-quality completion estimate allows a meaningful advantage for methadone; (2) the safety ranking of lofexidine over clonidine rests on three small direct comparisons without meta-analysis and on indirect comparisons across trials; (3) the practice advice to prefer lofexidine for outpatient withdrawal goes beyond these data; (4) the plain-language summary calls further placebo-controlled trials unethical on the strength of 148 participants in three trials; (5) the excess of adverse effects against methadone loses significance when the three high-risk trials are removed, although the point estimate holds. Elsewhere the discussion states its limits plainly, including bias against methadone from fixed trial tapers.

timeline.event: First publication of this Cochrane review (Gowing et al.), from a protocol published in 2000; new citations followed in 2008, 2009, 2014 and 2016 (History table).
Yu et al. US multisite placebo-controlled trial of lofexidine in inpatient withdrawal, stopped early for benefit; the largest placebo trial in this review (68 participants).
This update: 26 trials, 1728 participants, search to November 2015.
Companion Cochrane review of buprenorphine for managing opioid withdrawal, by the same lead author

replication.where_it_stands: The standard summary of randomized evidence on clonidine-type medicines for opioid withdrawal up to 2015. The placebo comparison is small but consistent; the comparison with methadone is low quality. Its trials predate the spread of illicitly manufactured fentanyl, so the review does not show how well these medicines work in people withdrawing from fentanyl or xylazine-adulterated supply. The companion buprenorphine review compares buprenorphine directly with these medicines and should be read with it.

funding.funder: Internal: Drug and Alcohol Services South Australia (two authors, LG and RA, are employees). External: none supplied.
funding.declared_conflicts: Robert Ali: his institution received untied educational grants from Reckitt Benckiser for research and scientific meetings, with no personal fees. The other three authors declare none known.
funding.affiliations_note: Boehringer Ingelheim (maker of clonidine) and Britannia Pharmaceuticals (maker of lofexidine) supplied information on trials (Acknowledgements). Six included trials had some pharmaceutical support, six reported non-industry funding and funding was unclear for 14; the multicentre trial behind two included reports was part-funded by Boehringer Ingelheim, and Britannia supplied medication and placebo for Yu 2008.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people withdrawing from illicitly manufactured fentanyl (including xylazine-adulterated supply), in outpatient as well as inpatient settings, comparing lofexidine, clonidine and buprenorphine-based withdrawal management with blinded withdrawal ratings, standardized monitoring of blood pressure, dizziness and falls, and follow-up beyond the episode for engagement in further treatment, relapse and overdose.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people dependent on opioids in managed withdrawal), interventions, four comparators and outcomes are specified.
Cochrane protocol published in 2000, before the review was first published in 2001; the changes to the search in this update are stated under Differences between protocol and review.
Only randomized controlled trials are eligible, without a stated reason (the excluded-studies table only notes that this version is restricted to them).

Five databases with strategies in appendices, reference lists, trial registries, conference proceedings and contacts with investigators; no language restriction; search within six months of publication.
One author assessed each potentially relevant study and all four authors confirmed the decisions; the first screening of 3377 records is not described as duplicated.
One author extracted the data, consulting the others only where uncertain.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The Characteristics of excluded studies table lists 34 studies with a reason for each. A further 252 full-text articles were excluded without listing because they were judged not potentially relevant; a strict reading of the item would make this 'no' and the overall rating critically low.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Setting, participants, group sizes, interventions with doses, comparators, outcomes, scheduled duration and funding notes for each trial (Characteristics of included studies).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding judged separately for subjective and objective outcomes, incomplete data, selective reporting, other bias) for every trial.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding reported for each trial where known (six with pharmaceutical support, six non-industry, 14 unclear).
Random-effects models in RevMan 5; the peak-withdrawal data against placebo were not pooled because of I2 98%; multi-arm trials were combined after checking that the arms were similar.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses leaving out high-risk trials for five outcomes (severe withdrawal and completion against placebo; severe withdrawal, adverse effects and drop-out against methadone).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE ratings in the summary tables; the discussion says the adverse-effect finding is weakened by high-risk trials and by few events.
I2 and chi-squared reported; subgroup analyses by opioid and by setting; the heterogeneity of withdrawal measures is discussed as the reason the peak placebo data were not pooled.
Not investigated; the authors state that small numbers of studies limited their ability to assess it.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Sources of support and each author's declaration are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is 'no' (15: publication bias not investigated), which under AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence; the other critical items are met, item 7 on a lenient reading. Items 3, 5 and 6 are non-critical weaknesses. This rates the review's conduct, not its trials: for the trials the card follows the review's own Cochrane appraisal and says so (10 of 26 trials at high risk of bias in at least one domain; the GRADE ratings it reports are moderate for both placebo outcomes and low to moderate against methadone). The review may be cited for the pooled estimates with the review's own GRADE ratings, for the observation that withdrawal comes and goes earlier with alpha2 agonists than with a methadone taper, and for the narrative comparison of blood-pressure effects of clonidine and lofexidine; it should not be cited for effects in fentanyl withdrawal, for outcomes after the episode, or for a ranking of the alpha2 agonists.

key_findings.finding: 26 randomized controlled trials (35 reports) with 1728 participants met the criteria; 1012 participants received an alpha2 agonist (607 clonidine, 215 lofexidine, 174 guanfacine, 16 tizanidine). Six trials compared an alpha2 agonist with placebo, 12 with reducing doses of methadone, 4 with symptomatic medicines and 5 compared alpha2 agonists; 10 trials were at high risk of bias in at least one domain.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Main results, 1st paragraph; Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Against placebo, severe withdrawal was less likely with clonidine or lofexidine: RR 0.32 (95% CI 0.18 to 0.57), 3 trials, 148 participants, GRADE moderate (downgraded for few events); illustrative risk 589 per 1000 with placebo against 188 per 1000. Leaving out the high-risk trial (Batey 1987) gave RR 0.28 (0.09 to 0.83), 117 participants.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › 1. Alpha2-adrenergic agonists compared with placebo › (a) Withdrawal syndrome, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text does not name the three trials; their group sizes in the Characteristics of included studies (Batey 1987, 31; Benos 1985, 49; Yu 2008, 68) add up to 148, and to 117 without Batey 1987 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Against placebo, completion of withdrawal treatment was more likely: RR 1.95 (1.34 to 2.84), 3 trials, 148 participants, GRADE moderate; illustrative 288 per 1000 with placebo against 561 per 1000. Without the high-risk trial RR 2.12 (1.40 to 3.19), 117 participants.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › 1 › (d) Completion of treatment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Against placebo, adverse effects were more common: sedation and dry mouth about twice as common with clonidine (Benos 1985); drowsiness and dizziness in 7 of 16 on clonidine against 0 of 15 on placebo (Batey 1987); with lofexidine, hypotension 18% against 0% and insomnia 42% against 9%, and 4 of 35 against 0 of 33 stopped for adverse effects (Yu 2008). In Yu 2008, 15 of 33 on placebo against 6 of 35 on lofexidine stopped because the medicine was not working.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 1 › (c) Adverse effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; (a) Withdrawal syndrome, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Against reducing doses of methadone, withdrawal severity did not differ significantly: severe withdrawal RR 1.18 (0.81 to 1.73), 5 trials, 340 participants, GRADE low; peak withdrawal score SMD 0.22 (-0.02 to 0.46), 2 trials, 263, moderate; overall severity SMD 0.13 (-0.24 to 0.49), 3 trials, 119, moderate.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (a) Withdrawal syndrome › Intensity of withdrawal, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In all eight trials that described the time course, withdrawal signs and symptoms appeared earlier and resolved sooner with an alpha2 agonist than with a methadone taper, with which peak withdrawal came at the end of the taper.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (a) Time course of withdrawal, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Time in treatment was shorter with an alpha2 agonist than with a methadone taper: SMD -1.07 (-1.31 to -0.83), 3 trials, 310 participants, GRADE low; SMD -1.04 (-1.44 to -0.64) without the high-risk trial (Jiang 1993).
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (b) Duration of treatment, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Hypotensive or other adverse effects were more frequent with an alpha2 agonist than with a methadone taper: RR 1.92 (1.19 to 3.10), 6 trials, 464 participants, GRADE low; illustrative 79 against 151 per 1000. Without the three high-risk trials RR 2.02 (0.62 to 6.64), 203 participants. Drop-out for adverse effects RR 3.62 (0.77 to 16.94), 4 trials, 153 participants, with no events in the methadone arms. In Jiang 1993, 89 of 100 participants on clonidine had dizziness on standing.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (c) Nature and incidence of adverse effects, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Completion did not differ significantly between alpha2 agonists and a methadone taper: RR 0.85 (0.69 to 1.05), 9 trials, 659 participants, GRADE low (two trials at high risk of selection bias; significant heterogeneity); illustrative 568 against 483 per 1000. Without San 1990 RR 0.91 (0.75 to 1.11). Subgroups: withdrawal from heroin RR 0.87 (0.61 to 1.25), from methadone RR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18); inpatient RR 0.87 (0.68 to 1.12), I2 67%; outpatient RR 1.09 (0.73 to 1.64), I2 0%.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › 2 › (d) Completion of treatment, 4th paragraph; Effect of opioid used; Effect of treatment setting; Data and analyses, Comparison 2

key_findings.finding: Clonidine against lofexidine (3 trials) and guanfacine (2 trials) could not be pooled. Withdrawal was similar; lofexidine lowered blood pressure less: postural hypotension in 8 of 14 on lofexidine against 13 of 14 on clonidine (Kahn 1997); doses withheld for low blood pressure on 4.1% against 8.9% of occasions (Lin 1997). In the home-based trial (Carnwath 1998), 17 of 26 on lofexidine against 12 of 24 on clonidine had an opiate-free urine sample four weeks after starting.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › 3. Clonidine compared to lofexidine or guanfacine › (a) Withdrawal syndrome; (d) Nature and incidence of adverse effects › Hypotension, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; (d) Completion of withdrawal

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that neither alpha2 agonists nor a methadone taper fully suppress the aches and pains, sleep disturbance, loss of energy, chills or anxiety of opioid withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Summary of main results › 2. (a) Withdrawal syndrome experienced, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Six trials received some pharmaceutical support, six reported non-industry funding and in 14 funding was unclear.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Janiri 1994 is listed among the excluded studies (and in the references to excluded studies), yet its completion data for clonidine against lefetamine are reported in Results as one of three studies with comparative completion rates.
reporting_issues.consequence: An excluded trial's result is presented among included-study results; it is narrative only and does not enter any pooled estimate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Participant characteristics paragraph refers to 'the 25 studies that met the inclusion criteria', while 26 trials were included.
reporting_issues.consequence: A leftover from an earlier version; no effect on the analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: The typical maximum daily amount of clonidine is given as two different figures in Results › Treatment regimens and in Implications for practice (both recorded in the exposure field of this card).
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency in a descriptive statement; no effect on the pooled results.

reporting_issues.issue: The methadone taper in Cami 1985 is described as going from a lower to a higher daily amount over ten days (Results › Predominant signs and symptoms), which cannot be a taper.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error in a study description.

reporting_issues.issue: The plain-language summary rates the placebo-comparison evidence as very low to moderate quality, but Summary of findings 2 shows only two outcomes, both moderate; the outcome rated very low (peak withdrawal score) appears in no table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers of the tables cannot see the very-low-quality rating that the summary mentions.

reporting_issues.issue: Summary of findings for the main comparison gives illustrative risks of 0 per 1000 for drop-out due to adverse effects in both arms, because the methadone arms had no events.
reporting_issues.consequence: The absolute effect for this outcome is uninformative; the relative estimate (RR 3.62, 0.77 to 16.94) is the only usable figure.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent), AI reader 112 (first reader)
verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7081129 (all sections, both summary-of-findings tables, the data-and-analyses tables and the characteristics of included and excluded studies rendered as text, appendices listed, acknowledgements, contributions, sources of support and declarations of interest read; Figures 1 to 3 and all forest plots are images and their values were not extracted)

design_detail: Cochrane systematic review (update of a review first published in 2000 from a protocol published the same year; searches to December 2016) of randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials using buprenorphine to manage opioid withdrawal, compared with reducing doses of methadone, alpha2-adrenergic agonists (clonidine or lofexidine), symptomatic medicines or placebo, or a different buprenorphine regimen. Random-effects meta-analysis (RevMan 5) with GRADE summary-of-findings tables for three comparisons. 27 trials, 3048 participants, 2172 of whom received buprenorphine.
can_establish: How buprenorphine compared with clonidine or lofexidine, and with a methadone taper, in withdrawal severity, time in treatment, adverse effects and completion of supervised withdrawal, mostly from heroin, in trials up to 2016, with the review's own GRADE ratings; and whether faster or slower reduction of buprenorphine changed completion.
cannot_establish: Effects in people withdrawing from illicitly manufactured fentanyl (no trial) or, with any confidence, from methadone or prescription opioids (the review says it could not assess this); effects outside supervised treatment; relapse or overdose after the episode (engagement in further treatment was reported by five trials and not pooled); the best dose or schedule (regimens too diverse); and whether trials are missing (no method for publication bias is described).

sample.recruitment: CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and Web of Science searched to December 2016 without language limits, plus reference lists, trial registries, conference proceedings and contacts with investigators. 14 trials in the USA, 3 in Germany, 2 each in the UK, India and Iran, and 1 each in Australia, Israel, Italy and Switzerland (Results › Participant characteristics).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized (and quasi-randomized) trials of buprenorphine to modify withdrawal signs and symptoms in people primarily dependent on opioids, against the comparators above, giving detailed drug and participant information. Excluded: buprenorphine combined with opioid antagonists given to induce withdrawal (separate review). One partially randomized trial contributed only its 14 randomized participants (Wang 1996); two trials whose comparisons were unique (different starting doses; oxazepam) were not analysed further.
sample.demographics: Average age 25 to 40 years in 21 trials, 47 in one, 17 to 20 in two adolescent trials, not reported in three. Men were half to three-quarters of participants in most trials, all or nearly all in four and under half in three. In 17 trials most or all participants were withdrawing from heroin or heroin and methadone; one trial was mostly prescription opioids (Sigmon 2013); two tapered buprenorphine after buprenorphine maintenance; seven did not report the opioid.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; completion is an outcome. Incomplete outcome data were judged high risk in one trial (Sigmon 2013) and unclear in one (Ponizovsky 2006).
sample.selection_effects: Ten of the 14 alpha2-comparison trials were inpatient; settings included an AIDS ward (Umbricht 2003, where discharge depended on the medical illness) and a prison (Wright 2011). Four trials excluded people dependent on other drugs; two trials were stopped early for benefit (Collins 2005; Ling 2005). No trial involved illicitly manufactured fentanyl.

exposure.measurement: Randomized allocation to buprenorphine (sublingual tablets, buprenorphine-naloxone tablets, sublingual solution or intramuscular injection) to manage withdrawal, or to a faster or slower buprenorphine reduction.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as the review reports them: sublingual tablets in 9 trials, buprenorphine-naloxone tablets in 5 (one switched from one to the other), sublingual solution in 3, intramuscular injection in 3, preparation not reported in 6. Maximum doses ranged from 0.3 to 3.6 mg by injection and from 1.2 to 16 mg sublingually; fixed regimens in most trials, tailored to need in two. Alpha2 comparison: buprenorphine for 3 days (three trials), 4 days (one), 5 days (three), 7 days (two), 10 days (three) or 13 days (one); one trial gave a single 8 mg dose before starting naltrexone. Methadone comparison: buprenorphine regimens from 3 days (intramuscular, 3.6 mg on day 1 tapering to 1.2 mg on day 3) to 20 or 21 days, maximum 2 to 16 mg a day sublingually. Rate-of-reduction comparison: inpatient regimens of one to five days (for example 8 mg then 24 mg on one day against 32 mg over three days); outpatient reductions over 7 to 56 days after stabilization (12 against 36 days; 7 against 28 days; 28 against 56 days; one, two or four weeks; 14 days against 8 weeks).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled differently by trial: four excluded people dependent on other drugs, some excluded alcohol or benzodiazepine dependence, two detoxified other drugs first, one sample was 60% cocaine dependent and two enrolled only people who used several drugs. Not analysed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: outcomes were measured during the withdrawal episode; abstinence at completion was an outcome in the rate-of-reduction comparison.

comparison.controls: Reducing doses of methadone (6 trials), clonidine (13 trials) or lofexidine (1 trial, Raistrick 2005), or a different rate of buprenorphine reduction (7 trials). Umbricht 2003 contributed to both the methadone and the clonidine comparisons.
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials; allocation was judged at uncertain risk in five of six methadone trials and 10 of 14 alpha2 trials for lack of information, and at high risk in two rate-of-reduction trials that did not conceal allocation.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; the planned subgroup analyses by drug and severity of dependence, polydrug use and comorbidity could not be done. None of the trials reported outcomes by sex.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison arms came from the same trial populations; other drug use was not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: Peak and mean overall withdrawal scores on scales that differed between trials (pooled as standardized mean differences); days in treatment; number with any adverse effect and number stopping for adverse effects; completion (number completing the scheduled period; in two trials, number receiving a naltrexone dose); number abstinent at completion of the buprenorphine reduction.
outcomes.validity_norms: No common withdrawal instrument; the authors calculated mean overall scores themselves for some trials and say this may have introduced error (Potential biases in the review process).
outcomes.operationalization: Adverse effects were defined as clinically significant withdrawal signs plus events not typical of withdrawal (such as hypotension and dry mouth). Completion definitions differed; naltrexone-based definitions may be stricter.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The 12 counts the pooled estimates in the Data and analyses tables (2 for methadone, 6 for alpha2 agonists, and inpatient and outpatient subtotals for 2 outcomes on rate of reduction).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Lack of blinding was judged high risk for subjective outcomes in 2 of 6 methadone trials, 6 of 14 alpha2 trials and 2 of 7 rate-of-reduction trials; duration and completion were treated as objective and at low risk in all trials.

analysis.effect_sizes: Against a methadone taper: days in treatment MD 1.30 days (95% CI -8.11 to 10.72), 2 trials, 82 participants, GRADE low; completion RR 1.04 (0.91 to 1.20), 5 trials, 457 participants, moderate (528 against 549 per 1000); severity and adverse effects not pooled. Against clonidine or lofexidine: peak withdrawal SMD -0.43 (-0.74 to -0.13), 6 trials, 521 participants, very low, I2 63% (SMD -0.50, -0.92 to -0.09, without three high-risk trials); mean overall withdrawal SMD -0.43 (-0.58 to -0.28), 7 trials, 902 participants, moderate (SMD -0.37, -0.58 to -0.16, without four high-risk trials); days in treatment SMD 0.92 (0.57 to 1.27), 4 trials (5 comparisons), 558 participants, moderate (inpatient 1.00, 0.33 to 1.67; outpatient 0.82, 0.57 to 1.06); any adverse effect RR 0.93 (0.70 to 1.26), 3 trials (4 comparisons), 493 participants, very low; stopping for adverse effects RR 0.20 (0.04 to 1.15), 3 inpatient trials, 134 participants, low (90 against 18 per 1000), events only in clonidine arms; completion RR 1.59 (1.23 to 2.06), 11 trials (12 comparisons), 1264 participants, moderate (453 against 721 per 1000), number needed to treat for one more completion 4 (2.8 to 6.7); inpatient RR 1.74 (1.05 to 2.89), 539; outpatient RR 1.45 (1.12 to 1.88), 725. Faster against slower buprenorphine reduction: completion inpatient RR 1.00 (0.84 to 1.18), 2 trials, 60, low; outpatient RR 0.86 (0.44 to 1.70), 4 trials, 647, I2 80%, very low; abstinence at completion inpatient RR 1.00 (0.81 to 1.23), 1 trial, 40, low; outpatient RR 0.94 (0.39 to 2.24), 4 trials, 610 (619 in Summary of findings 3), I2 81%, very low.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (aggregate trial data; subgroup analysis by setting only).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol published in Issue 2, 2000. Deviation stated: the protocol and earlier versions also admitted prospective controlled cohort studies; this update is restricted to randomized and quasi-randomized trials 'to ensure internal validity'. Of six planned subgroup factors only setting could be analysed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Severity and adverse effects against methadone could not be pooled; one trial collected adverse-effect data without reporting them (Wright 2011, judged uncertain for selective reporting). Engagement in further treatment was summarized narratively from five trials.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The methadone comparison rests on 82 to 457 participants per outcome; stopping for adverse effects rests on few events.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against clonidine or lofexidine, buprenorphine was followed by lower average withdrawal scores (SMD -0.43, moderate), longer time in treatment (SMD 0.92, moderate) and more completion (RR 1.59; about 72 against 45 in 100 in the review's illustration; moderate), with no detectable difference in the number with adverse effects (RR 0.93, very low) and a non-significant difference in stopping for adverse effects (RR 0.20, 0.04 to 1.15, low). Against a methadone taper, completion did not differ detectably (RR 1.04, 0.91 to 1.20, moderate). Whether faster or slower reduction of buprenorphine changes completion could not be determined (very low).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that buprenorphine is more effective than clonidine or lofexidine for severity, duration and completion, and that buprenorphine and methadone appear equally effective. These follow the moderate-quality estimates. Gaps: (1) the plain-language summary says people on buprenorphine ‘experience fewer side effects’, while the pooled number with adverse effects shows no difference (very low) and the drop-out difference is not significant; (2) the implication that buprenorphine may be associated with higher engagement in further treatment rests on four of five trials, not pooled, one of which built naltrexone into the buprenorphine arm's protocol; (3) ‘we did not detect any publication bias’ is stated without any described method. The effect size of 0.43 is called small to moderate in the abstract and moderate elsewhere.

timeline.event: First publication of this Cochrane review (Gowing et al.); new citations followed in 2006, 2008 and 2017, with a further search in 2009 (History table).

Ling et al. two open-label trials of buprenorphine-naloxone against clonidine in US community treatment programmes (113 inpatients, 231 outpatients), stopped early for benefit; together 344 of the 1264 participants in the completion estimate (editors' arithmetic).
Companion Cochrane review of alpha2-adrenergic agonists for opioid withdrawal, by the same lead author
This update: 27 trials, 3048 participants, search to December 2016.

replication.where_it_stands: The standard summary of randomized evidence on buprenorphine for managing opioid withdrawal up to 2016. The advantage over clonidine is consistent across settings and moderately certain; equivalence with a methadone taper rests on fewer, smaller trials. The trials predate widespread illicitly manufactured fentanyl, with which starting buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal, so the review cannot speak to fentanyl withdrawal. Two trials were stopped early for benefit, which can exaggerate effects.

funding.funder: Internal: Drug and Alcohol Services South Australia. External: Commonwealth Department of Health and Ageing, Australia.
funding.declared_conflicts: All four authors declare none known.
funding.affiliations_note: In the 2016 companion review one author (Robert Ali) declared untied educational grants to his institution from Reckitt Benckiser, a buprenorphine manufacturer; here he declares none. Among included trials, three had some pharmaceutical funding and three received study medicine from a company, 13 reported non-industry funding and seven were unclear (Results); the plain-language summary gives 14, 7 and 7.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials in people withdrawing from illicitly manufactured fentanyl, outpatient and inpatient, comparing buprenorphine-based withdrawal (including approaches that avoid precipitated withdrawal) with methadone and lofexidine, with blinded withdrawal ratings, standardized adverse-effect collection, outcomes reported by sex, and follow-up for engagement in further treatment, relapse and overdose in the months after.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, intervention, five comparator types and outcomes are specified.
Cochrane protocol published in 2000; the deviation (restriction to randomized and quasi-randomized trials) is stated and explained.
The restriction to randomized and quasi-randomized trials is explained as ensuring internal validity (Differences between protocol and review).
Five databases with strategies in appendices, reference lists, trial registries, conference proceedings, investigator contacts, no language limit; search two months before publication.
One reviewer assessed eligibility and all reviewers confirmed the decisions; screening of 3573 records is not described as duplicated.
One reviewer (LG or DM) extracted, consulting others where uncertain.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: 45 excluded studies are listed with reasons. Another 192 full-text articles were excluded without listing; a strict reading of the item would make this 'no' and the overall rating critically low.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Characteristics of included studies give setting, participants, interventions with doses and preparations, comparators, outcomes and notes for each trial.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane risk-of-bias tool in seven domains, with blinding judged separately for subjective and objective outcomes.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding and supply of study medicine by companies reported (counts differ between Results and the plain-language summary; see reporting issues).
Random-effects models; standardized mean differences where scales differed; separate inpatient and outpatient analyses where regimens differed; arms outside the review's comparisons excluded.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Sensitivity analyses leaving out trials at high risk of performance and detection bias for both withdrawal-score outcomes.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE downgrades for blinding of subjective outcomes are carried into the conclusions; early stopping of two trials is noted as a possible bias.
I2 reported, subgroup analyses by setting, and the divergent rate-of-reduction results discussed (different settings, follow-on naltrexone, clinic attendance).
The review states it detected no publication bias, but no funnel plot, test or other method is described in Methods or Results.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Sources of support and declarations of interest are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: One critical item is 'no' (15: no method for assessing publication bias, although its absence is asserted), which under AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence; the other critical items are met, item 7 on a lenient reading. Items 5 and 6 are non-critical weaknesses. This rates the review's conduct; for its trials the card follows the review's own Cochrane appraisal and GRADE ratings and says so (12 of 27 trials at high risk of bias in at least one domain; moderate certainty for overall withdrawal score, days in treatment and completion against alpha2 agonists, very low for adverse effects and peak score; low to moderate against methadone; very low to low for rate of reduction). The review may be cited for these pooled estimates with their ratings, and for the conclusion that the rate of buprenorphine reduction remains unresolved; it should not be cited for fentanyl withdrawal or for side-effect superiority.

key_findings.finding: 27 trials (49 reports) with 3048 participants were included, 2172 of whom received buprenorphine: 6 against reducing doses of methadone, 14 against clonidine or lofexidine (only Raistrick 2005 used lofexidine), and 7 comparing faster and slower buprenorphine reduction; 12 trials were at high risk of bias in at least one of seven domains.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Main results, 1st paragraph; Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Major comparisons

key_findings.finding: Against clonidine or lofexidine, completion of withdrawal treatment was more likely with buprenorphine: RR 1.59 (95% CI 1.23 to 2.06), 11 trials (12 comparisons), 1264 participants, GRADE moderate (downgraded for heterogeneity above 60%); illustrative 453 per 1000 with alpha2 agonists against 721 per 1000; number needed to treat for one additional completion 4 (2.8 to 6.7). Inpatient RR 1.74 (1.05 to 2.89), 539 participants; outpatient RR 1.45 (1.12 to 1.88), 725 participants.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › Buprenorphine versus alpha2-adrenergic agonists › Completion of treatment, 1st paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 2, outcome 6

key_findings.finding: Against clonidine or lofexidine, mean overall withdrawal score was lower with buprenorphine in all seven trials that reported it: SMD -0.43 (-0.58 to -0.28), 902 participants, GRADE moderate; without four high-risk trials SMD -0.37 (-0.58 to -0.16). Peak withdrawal score SMD -0.43 (-0.74 to -0.13), 6 trials, 521 participants, I2 63%, GRADE very low; without three high-risk trials SMD -0.50 (-0.92 to -0.09), 309 participants.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › Buprenorphine versus alpha2-adrenergic agonists › Intensity of withdrawal, 1st to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against clonidine or lofexidine, people on buprenorphine stayed in treatment longer: SMD 0.92 (0.57 to 1.27), 4 trials (5 comparisons), 558 participants, GRADE moderate (downgraded for different settings and heterogeneity); inpatient SMD 1.00 (0.33 to 1.67), outpatient SMD 0.82 (0.57 to 1.06).
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › Buprenorphine versus alpha2-adrenergic agonists › Duration of withdrawal treatment, 2nd paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 2, outcome 3

key_findings.finding: The number with any adverse effect did not differ: RR 0.93 (0.70 to 1.26), 3 trials (4 comparisons), 493 participants, GRADE very low. Stopping treatment for adverse effects occurred only in clonidine arms: RR 0.20 (0.04 to 1.15), 3 inpatient trials, 134 participants, GRADE low. Dizziness, dry mouth and lethargy were typical with clonidine; headache, constipation and nausea with buprenorphine. In Ling 2005, serious adverse events (mostly continued drug use or overdose leading to hospital stay) occurred in 14 of 157 outpatients on buprenorphine against 4 of 74 on clonidine.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › Buprenorphine versus alpha2-adrenergic agonists › Nature and incidence of adverse effects, 1st, 3rd, 4th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Against reducing doses of methadone, completion did not differ: RR 1.04 (0.91 to 1.20), 5 trials, 457 participants, GRADE moderate (fewer than 300 events); illustrative 528 against 549 per 1000. Days in treatment did not differ: MD 1.30 days (-8.11 to 10.72), 2 trials, 82 participants, GRADE low. Withdrawal severity and adverse effects could not be pooled; three trials reported no significant adverse effects in either arm.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › Buprenorphine versus tapered doses of methadone, all subsections

key_findings.finding: Faster against slower reduction of buprenorphine: completion inpatient RR 1.00 (0.84 to 1.18), 2 trials, 60 participants, GRADE low; outpatient RR 0.86 (0.44 to 1.70), 4 trials, 647 participants, I2 80%, very low; abstinence at completion outpatient RR 0.94 (0.39 to 2.24), 4 trials, 610 participants, I2 81%, very low. The larger outpatient trials disagreed in direction, and the authors leave the question unanswered.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 3; Results › Effects of interventions › Different rates of buprenorphine dose reduction › Completion of treatment; Discussion › Summary of main results › Different rates of dose reduction, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Engagement in treatment after withdrawal was reported by five trials (not pooled): four suggested higher engagement after buprenorphine than after clonidine or lofexidine (for example 47 of 58 against 37 of 56 in Lintzeris 2002), and one found similar rates (Ziaaddini 2012).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Buprenorphine versus alpha2-adrenergic agonists › Completion of treatment, 3rd to 8th paragraphs; Discussion › Summary of main results, Buprenorphine versus alpha2-adrenergic agonists, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: After buprenorphine was stopped in Lintzeris 2002, 5 of 53 participants had mild or transient withdrawal and 4 of 53 moderately severe rebound withdrawal; the authors read this as most people not experiencing rebound.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Summary of main results › Buprenorphine versus tapered doses of methadone, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The plain-language summary says that people on buprenorphine experience fewer side effects than with clonidine or lofexidine, while the abstract and results report no significant difference in the number with adverse effects (RR 0.93, 0.70 to 1.26, very low) and only a non-significant difference in stopping for adverse effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lay summary overstates the adverse-effect finding; claims should use the pooled estimates and their ratings.

reporting_issues.issue: Trial counts differ between the summary and data tables and the abstract and text: completion 11 trials against 12 studies, days in treatment 4 trials against 5 studies, adverse effects 3 trials against 4 studies, because the inpatient and outpatient arms of Ling 2005 are counted as two studies in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not an error in the estimates, but the counts must be quoted with their unit (trials or comparisons).

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity analysis for peak withdrawal score reports 'studies = 6' after three of the six trials were excluded.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical error; the sensitivity estimate rests on three trials (309 participants).

reporting_issues.issue: The outpatient analysis of abstinence at completion has 619 participants in Summary of findings 3 and 610 in Results and the Data and analyses table.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency; use 610 from the data table.

reporting_issues.issue: Funding counts for included trials differ: Results give 3 with pharmaceutical funding plus 3 with company-supplied medicine, 13 non-industry and 7 unclear (26 in all), the plain-language summary 7 company, 14 non-industry and 7 unclear (28).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither set adds up to the 27 included trials; the industry share is roughly a quarter either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Overall completeness and applicability refers to '14 of 26' studies, while 27 trials were included; the Discussion rates the withdrawal-intensity evidence low to moderate while Summary of findings 2 gives very low (peak) and moderate (overall).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small internal inconsistencies; the summary tables should be preferred.

reporting_issues.issue: Potential biases in the review process states that no publication bias was detected, but no method for detecting it is described anywhere in the review.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement cannot be checked; it is treated as publication bias not investigated (AMSTAR 2 item 15).

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6464315 (all sections, the three summary-of-findings tables, the data-and-analyses tables and the characteristics of included and excluded studies rendered as text, acknowledgements, contributions, sources of support and declarations read; Figures 1 to 3 and all forest plots are images and their values were not extracted)

design_detail: Retrospective description of the 26 cases coded as loperamide exposure in the ToxIC Registry of the American College of Medical Toxicology, a prospective registry of patients seen in person by medical toxicologists at 50 US sites. The Methods give the search period as the registry's start, 5 January 2010, to 5 December 2016; the abstract gives November 2011 to December 2016. Descriptive statistics only, no comparison group. Filed under heroin because the paper concerns loperamide taken to avoid opioid withdrawal and does not name the opioid. Read as the online-first PDF (a cover page, then article pages 1-6); the printed article is Clin Toxicol 2019;57(3):175-180, so page numbers here are those of the online-first PDF.
can_establish: What was recorded about 26 people with loperamide exposure who were seen by US medical toxicologists in 2010-2016: why they took it where this was known, the heart-rhythm and other problems they had, the treatment they received and whether they survived.
cannot_establish: How often loperamide taken in large amounts, or taken to avoid opioid withdrawal, leads to heart-rhythm problems (no count of people who took it and did not come to care); any threshold amount (recorded for only 9 of 26); whether loperamide relieves withdrawal (never recorded); or that loperamide alone caused each problem (no biological confirmation, other substances in 7 people).

sample.recruitment: Registry: patients cared for in person by a participating medical toxicologist at 50 US sites are entered by the toxicologist through an online form; loperamide cases were found by searching the registry's agent field (p. 2, 2.1 Study design and setting). No case came from the registry's sites outside the USA.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All registry cases coded as loperamide exposure, with or without symptoms, single-agent or with other substances; the diagnosis rests on the history and the consulting toxicologist's clinical impression (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Median age 27 (range 2-89, IQR 17.5-36; age known for 23); 14 men (53.9%) and 12 women; 17 aged 19-65, 3 aged 13-18, 4 under 7, 2 aged 66-89; first consultation in intensive care for 10 (38.5%), in the emergency department for 6, unknown for 4 (Table 3, p. 3). The Discussion describes those reporting misuse as predominantly young and white (p. 4), but ethnicity is not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (registry records). Missing values are shown as denominators: intent known for 18 of 26, amount for 9 of 26, exact QTc only for cases from 1 March 2015 (pp. 2-3).
sample.selection_effects: Severity bias by design: only people seen by a medical toxicologist are recorded, which the authors say likely overestimates severity and leaves out exposures with few or no symptoms (4.1 Limitations, p. 5). Participation and reporting by toxicologists are voluntary, so cases may be missed or recorded in error. People who took loperamide for withdrawal without harm, or who were treated without a toxicologist, are invisible.

exposure.measurement: Report of the patient and/or the treating clinicians, as entered by the toxicologist. The Methods say confirmatory laboratory testing was not performed (p. 2); the Limitations say exposure was not confirmed in biological samples in the vast majority of cases (p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as recorded: oral loperamide; amount reported in 9 of 26 cases, from 4 mg (a child's exploratory ingestion) to 400 mg; among people taking it to avoid withdrawal, 160-400 mg a day, most often 200 mg (n = 4); every person with a ventricular dysrhythmia whose amount was recorded had taken 200 mg or more (Results 3.1 and 3.2, p. 3). The Discussion gives the label maximum as 16 mg a day (p. 4). Duration of use, and the opioid and amount people were withdrawing from, are not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: 19 (73%) were single-agent exposures; the other 7 people account for 21 mentions of other substances, among them antihistamines (3), dextromethorphan (2), cimetidine (2), metoclopramide (2), vitamins (2), diazepam, methylphenidate, risperidone and a hydrocarbon (Table 4, p. 3). Outcomes by single versus several substances are reported only for ventricular dysrhythmias (5 of 6 single-agent).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; patients were assessed during the episode.

comparison.controls: None. There is no group of people who took loperamide without harm or without coming to care, and no comparison with people withdrawing without loperamide.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Heart disease, baseline ECGs and electrolytes, other medicines that prolong the QT interval beyond the listed co-ingestants, the opioid used before withdrawal, and whether methadone or buprenorphine treatment was available to the person (the authors say the last is not known in this study, p. 5).

outcomes.instruments: Registry fields completed by the treating toxicologist: severe vital-sign thresholds (Table 1) and clinical definitions (Table 2: prolonged QTc 500 ms, prolonged QRS 120 ms, acidosis, kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, haemolysis and others), toxidrome, signs and symptoms, treatment and outcome (p. 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors did not review the ECGs; neither the uncorrected QT nor the correction method was available; exact QTc values were collected only from 1 March 2015 (pp. 2 and 5). Vital signs are not age-adjusted, so children may be misclassified (p. 5).
outcomes.operationalization: Toxicity is the consulting toxicologist's clinical impression. Intent (misuse/abuse, self-harm, exploratory) and circumstances (more than labelled, avoiding withdrawal, a pleasurable sensation; several possible per person) are registry codes.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; the authors note that not being blinded to the study hypothesis may produce information bias (p. 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and percentages only. Prolonged QTc 10 of 26 (38.5%), half of them with ventricular dysrhythmias; prolonged QRS 6 (23.1%); first-degree AV block 2; myocardial injury and infarction 1 (3.8%); coma or CNS depression 11 (42.3%); respiratory depression 5 (printed as 15.4%; 19.2% by editors' calculation); specific toxicological treatment 17 (65%); 4 intubated, 2 paced, 1 resuscitated; no deaths (pp. 3-4; Table 5).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registry research judged exempt from review by the Western Institutional Review Board, with local permissions at participating sites; no protocol registration (p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Treatments and outcomes are reported for the whole series, not by intent: what happened to the 6 people who took loperamide to avoid withdrawal is not reported separately.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 26 people seen by toxicologists after loperamide exposure, some of whom had taken very large amounts to avoid opioid withdrawal or for a pleasurable effect, prolonged QTc, wide QRS and ventricular dysrhythmias were common, several needed intubation, pacing or resuscitation, and none died. The amount was known for only 9 people and there is no comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion names an amount above which loperamide may cause significant cardiovascular effects (p. 1) and the title speaks of 'high doses and high risk'. A threshold cannot be drawn from 9 recorded amounts without a comparison, and risk cannot be estimated without a denominator. The Introduction calls the series a 'sizable cohort' (p. 2) and the Discussion a prospectively collected cohort (p. 4); it is a registry case series of 26. That most toxicity was due to misuse rests on 12 of the 18 cases with known intent.

timeline.event: Daniulaityte et al., a web-forum study cited by the authors for online discussion of loperamide to self-treat opioid withdrawal and for euphoric effects.
Eggleston et al., MMWR report of cardiac dysrhythmias after loperamide misuse in New York, 2008-2016 (cited, not read).
Swank et al., FDA adverse-event reports: 48 cases of loperamide cardiotoxicity, most in misuse to produce euphoria or prevent withdrawal (as described on p. 4; not read).
Wu and Juurlink, clinical review of loperamide toxicity (cited, not read).
This registry series: 26 cases with bedside detail from medical toxicologists.

replication.where_it_stands: As the authors describe them, other case reports, poison-centre data and FDA adverse-event reports show the same picture of heart-rhythm problems after very large amounts. None of these sources has a denominator, so the risk for a person who uses loperamide this way is unknown; none measured whether loperamide relieves withdrawal.

funding.funder: No specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors (Disclosure statement, p. 5).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest reported; no relevant financial relationships (p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: Emergency medicine departments in New Jersey, the New Jersey Poison Information and Education System, and the American College of Medical Toxicology, which runs the ToxIC registry.

what_would_settle_it: A study with a denominator, for example poison-centre and emergency records linked to a survey of people who use loperamide to manage opioid withdrawal, recording amounts, other medicines and ECGs, to estimate how often heart-rhythm problems occur; and a controlled study of whether loperamide relieves withdrawal at all compared with approved treatments.

domains.note: Only cases seen by a medical toxicologist and voluntarily entered in the registry; the authors say this likely overestimates severity (p. 5).
Self-report or clinician report without laboratory confirmation; amount recorded for 9 of 26; 7 people had taken other substances.
Defined ECG and vital-sign thresholds recorded by the treating toxicologist, but ECGs not reviewed, correction method unknown and exact QTc only from March 2015.
Intent unknown in 8; the opioid people were withdrawing from, the duration of use and the outcomes of the withdrawal group are not reported.
The abstract and the Results disagree on the search period and on several counts; Tables 4 and 5 contain percentage and labelling errors (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a registry case series (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The series can be cited as a description of what happened to 26 people seen by toxicologists after loperamide exposure, including people who took it to avoid opioid withdrawal. It cannot be cited for how often these problems occur, for a safe or unsafe amount, for loperamide being the sole cause in each case, or for whether loperamide relieves withdrawal, which was never recorded.

key_findings.finding: 26 cases coded as loperamide exposure; intent known for 18: 12 (67%) misuse, 3 (17%) attempted self-harm, 3 (17%) exploratory ingestions by children. Circumstances of misuse, more than one possible per person: taking more than labelled (8), trying to avoid opioid withdrawal (6), seeking a pleasurable sensation (4).

key_findings.note: The abstract gives 7, not 8, for taking more than labelled (p. 1).

key_findings.finding: The amount taken was recorded for 9 of the 26 people; amounts appear in this card only as study conditions (exposure field).
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Patients, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 20 (76.9%) had signs or symptoms attributed to loperamide by the treating toxicologist; 6 had none.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Clinical presentations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Prolonged QTc (500 ms or more) in 10 of 26 (38.5%), 5 of whom had ventricular dysrhythmias; of the 10, 9 were coded misuse (one aged 17) and 1 self-harm. Of those with ventricular dysrhythmias, 5 of 6 had taken loperamide alone; all but one had prolonged QTc, 566-749 ms. Prolonged QRS (120 ms or more) in 6 (23.1%); first-degree AV block in 2; myocardial injury and infarction in 1 (3.8%). No deaths.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Clinical presentations, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); thresholds from Table 2 (p. 2)
key_findings.note: The abstract gives seven ventricular dysrhythmias and splits the 10 prolonged QTc cases as 6 misuse and 1 self-harm (p. 1).

key_findings.finding: The two highest QTc values (749 and 725 ms) were in the two people whose other substances included cimetidine.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Clinical presentations, 2nd paragraph; Table 4
key_findings.note: Two cases, no comparison. Recorded as an interaction observation only; the editors leave out the mechanism the paper gives, under the rule against information on strengthening a drug's effects.

key_findings.finding: Table 5: coma or CNS depression 11 (42.3%); respiratory depression 5 (printed 15.4%); bradycardia 4 (15.4%); bradypnoea 4 (15.4%); hypotension 3 (11.5%); tachycardia 2 (7.7%); rhabdomyolysis 3 (11.5%); acute kidney injury 3 (11.5%); aspiration pneumonitis 2 (7.7%); seizure 1; delirium or toxic psychosis 1; raised anion gap metabolic acidosis 2; hypoglycaemia 1; haemolysis 1; marked leukocytosis 1.
key_findings.locator: Table 5
key_findings.note: 5 of 26 is 19.2% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: 17 (65%) needed specific toxicological treatment: an opioid antagonist in 6 (23%), benzodiazepines in 3 (11%), sodium bicarbonate in 4 (15%), isoproterenol in 2 (8%), amiodarone in 1 (4%). Four (15%) were intubated, 3 of them with ventricular dysrhythmias; 2 (8%) had pacemaker intervention, both with ventricular dysrhythmias; 1 needed cardiopulmonary resuscitation, intubation with ventilation, vasopressors and pacing, and survived.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Treatments, 1st paragraph (starts on p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Figure 1: loperamide cases per 10,000 registry cases rose from 1.74 in 2011 to 3.26 (2012), 5.61 (2013), 6.44 (2014), 7.32 (2015) and 12.4 (2016); cases due to misuse from 0 to 1.63, 4.21, 5.15, 5.85 and 8.29.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 (values read from the data labels on a 110 dpi rendering)
key_findings.note: The figure starts in 2011 although the Methods give a search from January 2010.

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: only patients seen at the bedside by medical toxicologists, likely overestimating severity; voluntary participation, so under-reporting or errors are possible; treatment decisions sometimes by the primary team; no age-adjusted vital signs; authors not blinded; ECGs not reviewed and QT correction unknown; exposure not biologically confirmed in the vast majority.
key_findings.locator: 4.1 Limitations, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.consequence: The period the 26 cases cover, and so the yearly trend, is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Taking more than labelled is n = 7 in the abstract (p. 1) and eight in the Results (p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Results figure is used.

reporting_issues.consequence: The Results breakdown is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports seven ventricular dysrhythmias, five of them single-agent; the Results imply six (5 of 6 single-agent; half of the 10 with prolonged QTc) (p. 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number with ventricular dysrhythmias is 6 or 7; claims say 'six or seven' or use the Results.
