reporting_issues.consequence: Either the count or the percentage is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 lists 'Single exposure (loperamide only)' 19 (73) and 'Co-Ingestions' 21 (80); the 21 is the number of co-ingestant mentions among the other 7 people, not patients, and 2 of 26 is printed as 7% (7.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as 19 single-agent and 7 multi-substance exposures.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say confirmatory laboratory testing was not performed (p. 2); the Limitations say exposure was unconfirmed in the vast majority of cases (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether any case was confirmed is unclear; treat exposure as unconfirmed.

design_detail: Cross-sectional client survey (2018 Harm Reduction Client Survey, British Columbia, Canada; May to August 2018) of people who use drugs attending 27 harm-reduction supply distribution sites, each surveying for two weeks. Prevalence of using drugs alone in the past 7 days, its correlates (chi-square tests and a multivariable logistic regression), and reasons for using alone from a fixed-option item, with free-text answers to 'other' coded by thematic analysis and merged with the fixed options. The free-text coding is a brief categorisation, not a qualitative study; the card appraises the prevalence estimate with the JBI checklist and describes the correlates and reasons.
can_establish: How common any use of drugs alone in the past week was in 2018 among clients of harm-reduction supply sites across British Columbia, which characteristics went with it in this sample, and which reasons clients gave when offered a short list of options.
cannot_establish: How common using alone is among people who use drugs who do not attend these sites; whether using alone, housing or crack/cocaine use cause one another (cross-sectional associations from a selected model in 306 complete cases); or whether using alone raises the risk of overdose or death, which this survey did not measure at the level of occasions.

sample.recruitment: Community: clients of harm-reduction supply distribution sites in all five regional health authorities of British Columbia. Two-stage convenience sampling: 37 sites approached, 10 declined for lack of capacity, 27 took part and surveyed attending clients over two weeks; clients were paid 5 Canadian dollars for a 10-minute survey and sites 5 dollars per participant (Methods › Data collection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Characteristics of participants who reported using drugs alone, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 19 or older, attending a harm-reduction supply distribution site, used illicit drugs in the past 6 months, able to give verbal consent. Respondents with a missing or prefer-not-to-say answer on using alone were excluded (Methods › Data collection, 2nd paragraph; Study variables, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Men 62.6%, women 34.8%, 9 other genders; age 19–29 19.3%, 30–39 28.3%, 40–49 26.1%, 50 or older 26.1%; medium or large urban sites 72.7%; regularly housed 62.8%, not regularly housed 34.3%; not employed 78.5%; naloxone kit 67.4%; preferred injection 33.8%, non-injection 60.4% (smoking, inhaling or snorting 56.5%). Ethnicity and Indigenous identity are not reported (Results › Characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). 72 of 486 (14.8%) excluded for a missing or prefer-not-to-say answer on the outcome; the multivariable model used 306 of 414 (26% further excluded for missing covariates); no comparison of excluded with included respondents.
sample.selection_effects: Clients already in contact with harm-reduction services, recruited by convenience at sites with capacity to take part; people who come to sites more often had more chance of being surveyed. The authors note that people more affected by stigma, who may hide their use and avoid services, are under-represented (Discussion, 11th paragraph). The response rate among clients approached is not reported.

exposure.measurement: Using alone (the study's outcome and the circumstance of interest here) was measured with one self-report item, the percentage of the time drugs were used alone in the last 7 days (0%, 1–25%, 26–50%, 51–75%, 76–100%, prefer not to say), dichotomised as any versus none. The paper does not say how alone was defined for respondents (for example whether someone nearby who could respond counted) (Methods › Study variables, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Self-reported use in the past 7 days: opioids 70.0%, crystal methamphetamine 72.9%, crack or powder cocaine 37.7%, benzodiazepines 13.5%, alcohol 42.3%; polysubstance use (opioids with stimulants, opioids with benzodiazepines, or stimulants with benzodiazepines) 64.5%. Each drug and polysubstance use were candidate correlates; opioid, crystal methamphetamine and crack/cocaine use entered the final model (Table 1; Table 2).

comparison.controls: Within-sample comparison: the 314 respondents who used alone at least once in the past 7 days against the 100 who did not.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: For the correlates: mental health, income, ethnicity or Indigenous identity, living arrangement (for example living alone), dependence, source of drugs and access to an overdose prevention site were not measured or not modelled.

outcomes.instruments: 2018 Harm Reduction Client Survey (questionnaire; administration procedures described in earlier papers, not here). Reasons item, asked only of those who used alone, with options: safer to be alone; more convenient and comfortable to use at home; do not want others to know; other (free text); prefer not to say; more than one could be chosen (Methods › Study variables, 4th paragraph). Overdose: self-reported opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months.
outcomes.validity_norms: Survey items are not reported as validated.
outcomes.operationalization: Using alone = any use alone in the past 7 days. The reason labelled convenience and comfort is a pre-worded option that joins convenience, comfort and using at home; free-text answers synonymous with an option were recoded into it, and two new themes were added (was alone or had no one to use with; did not want to share or cheaper to use alone) (Methods › Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph; Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 15 characteristics compared by chi-square at p<0.05; candidates for the model screened at p<0.25 in bivariate regressions, then backwards selection by Akaike's information criterion, with age and gender forced in (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

analysis.effect_sizes: Prevalence 314/414 = 75.8% (no interval printed; Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7%, editors' calculation). Adjusted odds ratios for using alone (n=306): no regular housing 2.27 (95% CI 1.20 to 4.27); crack/cocaine use 2.10 (1.15 to 3.82); not significant: opioid use 1.59 (0.87 to 2.88), crystal methamphetamine 1.58 (0.86 to 2.88), overdose in past 6 months 1.71 (0.79 to 3.69), men vs women 1.40 (0.80 to 2.44), age groups 0.83 to 1.10 (Table 2). The printed intervals are consistent with their point estimates (editors' check of log-symmetry).
analysis.covariates: Final model: age, gender, housing, opioid use, crystal methamphetamine use, crack/cocaine use and overdose in the past 6 months (Table 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or analysis plan mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 15 characteristics are shown in Table 1. The final model omits polysubstance use (bivariate p<0.01), alcohol, employment and health authority without saying why each was dropped (presumably the backwards selection; polysubstance use is built from the drug variables). Reasons were compared only by gender and age.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 100 respondents who did not use alone, adjusted odds ratios are imprecise (for example housing 1.20 to 4.27). Site clustering is not mentioned in the analysis.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Three-quarters of 414 clients of 27 harm-reduction supply sites in British Columbia (2018) reported using drugs alone at least once in the past week, and nearly half more than a quarter of the time; prevalence did not differ by age, gender, region, urbanicity or injecting. In 306 complete cases, no regular housing and past-week crack/cocaine use were associated with using alone. Given a short list of options, 44.3% of those who used alone (52.7% of those who gave any reason) chose the option that it is more convenient and comfortable to use at home; 14.0% cited stigma and 9.6% safety, and written answers coded by the authors added having no one to use with (11.7%) and not wanting to share (8.6%).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls using alone ubiquitous among people accessing harm-reduction services, which the sample supports for site clients but not beyond them. The title and Conclusion foreground convenience and comfort, which rests on one pre-worded option that bundles three ideas. The Conclusion then states that access to a safer supply of drugs is paramount; the survey did not ask about supply, and the argument rests on cited work. The Discussion explains the crack/cocaine association by a lower perceived risk with stimulants, which was not measured.

timeline.event: Harm Reduction Client Survey fielded at 27 sites in British Columbia (May to August).
Karamouzian et al. (2020), from the same survey, reported known fentanyl use among site clients; the Background cites it for two-thirds of those who used alone reporting fentanyl use; not read here.

replication.where_it_stands: The survey quantifies, for clients of supply sites in one province and one year, what earlier, mostly small qualitative studies described. Other studies of using alone on the editors' reading list (Rosen et al., 2023, on women who inject drugs; Ataiants et al., 2020, on circumstances of overdose) were not read here. The editors' list records no trial of services for people who use alone.

funding.funder: Health Canada's Substance Use and Addictions Program (SUAP), Grant 1819-HQ-000054, for the Harm Reduction Client Survey project, of which JAB is principal investigator; the funders had no role in the analysis or preparation of the manuscript (Funding). M. Karamouzian was supported by Vanier Canada Graduate and Pierre Elliott Trudeau Foundation doctoral scholarships (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: British Columbia Centre for Disease Control (affiliation of the principal investigator and of six of the eight authors); University of British Columbia; British Columbia Centre on Substance Use; McMaster University; Kerman University of Medical Sciences. The survey was funded by the federal health department; recorded as context, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective, event-level data (daily diaries or ecological momentary assessment) from people who use drugs, recording on each occasion whether anyone able to respond was present, linked to non-fatal and fatal overdose; and controlled evaluations of services for people who use alone (check-in, phone or app-based response, supervised or housing-based consumption) with overdose and death as outcomes.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The target is people accessing harm-reduction services in British Columbia and the frame is supply distribution sites, but sites were chosen by convenience and 10 of 37 declined for lack of capacity.
Convenience sampling of clients attending during a two-week window; frequent attenders more likely to be included.
414 gives a 95% interval of about plus or minus 4 points for the overall prevalence (editors' calculation); subgroups, for example the 56 who used benzodiazepines, are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, gender, region, urbanicity, housing, employment, naloxone and drug use by group in Table 1, and a map of sites; ethnicity and Indigenous identity not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 14.8% of completed surveys excluded for a missing or prefer-not-to-say outcome (those preferring not to say may differ in using alone); the model used 306 of 414; no comparison of excluded with included respondents.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: A single, unvalidated self-report item; alone is not defined for respondents; any single occasion in a week counts.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same item in the same questionnaire at every site; administration procedures are described only in earlier papers.

Prevalence given without an interval; the regression used data-driven variable selection, complete cases and no allowance for clustering by site; reason percentages use all 314 who used alone, including 50 who gave no reason.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: The proportion of approached clients who agreed is not reported; site-level participation was 27 of 37.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For its stated population, clients of harm-reduction supply sites in British Columbia in 2018, the prevalence estimate is direct and large, and its likely biases (convenience sampling, unknown response, exclusion of prefer-not-to-say answers, an undefined single item) are unlikely to change the conclusion that most clients used alone at least sometimes, though they make the exact figure uncertain. It cannot be generalized to people who use drugs and do not attend services. The correlates come from a data-driven model in complete cases and are associations only. The reasons depend on the wording of the options offered. Cite as: about three-quarters of supply-site clients reported using alone at least once in the past week, mostly giving convenience and comfort of using at home as a reason.

key_findings.finding: 486 clients completed the survey at 27 sites (37 approached, 10 declined); after excluding 37 missing and 35 prefer-not-to-say answers on using alone, 414 were analysed.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data collection, 2nd paragraph; Results › Characteristics of participants who reported using drugs alone, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 314 of 414 (75.8%) reported using drugs alone at least once in the past 7 days, and 198 (47.8%) more than 25% of the time.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of participants who reported using drugs alone, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: No interval printed; Wilson 95% CI 71.5% to 79.7% (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Those who used alone did not differ significantly from those who did not by age, gender (men 64.6% vs 56.0%, p=0.16), health authority, urbanicity, employment, naloxone kit (67.8% vs 66.0%) or preferred method (injection 34.4% vs 32.0%, p=0.87).
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted differences, used alone vs not: no regular housing 37.6% vs 24.0% (p<0.01); opioid or stimulant overdose in past 6 months 22.9% vs 15.0% (p=0.03); past-week opioids 73.2% vs 60.0% (p=0.04), crystal methamphetamine 76.8% vs 61.0% (p<0.01), crack/cocaine 41.4% vs 26.0% (p=0.01), polysubstance use 68.5% vs 52.0% (p<0.01); benzodiazepines 14.6% vs 10.0% (p=0.29) and alcohol 44.6% vs 35.0% (p=0.15) did not differ significantly.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for age, gender and the other retained variables (n=306), using alone was associated with having no regular housing (AOR 2.27, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.27) and past-week crack/cocaine use (AOR 2.10, 1.15 to 3.82); opioid use (1.59, 0.87 to 2.88), crystal methamphetamine use (1.58, 0.86 to 2.88) and a recent overdose (1.71, 0.79 to 3.69) were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Factors associated with using drugs alone, 1st paragraph; Table 2 and its footnote

key_findings.finding: Reasons for using alone, as a share of all 314 who used alone (more than one allowed): convenience and comfort 139 (44.3%); not wanting others to know or stigma 44 (14.0%); being alone or having no one to use with 37 (11.7%); safer to be alone 30 (9.6%); not wanting to share or cheaper 27 (8.6%); other 19 (6.1%); prefer not to say 31 (9.9%); no response 19 (6.1%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 2nd paragraph; Table 3
key_findings.note: Of the 264 who gave a reason, 139 (52.7%) chose convenience and comfort (editors' calculation). 37/314 is 11.8%, printed as 11.7%. Being alone or having no one to use with, and not wanting to share or cheaper, were coded from written answers (Table 3, footnote a), not offered as options; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Reasons did not differ by gender or age, except stigma or not wanting others to know, given more often by those under 50 than by those 50 or older (16.9% vs 5.3%, p=0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of 121 who chose other, 113 wrote a reason; most matched an existing option and were recoded, two new themes were created (was alone or had no one to use with; did not want to share or cheaper), and 19 answers could not be coded. Free-text answers included having no access to an overdose prevention site, not being allowed to use in a transition home, and severe pain.
key_findings.locator: Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Among those who used alone, 67.8% (213) had a naloxone kit and 22.9% (72) reported an opioid or stimulant overdose in the past 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Table 1
key_findings.note: The Discussion gives 67.4%, the whole-sample figure; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Background figures cited from British Columbia Coroners Service reports, not data of this study: in 2019 the place of injury was determined to be a private residence for more than half of illicit drug overdose deaths and another residence (single-room hotels, shelters, supportive housing) for 26.5%; a 2018 report of coroners' investigations found 69% of people who died of an overdose in 2016–2017 were using alone; fentanyl was detected in more than 80% of drug toxicity deaths from 2017.
key_findings.locator: Background, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (references 9 and 13)
key_findings.note: Who counted and decided: the provincial coroners' service. The paper does not define these deaths, say how using alone was established in coroners' investigations, or say how many deaths were tested; fentanyl is reported as detected, not as the cause.

key_findings.finding: Practices that let someone respond when a person uses alone (telling friends or neighbours, leaving the door unlocked, asking to be checked on) are mentioned in the Discussion from earlier work (Tsang et al., 2019); this survey did not measure them.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors note that answers are self-reported and open to social-desirability bias, that the sample is of people already connected to harm-reduction services, and that people more affected by stigma may not use these services.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 11th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says 67.4% of participants who used alone had a naloxone kit; Table 1 gives 67.8% (213 of 314) for that group, and 67.4% (279 of 414) for the whole sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the Table 1 figure for the group that used alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say candidate variables were those with p<0.25 in bivariate logistic regressions, followed by backwards selection on Akaike's criterion; the Results say covariates not statistically significant in bivariate analyses were excluded. Polysubstance use (bivariate p<0.01) is absent from the final model without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The model-building rule is unclear; the two significant associations should be cited as associations from a selected model, not as independent risk factors.

reporting_issues.issue: The final model used 306 of the 414 respondents (26% excluded for missing or prefer-not-to-say covariates), with no comparison of excluded and included respondents and no allowance for clustering by site.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted odds ratios may be biased and their intervals too narrow.

reporting_issues.issue: Reason percentages are computed over all 314 who used alone, including 50 who gave no reason (31 prefer not to say, 19 no response); the headline 44.3% for convenience and comfort is 52.7% of those who gave a reason (editors' calculation). The option itself read more convenient and comfortable to use at home, joining three ideas.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the reason as the option was worded and say which denominator is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The prevalence of using alone (75.8%) and the reason percentages are printed without confidence intervals.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the editors' interval (71.5% to 79.7%) or none; do not imply precision beyond the sample.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 places two reasons that respondents could give only in writing (was alone or had no one to use with, 37; do not want to share or cheaper to use alone, 27; footnote a: identified through thematic analysis of free-text responses) beside the three reasons offered as options, all as shares of the 314 who used alone, and the Abstract and Results list all five in one ranked sentence.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 3 and its footnote a; Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract › Results)
reporting_issues.consequence: Only the 121 who chose other (113 of whom wrote a reason) could give the two coded reasons, so their shares are not comparable with the offered options and are probably undercounts; do not rank them against the offered options.

reporting_issues.issue: The oldest age band is labelled '> 50' in Tables 1 and 2 but described as 50 years or older in the Results text (26.1%) and in the comparison of reasons by age (under 50 against 50 or older).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Table 2; Results › Characteristics of participants who reported using drugs alone, 2nd paragraph; Results › Reasons for using drugs alone, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; whether people aged exactly 50 were in the oldest band is unclear. Cite the band as the text does (50 or older) and the comparison as printed.

design_detail: Narrative review, with no stated search, selection criteria or appraisal, of published series, conference papers and official statistics (mostly 1967–1996, from the USA, Australia and Europe) on deaths attributed to heroin 'overdose': who dies, the circumstances, and the proposed mechanisms (true overdose relative to tolerance; contaminants; pulmonary oedema; use of other central nervous system depressants). The authors' own New South Wales series of 152 heroin-related deaths in 1992 (Zador, Sunjic & Darke, 1996) supplies many of the figures. The review argues that 'overdose' wrongly implies one mechanism for all such deaths and proposes 'multiple drug toxicity' for many of them. No figures are pooled.
can_establish: What the toxicology and circumstance studies available in 1996, as selected by the authors, reported about deaths attributed to heroin overdose: morphine was the only drug detected in a minority of cases (23–48% across six studies), alcohol and benzodiazepines were often detected, many deaths were not instant and happened with others present, and the authors' case for a multiple-drug account and better classification.
cannot_establish: Whether alcohol, benzodiazepines or other drugs caused or contributed to any death, or how morphine levels in these deaths compare with those of living people who use heroin (the authors say such data were scarce): nothing is pooled or appraised, the breadth of each laboratory's screening is unknown, tolerance was not measured in any cited study, and time from injection to death, post-mortem redistribution and specimen site are not weighed as explanations for low post-mortem morphine.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited sources include medical examiner and coroner series (for example New York City, Michigan, New South Wales, Western Australia, Texas, Vienna, Stockholm), a psychological-autopsy study of US soldiers in Europe, two conference papers (Chan et al., 1988; Fugelstad, 1994), cohort studies of mortality, and an Australian government statistical update.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No criteria stated; studies chosen by the authors.
sample.demographics: As cited: men over-represented, up to over 80% of recorded deaths in some series; mean age at death 27, 28, 30, 33 and 38 years in the studies named (about 30 in most); in the authors' series 80% were classed as dependent, regular heroin use and 17% as recreational use (p. 1766).
sample.selection_effects: Selection is the authors' own and leans on their New South Wales 1992 series, the source of most figures on circumstances, morphine and alcohol levels, benzodiazepines and treatment status. Two important sources are conference papers. The deaths described are those that medical examiners, coroners or researchers attributed to heroin overdose; how each source defined a heroin-related death, what was screened for, and in what share of deaths, is not given.

exposure.measurement: Post-mortem toxicology as reported by each cited study: blood morphine, blood alcohol concentration, benzodiazepines, quinine and other contaminants. Blood is named broadly for morphine and alcohol; Steentoft et al. is described as autopsy material with morphine in µmol/kg. Sampling sites, analytical methods, free versus total morphine and post-mortem intervals are not described. Circumstances come from case files and, in one study, psychological autopsies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Heroin amounts are unknown in all cited deaths; injection is the route in most. The authors cite one Dutch report comparing two groups of people who use heroin (Surinamese-born and Dutch-born) on self-reported non-fatal overdose (6% and 29%) and injecting (4% and 37%) and suggest a link between route and overdose (p. 1769); the groups differ in more than route.
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the review: morphine as the only drug detected in 23–48% of deaths across six studies; alcohol detected in 29–75% across 13 studies, mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported; diazepam detected in12% (not sole exposure) in one study and benzodiazepines in22%,27% and55% in three others. Which drugs each laboratory screened for is not reported, so 'morphine only' depends on each panel.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Recent abstinence (for example after prison or detoxification) is not discussed; treatment status is reported only as methadone maintenance at the time of death (2% of the authors' 1992 series; 75% never in methadone treatment).

comparison.controls: As cited: people who used heroin and died of other causes such as trauma or homicide (Monforte, 1977); survivors of overdose (three studies, cited without figures); a laboratory 'toxic level' for people without opioid tolerance (0.16 mg/L) in the authors' series; deaths with and without alcohol in five studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance, recent pattern of use and time from last injection to death are unknown or unreported for most cited deaths.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison deaths in Monforte (1977) are not described for other drugs.

outcomes.instruments: Cited outcomes: blood morphine (mg/L or µmol/kg), blood alcohol (g/100 mL), detection of benzodiazepines, quinine and other contaminants, presence of others at death, interval from injection to death, help-seeking, and methadone treatment status.
outcomes.validity_norms: No appraisal of analytical methods, specimen site, free versus total morphine or post-mortem interval. The 0.16 mg/L 'toxic level' is the analysing laboratories' figure for people without opioid tolerance, not a validated threshold.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Overdose' is used as the cited sources used it, for deaths attributed to heroin overdose by investigating authorities or researchers; the authors' alternative, 'multiple drug toxicity', is proposed without criteria.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, nothing pooled. Annual mortality of people who use heroin 1–3% in longitudinal studies, 6 to 20 times that of peers of the same age and sex; opioid-related deaths in Australia up 180% between 1981 and 1990 (official statistics). Others present at death in 58% (authors' series), 61% (Walsh, 1991), 79% (Drew, 1982) and more than half (Manning et al., 1983). Collapse immediately after injection in 23% (Manning et al., 1983) and death classed as instant in 14% (authors' series); death over more than 3 hours in 22% (authors' series) and 52% (Garriot & Sturner, 1973); interval over 2 hours in 44% (Nakamura, 1978). Help sought only 3 hours after the final injection in 42% (Manning et al., 1983); medical help sought before death in 10% and no intervention in 79% (authors' series, cited as 1995). Monforte (1977): 74% of fatal overdose cases had blood morphine no higher than people who used heroin and died of other causes. Authors' series: a third below 0.16 mg/L; median morphine 0.17 mg/L with alcohol against 0.34 mg/L without (called significant; no statistic given); r = −0.28 between blood alcohol and morphine. Ruttenber et al. (1990): r = −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths. Morphine with and without alcohol elsewhere: means 0.43 and 0.52 mg/L (Chan et al., 1988), medians 0.4 and 0.7 µmol/kg (Steentoft et al., 1988), medians 0.4 and 0.6 mg/L (Richards et al., 1976). Quinine in 19% (New York City) and 57% (Michigan), at therapeutic levels in almost all; no contaminants in the authors' 152 deaths. Methadone: about three times the relative risk of death attributed to overdose for people never in methadone maintenance than for those in it (Fugelstad et al., 1995).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The claim that morphine levels in deaths are no higher than in survivors cites three studies without figures, one a conference paper. The review's pharmacology section lists time since the last dose among the determinants of blood morphine, and its circumstances section reports many deaths hours after injection, but neither is weighed as an explanation for low post-mortem morphine; post-mortem redistribution and specimen site are not discussed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across the cited series, morphine was the only drug detected in 23–48% of deaths attributed to heroin overdose, alcohol was detected in 29–75% (mean blood alcohol 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL where reported) and diazepam in12% in one study and benzodiazepines in22%,27% and55% in others; morphine concentrations were lower in alcohol-positive deaths in five studies, with weak correlations of −0.14 and −0.28 where reported; one 1977 series found 74% of overdose deaths with morphine no higher than in people who used heroin and died of other causes; many deaths were not instant, and others were often present.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that these deaths “are likely to have morphine levels no higher than those who survive”, or than people who use heroin and die of other causes, and that 'overdose' is in many cases a misleading term (p. 1765). The body goes further: a great many 'overdoses' are 'in fact fatalities due to multiple drug use', and heroin may be no more than a contributory cause in many, perhaps most, cases (p. 1769). The evidence is the presence of other drugs and low morphine levels, not their causal role. (1) The survivor comparison rests on three studies cited without numbers, while the review says very little is known about morphine levels in living, intoxicated people (p. 1769). (2) Its own figures show many deaths hours after injection, when blood morphine would already have fallen (it names time since the last dose as a determinant, p. 1766), an explanation for low levels that is not considered. (3) Tolerance at death was measured in no cited study. (4) Whether the other drugs were present at levels that mattered is not assessed beyond mean blood alcohol. The prevention proposals (reducing concurrent depressant use, methadone treatment, encouraging people present to call an ambulance, police not arresting at overdose scenes, resuscitation training) are not evaluated in the paper.

timeline.event: Monforte, Michigan series: 74% of fatal heroin overdose cases had blood morphine no higher than people who used heroin and died of other causes (as described in this review).
Ruttenber, Kalter & Santinga: inverse correlation of blood alcohol and morphine (r = −0.14) in 505 alcohol-positive heroin-related deaths (as described in this review).
Pounder & Jones, 'Post-mortem drug redistribution — a toxicological nightmare' (in the project's library; not cited by this review; relevant to whether post-mortem levels reflect levels at death).
Zador, Sunjic & Darke, heroin-related deaths in New South Wales in 1992 (152 deaths), the authors' own primary source for many of the review's figures (not read).
This review.
White & Irvine, review of the mechanisms of fatal opioid overdose (in the project's library; not read in this round).
Stam et al., analysis of issues in the classification and reporting of heroin-related deaths in Australia, published with a commentary by Darke (in the project's library; not read in this round).

replication.where_it_stands: An influential argument rather than a synthesis. It documented that deaths labelled heroin overdose often have other depressants present and modest morphine levels, and asked for better classification and reporting. Whether those findings mean that the other drugs caused the deaths, or reflect delayed death, redistribution, changes in tolerance or laboratory practice, is not settled here. Later work comparing blood morphine in heroin-related deaths with that of people currently using heroin (Darke et al., 1997, listed on the project's _Tolerance map; not read) should be read with it.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article. The authors thank Joanne Ross and Wayne Hall for their help in preparing the paper (Acknowledgments, p. 1770).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Shane Darke, National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, University of New South Wales; Deborah Zador, Drug and Alcohol Services, Central Sydney Area Health Service, New South Wales (p. 1765). Both are authors of the New South Wales 1992 series that supplies many of the figures. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A study of deaths and non-fatal overdoses in the same population, with femoral blood taken as soon as possible, the interval from last use to death or treatment recorded, full toxicology with concentrations (including 6-monoacetylmorphine and free morphine), a marker of recent use or tolerance such as hair analysis, and blood from living people who use heroin sampled at the time of use, analysed to estimate how much each concurrent depressant adds to the risk of death.

domains.note: No search, sources, dates or criteria; studies chosen by the authors.
No appraisal of analytical methods, specimen sites, screening panels, post-mortem interval or case definitions; conference papers carry the same weight as peer-reviewed series.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors' New South Wales 1992 series (152 deaths) supplies most figures on circumstances, morphine, alcohol, benzodiazepines and treatment; many other sources are cited, but it is the most used.

The multiple-drug account is labelled a theory and hedged in places, but the abstract and conclusions present low morphine and the presence of other drugs as showing that heroin was often only contributory; prevention proposals are presented alongside the evidence without being tested.

domains.domain: Balance of explanations for deaths at low morphine levels (concurrent depressants against delayed death, post-mortem redistribution, specimen site and reduced tolerance)
domains.note: Contaminants and pulmonary oedema are weighed and set aside, but explanations other than concurrent depressants are under-represented: the delayed deaths the review itself reports, redistribution, specimen site and reduced tolerance after a break in use are not considered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review is a clear and influential argument, but its selection is unsystematic and weighted toward the authors' own series, no cited study is appraised, and explanations for low post-mortem morphine other than concurrent depressants are not weighed. Cite it for the figures it reports (second-hand, with the primary sources named), for the argument that 'overdose' implies a single mechanism, and for its call for better classification and reporting of opioid-related deaths; not for the claim that other drugs caused these deaths, nor for morphine levels in deaths being no higher than in survivors.

key_findings.finding: Morphine was the only drug detected at autopsy in 23% (Monforte, 1977), 27% (authors' series), 35% (Richards et al., 1976), 38% (Wahbah et al., 1993), 40% (Steentoft et al., 1988) and 48% (Nakamura, 1978) of deaths attributed to heroin overdose.
key_findings.locator: A new perspective: polydrug use theory, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand. Which drugs each laboratory screened for is not stated, so the proportions depend on each panel.

key_findings.finding: Alcohol was detected in 29% to 75% of deaths attributed to overdose in the studies listed (29% Risser & Schneider; 31% Nakamura; 34% Cherubin; 40% Baden; 45% authors' series; 47% Baselt; 48% Walsh; 50% Garriot & Sturner; 68% Manning & Ingraham and Monforte; 74% Goldberger and Ruttenber & Luke; 75% Fugelstad). Mean blood alcohol where reported was 0.09–0.16 g/100 mL, and 22% of the authors' series had more than 0.20 g/100 mL. Editors' count: 13 studies are listed.
key_findings.locator: A new perspective: polydrug use theory, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Whether the mean concentrations are over all deaths or over alcohol-positive deaths is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Blood morphine was lower in deaths where alcohol was detected: authors' series median 0.17 against 0.34 mg/L (called significant; no statistic given); Chan et al. (1988) means 0.43 and 0.52 mg/L; Steentoft et al. (1988) medians 0.4 and 0.7 µmol/kg; Richards et al. (1976) medians 0.4 and 0.6 mg/L; correlations between blood alcohol and morphine of r = −0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths (Ruttenber et al., 1990) and r = −0.28 (authors' series). The authors say the clinical significance is unclear.
key_findings.locator: A new perspective: polydrug use theory, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepines: diazepam in 12% of deaths (Monforte, 1977); benzodiazepines in 55% of a Swedish sample (Fugelstad, 1994, a conference paper), 27% of the authors' series and 22% in Richards et al. (1976).
key_findings.locator: A new perspective: polydrug use theory, 5th paragraph (p. 1768, continuing on p. 1769)
key_findings.note: The Swedish figure is printed in words ('Fifty-five per cent', p. 1768).

key_findings.finding: Morphine levels: Monforte (1977) found 74% of fatal heroin overdose cases with blood morphine no higher than in a similar group of people who used heroin and died of other causes (trauma, homicide); a third of the authors' series were below the laboratories' toxic level for people without opioid tolerance (0.16 mg/L); three studies (Fugelstad, 1994; Gutierrez-Cebollada et al., 1994; Aderjan et al., 1995) are cited, without figures, for levels no higher than in survivors of overdose.
key_findings.locator: Mechanisms of heroin-caused deaths › True overdose, 1st–2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: By its title in the reference list (p. 1770), one of the three, Aderjan et al. (1995), measured morphine and its glucuronides in the serum of living people who use heroin as well as in heroin-related deaths; the review gives no figures from it.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that very little information is available on blood morphine levels in living, intoxicated people who use heroin, and say that research into the toxicological differences between them and fatal cases would contribute substantially to knowledge of opioid-related deaths; the question they call of primary importance is how heroin and other central nervous system depressants together relate to these deaths.
key_findings.locator: Research implications, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Timing: 23% collapsed immediately after injection (Manning et al., 1983) and 14% of the authors' series were classed as instant deaths, while 22% died over more than 3 hours; intervals of more than 3 hours in 52% (Garriot & Sturner, 1973) and more than 2 hours in 44% (Nakamura, 1978).
key_findings.locator: Circumstances of fatalities attributed to overdose, 3rd paragraph (starts p. 1766)

key_findings.finding: Others present and help: others were present at death in 58% (authors' series), 61% (Walsh, 1991), 79% (Drew, 1982) and more than half (Manning et al., 1983); help was sought only 3 hours after the final injection in 42% (Manning et al., 1983); in the authors' series medical help was sought before death in 10% and there was no intervention in 79%.
key_findings.locator: Circumstances of fatalities attributed to overdose, 2nd paragraph (p. 1766) and 4th paragraph (p. 1767)
key_findings.note: The 10% and 79% are attributed in the text to 'Zador et al. (1995)', which is not in the reference list; presumably the 1996 series.

key_findings.finding: Who died: men were over-represented (up to over 80% in some series); mean age at death in the late twenties and early thirties (27–38 years in the studies named); in the authors' series 80% were classed as dependent, regular heroin use and 17% as recreational use; weekend over-representation was found in some studies but not the authors'.
key_findings.locator: Characteristics of fatalities attributed to overdose, 1st–3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Treatment: only 2% of heroin-related deaths in New South Wales in 1992 were in methadone maintenance at death and 75% had never been in methadone treatment (authors' series); Fugelstad et al. (1995) found about three times the relative risk of death attributed to overdose for people never in methadone maintenance compared with those currently in it.
key_findings.locator: The prevention of heroin-related deaths, 2nd paragraph (p. 1769); reference list (p. 1771)
key_findings.note: The reference list title shows the Fugelstad et al. (1995) cohort consisted of HIV-infected people who injected drugs in Stockholm, which the text does not say.

key_findings.finding: Contaminants: quinine was found in 19% of New York City cases (Cherubin et al., 1972) and 57% of Michigan cases (Monforte, 1977), at therapeutic levels in almost all; studies outside the eastern USA reported no impurities, and the authors' series found no contaminants in injecting equipment or at autopsy in 152 heroin-related deaths.
key_findings.locator: Mechanisms of heroin-caused deaths › Contaminants, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Classification and reporting: heroin deaths may be recorded with clinically unhelpful terms such as 'narcotism'; official statistics recorded only that a death was due to opiates, without the type of opiate or whether several drugs were detected; the authors propose recording causes such as morphine only, or combined effects of heroin and alcohol.
key_findings.locator: Research implications, 3rd paragraph (p. 1769, continuing on p. 1770)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: a 'true overdose' involving only heroin appears to be a minority of deaths attributed to overdose; the term wrongly implies that an amount of heroin beyond the person's tolerance is the underlying cause in all cases; 'multiple drug toxicity' is proposed as more accurate in many cases.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions, 1st–2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Background mortality cited: annual mortality of 1% to 3% among people who use heroin in longitudinal studies, 6 to 20 times that expected for peers of the same age and sex; opioid-related deaths in Australia rose by 180% between 1981 and 1990.
key_findings.locator: Mortality and heroin use, 1st paragraph (starts p. 1765)

reporting_issues.issue: Citation years that do not match the reference list: 'Zador et al. (1995)' for the help-seeking figures (only a 1996 Zador paper is listed), 'Kintz et al., 1995' (listed as 1989) and 'Drew, 1983' (listed as 1982).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sources of these statements must be traced by content; the 10% and 79% help-seeking figures presumably come from the 1996 series.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's statement that morphine levels in deaths are no higher than in survivors rests in the body on three citations without figures, one a conference paper, while the Research implications section says data on living, intoxicated people are scarce.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract presents as a finding what the body supports only weakly.

reporting_issues.issue: The median morphine difference with and without alcohol in the authors' series (0.17 against 0.34 mg/L) is called significant without a test, sample size or statistic, and mean blood alcohol concentrations are given without saying whether they are over all deaths or over alcohol-positive deaths.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size and reliability of these comparisons cannot be judged from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The correlation of r = −0.14 between blood alcohol and morphine in 505 deaths (Ruttenber et al., 1990) is offered as support for the polydrug mechanism; editors' calculation: r squared is about 0.02, about2% shared variance in a simple linear description, not2% causally attributable to alcohol.
reporting_issues.consequence: A weak association; it cannot carry a causal argument.

reporting_issues.issue: The three-fold relative risk of death for people never in methadone maintenance is presented without noting that, per the reference title, the cohort consisted of HIV-infected people who injected drugs in Stockholm.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure may not apply to people who use heroin generally.

design_detail: Published under the journal heading 'Case Report' (p. 53): a two-part study from the doping-control setting of the Institute of Biochemistry, German Sport University Cologne. (1) Product analysis: eight poppy-seed products bought in Germany (seven listed by trade name, from supermarkets and health-food shops, and one baking mixture from a bakery, the text calling all eight poppy-seed specimens; purchase dates not given, manuscript received October 2001) analysed for morphine and codeine by GC-MS. (2) Uncontrolled excretion study: the batch with by far the most morphine (product 3, 151.6 µg/g) was baked into a poppy-seed cake, and nine healthy volunteers ate different numbers of pieces (12.5 to 52.3 g of seeds per person, over 10 to 120 minutes). Their urine was collected for 24 hours plus a final sample at about 44-48 hours and analysed for total morphine (after enzymatic hydrolysis) and codeine by GC-MS. Results were judged against the 1 µg/mL urinary morphine limit of the IOC. No control cake, no randomization, no pre-consumption urine reported, no immunoassay screening. Design recorded as 'case-series': every volunteer ate cake from the same batch and there is no comparison condition, unexposed group or baseline sample, so the excretion study is an uncontrolled series of nine people, published as a case report. METHODS 5.3 gives case series and case reports no risk-of-bias instrument, so the card states the design's limits with the editors' domains (stored as 'none-applicable'). The first pass recorded 'human-laboratory' with RoB 2, which judges randomized comparisons.
can_establish: That, in these nine volunteers, eating cake made with one unusually morphine-rich batch of poppy seeds produced urinary total morphine above the 1 µg/mL sports-doping limit in every person, how high and for how long, and how much morphine eight poppy-seed products bought in Germany contained (purchase dates not given; manuscript received October 2001).
cannot_establish: How likely a positive test is after ordinary poppy-seed foods (the batch used held about 18 to 250 times more morphine than the other seven products, editors' arithmetic); results at workplace screening and confirmation cut-offs or with immunoassays (only GC-MS against the 1 µg/mL limit was used); how morphine from poppy seeds can be told apart from heroin or morphine use (no marker such as thebaine was measured); or how much morphine survived baking (the cake itself was not analysed).

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond '9 healthy volunteers' (Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 1st paragraph, p. 54). No ethics approval or informed-consent statement is printed.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not reported: no criteria, no screening for opioid use or codeine-containing medicines, and no statement on avoiding other poppy-seed foods during the study.
sample.demographics: Aged 25-48; 2 women (62 and 68 kg) and 7 men (67-88 kg) (Table II, p. 54).
sample.attrition: None reported; all nine volunteers have tabulated results, with 8 to 10 urine samples each (Table III, p. 55).
sample.selection_effects: A small convenience group whose recruitment and relationship to the laboratory are not reported. The seed batch was chosen because it held by far the most morphine of the eight products (151.6 µg/g against 0.6-8.4 µg/g), and other batches from the same manufacturer held 1.1 µg/g (p. 54), so the excretion results describe a high-end exposure, not typical poppy-seed foods.

exposure.measurement: Seeds eaten known from the precise preparation of the cake pieces; morphine eaten calculated from the seeds' measured content (Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 1st paragraph, p. 54). Seed morphine by GC-MS after enzymatic hydrolysis (Materials and methods, p. 53). Morphine in the baked cake was not measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study condition, a single occasion: poppy seeds eaten in cake, 12.5 to 52.3 g per person, eaten over 10 to 120 minutes. Morphine eaten as printed in Table II: 1.6 to 6.8 mg; as printed in the Table III headings: 1.8 to 7.7 mg; the two tables disagree for every volunteer (pp. 54-55; see reporting issues).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported: no information on other drugs, medicines (including codeine) or other poppy-seed foods before or during the study.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported: no pre-consumption urine sample is shown.

comparison.controls: None: no control cake, no unexposed group and no pre-consumption sample. The only contrasts are over time within each person and between people who ate different amounts.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not a premorbid question. Not measured or not reported: pre-consumption urine morphine; urine dilution (no creatinine or specific gravity); urine volumes; morphine in the baked cake; codeine in each sample.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no controls); the volunteers' other drug and medicine use is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: GC-MS (HP5890 gas chromatograph with HP5971 mass-selective detector) after enzymatic hydrolysis (beta-glucuronidase/arylsulfatase from Helix pomatia), liquid-liquid extraction and trimethylsilylation; ethylmorphine as internal standard; quantitation ions m/z 429 (morphine-bis-TMS), 371 (codeine-TMS) and 385 (internal standard); identity confirmed by three diagnostic ions each (Materials and methods, p. 53; Excretion study, 2nd paragraph, p. 54).
outcomes.validity_norms: Sample preparation described as comparable to published methods (refs 11-13). No limit of detection or quantification, calibration range, precision or accuracy is given; values above 4 µg/mL were estimated from the calibration curve because such concentrations had not been expected (p. 54).
outcomes.operationalization: A positive doping result was urinary morphine above 1 µg/mL, the IOC limit (Table III footnote, p. 55). Concentrations are total morphine after hydrolysis, not corrected for urine dilution. No immunoassay screening and no workplace cut-offs were applied.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests; urinary morphine is tabulated per sample, urinary codeine is given only as a range, seed morphine per product. 3 = urinary morphine, urinary codeine and seed morphine.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only. Seed morphine 0.6 to 151.6 µg/g (median of the eight products 3.1 µg/g, editors' calculation) (Table I, p. 54). Peak urinary morphine per volunteer 1.93 to 10.04 µg/mL, reached 4 to 11 hours after eating (Table III, p. 55). Editors' count from Table III: 51 of 80 samples above 1 µg/mL (2 to 8 per volunteer); 13 above 4 µg/mL (estimated values), from 5 volunteers; the last sample above 1 µg/mL came 10.25 to 24 hours after eating in eight volunteers and at 47.5 hours in one (V8). Wilson 95% intervals (editors' calculation): nine of nine volunteers positive, 70% to 100%; one of nine still positive at about 48 hours, 2% to 44%. Peaks did not rise steadily with the amount eaten: the volunteer who ate the most seeds (52.3 g) peaked at 5.88 µg/mL, the one who ate 38.1 g at 10.04 µg/mL.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Every urinary morphine value is shown (Table III). Codeine is reported only as a range (urine) or as negligible (seeds); the second package of batch 3 is described only as comparable; the 1.1 µg/g for other batches of the same manufacturer is given without the number of batches tested.
analysis.power: Not addressed; nine volunteers, each eating a different amount.

interpretation_gap.results_show: All nine volunteers who ate cake made with an unusually morphine-rich seed batch had urine above the 1 µg/mL doping limit in at least two samples, mostly within the first day; peaks ranged from 1.93 to about 10 µg/mL, the values above 4 µg/mL being extrapolated. One volunteer was still above the limit at 47.5 hours; the other eight were at 0.20-0.36 µg/mL by 44-48 hours.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports peak values of approximately 10.0 µg/mL (p. 53): one volunteer reached about 10 µg/mL, an estimate above the calibrated range, while the other eight peaked at 1.93-5.90 µg/mL; and it calls the positive specimens several, where 51 of 80 samples exceeded the limit (editors' count). The Conclusions state that morphine can exceed the threshold 48 hours after eating poppy-seed cake and that positive results are possible up to two days later, conceding that this was shown in only one volunteer after a high amount (p. 55). The study used the one batch with 151.6 µg/g; the other seven products held 0.6-8.4 µg/g, so the same amounts of the other products would have given far less morphine; the abstract mentions one selected batch but not that it held far more morphine than the rest, and ends with a general statement about products containing poppy seeds. The advice that athletes avoid poppy-seed foods before and during competition (p. 55) is a precaution beyond the data. The paper says nothing about workplace testing cut-offs or immunoassays, and its remark on telling poppy seeds from heroin by thebaine comes from another study (p. 55).

timeline.event: Fritschi & Prescott (1985): urinary morphine peaks of 18 µg/mL after poppy-seed consumption, as cited by this paper (p. 54); not read for this card.
Hayes et al. (1987): morphine in commercial poppy seeds of 17 to 294 µg/g, as cited (p. 54); Struempler (1987) and Pettitt et al. (1987) also cited; not read for this card.
The IAAF first mentions a 1 µg/mL urinary morphine limit; the IOC adds it to its medical code in 1998 (as described, p. 53).
Cassella et al. (1997): thebaine found in urine after poppy-seed consumption but not after morphine, codeine or street heroin, as described by this paper (p. 55); not read for this card.
This study (manuscript received 5 October 2001, published January/February 2003).

replication.where_it_stands: The authors say earlier studies found comparable seed contents and urine concentrations (pp. 54-55); those studies were not read for this card, hence 'partially replicated' rests on the authors' account. This paper shows the possibility at the 1 µg/mL sports limit with one high-morphine batch; how often ordinary poppy-seed foods cause positives at current sport or workplace cut-offs is not addressed here, and later studies were not read.

funding.funder: Bundesinstitut für Sportwissenschaft, Bonn, Germany (financial support; Acknowledgment, p. 55).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the Institute of Biochemistry, German Sport University Cologne; the corresponding author's address at publication was at UCLA (p. 53). The funder is a German federal sport-science institute and the paper is framed around doping control. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A controlled feeding study with several common poppy-seed foods of measured morphine content after baking, a pre-consumption sample and a poppy-free control, in more volunteers, with urine tested by immunoassay and GC-MS at current sport and workplace cut-offs, results normalized for dilution, and markers that distinguish poppy seeds from heroin or morphine use measured in the same samples.

domains.note: Nine healthy volunteers aged 25-48 (2 women, 7 men); how they were recruited, their relationship to the laboratory and any screening for opioid or codeine use are not reported (p. 54). All nine have tabulated results.

domains.domain: Choice and measurement of the exposure
domains.note: The batch was chosen because it held by far the most morphine of the eight products (151.6 µg/g against 0.6-8.4 µg/g), as the paper states (p. 54), so the exposure is high-end by design. Seeds eaten are known from the precise preparation of the pieces, but the morphine eaten is printed differently in Tables II and III for every volunteer, and morphine in the baked cake was not measured.

GC-MS with an internal standard and three diagnostic ions is specific, but no validation data (detection or quantification limits, calibration range, precision) are given; the 13 values above 4 µg/mL, including the about 10 µg/mL peak, were extrapolated beyond the calibration curve; no correction for urine dilution, so whether a given sample crosses 1 µg/mL partly reflects hydration.

The text says all urine was collected for 24 hours, but Table III lists 8 to 10 samples per volunteer without saying whether every void is shown; nothing between 24 hours and the final sample (43.75-48 hours); urine volumes not reported.

No control cake, no unexposed group and no pre-consumption urine; volunteers were not reported to be screened for opioid or codeine use, and whether other poppy-seed foods or codeine medicines were avoided during the 48 hours is not stated, so absence of morphine before eating is assumed, not shown. The amounts eaten were not allocated by any stated rule, and the paper makes no comparison between amounts.

Eight products bought in Germany, one package each except batch 3 (a second package comparable), purchase dates not given; how many other batches of the same manufacturer lie behind the 1.1 µg/g is not given; seed morphine measured with the same GC-MS method, without validation data (pp. 53-54). The figures describe these products, not the market.

The abstract's peak values of approximately 10.0 µg/mL are one volunteer's extrapolated value, and its closing statement covers products containing poppy seeds in general on the basis of one unusually morphine-rich batch; the advice that athletes avoid poppy-seed foods goes beyond the data. The Conclusions concede that the 48-hour result was shown in one volunteer after a high amount (p. 55).

Morphine intakes differ between Table II and Table III for every volunteer; the final sample is dated 46-48 hours in the text but 43.75-48.00 hours in Table III; codeine is given only as a range or as negligible; the second analysis of batch 3 is reported only as comparable; no ethics or consent statement is printed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard instrument applies to an uncontrolled series of volunteers who all ate the same food (METHODS 5.3: case series and case reports have no instrument, and the card states the design's limits), so the editors' domains above describe those limits and the overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. RoB 2, used in the first pass, judges a randomized comparison and ROBINS-I a non-randomized one; here there is no comparison of any kind. The overall judgment is high because nothing was compared: there is no control, no unexposed group and no baseline sample. For the descriptive finding, that urinary morphine after eating this cake exceeded 1 µg/mL in these nine people, the lack of a comparison matters less, because the time courses rise and fall after eating as expected; the measurement and reporting concerns (extrapolated high values, no dilution correction, two different intake figures) mainly affect the exact concentrations and amounts. Citable for: eating cake made with a high-morphine batch of poppy seeds (151.6 µg/g; 12.5 to 52.3 g of seeds) produced urinary morphine above 1 µg/mL in all nine volunteers, up to about 10 µg/mL, mostly for less than a day, in one person for about 48 hours; and for the morphine content of eight products bought in Germany. Not citable for: how often typical poppy-seed foods cause positive tests, results at workplace cut-offs, or telling poppy-seed use from heroin use.

key_findings.finding: All eight poppy-seed products (seven listed by trade name, from supermarkets and health-food shops, and one baking mixture from a bakery, the text calling all eight poppy-seed specimens; origins Denmark, Hungary, Turkey or unknown) contained morphine and codeine. Morphine content by product (µg/g): 8.4, 6.9, 151.6, 2.1, 4.1, 0.8, 0.9 and 0.6. Product 3 (bought in a supermarket, origin unknown) held 151.6 µg/g; a second package of the same batch gave comparable results, while other batches from the same manufacturer held only 1.1 µg/g. Codeine was negligible in all products.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Morphine content of poppy seeds, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 53); Table I

key_findings.finding: Batch 3 was used in a typical poppy-seed cake; nine healthy volunteers aged 25-48 (2 women, 7 men) ate different numbers of pieces, and because the pieces were prepared precisely, the seeds and morphine each person ate were known. All urine was collected in portions for 24 hours after eating and a final sample was taken after 46-48 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 1st and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table III lists the final samples at 43.75 to 48.00 hours (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Per volunteer (sex, body weight, poppy seeds eaten, morphine intake, minutes taken to eat): V1 woman, 62 kg, 12.5 g, 1.6 mg, 20; V2 man, 79 kg, 16.8 g, 2.2 mg, 10; V3 woman, 68 kg, 16.3 g, 2.1 mg, 20; V4 man, 81 kg, 29.9 g, 3.9 mg, 40; V5 man, 77 kg, 31.9 g, 4.2 mg, 60; V6 man, 88 kg, 30.5 g, 4.0 mg, 45; V7 man, 83 kg, 36.4 g, 4.8 mg, 30; V8 man, 70 kg, 38.1 g, 5.0 mg, 60; V9 man, 67 kg, 52.3 g, 6.8 mg, 120.
key_findings.locator: Table II
key_findings.note: The Table III headings give different morphine amounts for every volunteer (1.8, 2.4, 2.5, 4.7, 4.5, 4.4, 5.3, 5.6 and 7.7 mg); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Every volunteer had urinary morphine above the IOC limit of 1 µg/mL in at least two samples, and most stayed above it for several hours. Peak concentrations (µg/mL, hours after eating): V1 1.93 (11.00), V2 5.88 (4.25), V3 2.75 (4.50), V4 3.91 (6.00), V5 5.76 (4.00), V6 3.53 (6.00), V7 5.90 (6.00), V8 10.04 (6.00), V9 5.88 (6.00).
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 4th paragraph (p. 54); Table III (p. 55)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table III: 51 of 80 samples exceeded 1 µg/mL, 2 to 8 per volunteer (Wilson 95% interval for nine of nine volunteers positive: 70% to 100%). The PDF's text layer misreads several Table III values (for example 5.76 as '5,76' and 1.39 as '139'); all values here were read from the rendered page.

key_findings.finding: One volunteer (V8, 38.1 g of seeds) reached about 10.0 µg/mL and was still above the limit at 47.50 hours (1.21 µg/mL). In the other eight, the last sample above 1 µg/mL was taken 10.25 to 24.00 hours after eating, and the final samples (43.75 to 48.00 hours) held 0.20 to 0.36 µg/mL. The volunteer who ate the most seeds (V9, 52.3 g) peaked at 5.88 µg/mL and was at 0.25 µg/mL by 44.00 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 4th paragraph (p. 54); Table II (p. 54); Table III (p. 55)

key_findings.finding: Urine concentrations within a person rose and fell between consecutive samples rather than declining smoothly: for example V2 had 1.03 µg/mL at 8.00 hours, 0.37 at 9.50 and 1.53 at 12.00; V5 had 1.98 at 6.00 hours, 0.71 at 8.00 and 1.72 at 10.00. No creatinine, specific gravity or urine volume is reported.
key_findings.locator: Table III
key_findings.note: Editors' reading: such swings are consistent with changing urine dilution, which the paper does not report or discuss; whether one sample crosses 1 µg/mL can depend on when it is given.

key_findings.finding: Values above 4 µg/mL were estimated from the calibration curve, because concentrations that high had not been expected before the study.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table III: 13 of 80 samples, from 5 volunteers (V2, V5, V7, V8, V9), exceed 4 µg/mL, including the 10.04 µg/mL peak.

key_findings.finding: Urinary codeine ranged from 0.06 to 0.82 µg/mL; no per-sample codeine values are given.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The paper judges every urine result only against the 1 µg/mL urinary morphine limit of the IOC: values above 1 µg/mL are printed in bold as positive under the IOC rules. It reports only GC-MS results, with no immunoassay screening, and uses or discusses no other screening or confirmation cut-off.
key_findings.locator: Abstract and Experimental › Materials and methods (p. 53); Results and Discussion › Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 54); Table III footnote (p. 55)

key_findings.finding: The 1 µg/mL urinary morphine limit was first mentioned by the IAAF in 1996 and added by the IOC to its medical code in 1998, based on studies of morphine formed from permitted codeine medicines and of alkaloids in commercial poppy seeds.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors cite earlier reports of 17 to 294 µg/g morphine in commercial poppy seeds and of urinary morphine peaks of 18 µg/mL after poppy seeds, and a study by Cassella et al. (their reference 15) in which thebaine appeared in urine only after poppy-seed consumption, not after morphine, codeine or street heroin. Thebaine was not measured in this study.
key_findings.locator: Results and Discussion › Excretion study with poppy seed cake, 5th paragraph (begins on p. 54, continues on p. 55)

key_findings.finding: Abstract: after the cakes were eaten, several urine specimens held more than 1 µg/mL morphine and peak values of approximately 10.0 µg/mL were detected; because the IOC limit is 1 µg/mL, high-performance athletes could possibly test positive in doping control after eating products containing poppy seeds.
key_findings.locator: Abstract

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: athletes may be sanctioned for urinary morphine above the 1 µg/mL limit caused by poppy-seed foods; even 48 hours after eating poppy-seed cake the level can exceed the threshold, though this was shown in only one volunteer after a high amount; athletes should avoid such foods before and during competitions.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Funding as printed: financial support from the Bundesinstitut für Sportwissenschaft, Bonn, Germany. No conflict-of-interest, ethics-approval or consent statement is printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The morphine each volunteer ate differs between Table II (1.6, 2.2, 2.1, 3.9, 4.2, 4.0, 4.8, 5.0 and 6.8 mg for V1-V9) and the Table III headings (1.8, 2.4, 2.5, 4.7, 4.5, 4.4, 5.3, 5.6 and 7.7 mg), by 0.2 to 0.9 mg, and the paper does not explain the difference. By the editors' arithmetic neither matches seeds eaten times the measured 151.6 µg/g (1.90 to 7.93 mg): Table II implies about 130 µg/g and Table III 141 to 157 µg/g, and Table III gives V4 (29.9 g of seeds) more morphine than V5 (31.9 g).
reporting_issues.consequence: The morphine amount each person ate is uncertain by up to about 20% (editors' arithmetic). Cite the seed amounts, which are given once and are consistent, and give morphine intake as the range of the two tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract speaks of peak values of approximately 10.0 µg/mL and of several positive specimens, but only one volunteer (V8) reached about 10 µg/mL, a value estimated beyond the calibration curve; the other peaks were 1.93 to 5.90 µg/mL, and 51 of 80 samples, not several, exceeded the limit (editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline 10 µg/mL is one person's extrapolated value; the typical peak was 2 to 6 µg/mL.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the final sample was taken after 46-48 hours; Table III lists final samples at 43.75, 44.00 and 45.00 hours for three volunteers (V6, V9, V7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the statement about 48 hours rests on V8's sample at 47.50 hours.

reporting_issues.issue: No validation data (detection or quantification limits, calibration range, precision, accuracy) are reported, and values above 4 µg/mL were extrapolated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether samples exceed 1 µg/mL is not affected, but the 13 values above 4 µg/mL, including the maximum, are approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: No pre-consumption urine, no creatinine or specific gravity and no urine volumes are reported, and Table III lists 8 to 10 samples per volunteer although all urine was said to be collected for 24 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of morphine before eating is assumed; concentrations cannot be adjusted for dilution, which may explain swings between consecutive samples; it is unclear whether every void is shown.
