design_detail: Systematic review of take-home naloxone (THN) programmes that trained people who use opioids in overdose prevention and reported overdose outcomes, with the evidence judged against the nine Bradford Hill criteria for causation and five feasibility and implementation criteria taken from a WHO report on needle and syringe programmes. Searches: Medline and PsycInfo (via OVID) and PubMed, January 1946 to the third week of June 2015, one Boolean string replicated from an earlier review (Clark et al., 2014), English only, plus the reference lists of three reviews. 22 observational studies included (one interrupted time series, 16 pre–post, three case series, two cross-sectional; none randomized; two controlled). The authors dismissed meta-analysis in favour of narrative synthesis, but report unweighted pooled counts of naloxone administrations, deaths and adverse reactions across 17 non-duplicated studies with 95% confidence intervals. Study selection, data extraction and quality appraisal by the first author under the senior author's supervision. Appraised with AMSTAR 2 as a systematic review without formal meta-analysis; the pooled counts are treated as a quantitative synthesis for items 11, 12 and 15.
can_establish: What the published, mostly uncontrolled literature to June 2015 reports about naloxone use by trained lay people (2336 administrations in 17 studies, with deaths and adverse reactions as recorded), and how the authors judged that literature against the Bradford Hill criteria.
cannot_establish: That take-home naloxone reduces overdose mortality by any known amount: survival after a bystander's naloxone (about 96–99%) is not deaths prevented, because most overdoses are survived (the review cites one fatal overdose per 20 overdose events, a ratio for overdoses in general, not for overdoses left without intervention) and no included study compared similar overdoses with and without naloxone; the only evidence on population death rates is one ecological interrupted time series (Walley et al., 2013).

sample.recruitment: Database search (Medline 150 and PsycInfo 772 records via OVID, PubMed 475), January 1946 to the third week of June 2015, English-language peer-reviewed papers; five studies added from the reference lists of three reviews (pp. 1178–1179; Figure 1). Participants in the included studies: people who use opioids, mostly heroin, trained by programmes in the USA (15 studies), Canada (2), the UK (4) and Jersey and Berlin (1); some programmes targeted people leaving detoxification or prison, people who are homeless, methadone patients and HIV education centre attendees (pp. 1179, 1184).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: original quantitative or mixed-method studies (randomized or observational) of THN programmes that trained people who use opioids in overdose prevention and reported overdose outcomes. Excluded: studies of buprenorphine/naloxone, case reports, papers without primary data, papers not about people who use heroin or opioids, naloxone or overdose (p. 1179); non-English records at screening, without a stated reason (Figure 1, p. 1178). Full papers excluded: case study 1, not relevant 8, population 2, qualitative 4, review article 4.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Within studies, follow-up ranged from 5% to 100% of participants (Table 4); in the 10 pre–post and case-series studies with unsystematic follow-up, naloxone use was recorded for 1973 of 8602 recipients (22.9%), which the authors read as the share returning for refills after use (p. 1185).
sample.selection_effects: English only; no trial-registry or expert search; grey literature searched only afterwards as a check, by the authors' account probably not exhaustively (p. 1185). The included studies are mostly programme reports relying on self-report and unsystematic follow-up, so naloxone uses with good outcomes may be over-represented, as the authors note (p. 1185). Four studies from projects with several papers were left out of the pooled counts to avoid double counting (Doe-Simkins 2009, Dwyer 2015, Lankenau 2013 and the Walley 2013 methadone-patient study).

exposure.measurement: Programme participation and naloxone kits, as each study reported them; naloxone use and its outcome mostly by participants' self-report at refill or follow-up. Only the interrupted time series (Walley et al., 2013) used vital statistics (p. 1185).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Kits distributed per study from 19 to 3500; share of kits used from 0% to 67% (Table 3, p. 1181). Naloxone formulation and route were not synthesized.
exposure.polysubstance: Not synthesized. The review notes that naloxone acts on opioid overdose only (no effect in one cocaine intoxication; one death after naloxone with non-opioids present) and that the included studies reported primarily on heroin overdoses, so effects for long-acting opioids such as methadone are unclear (pp. 1183, 1185).

comparison.controls: None in 20 of the 22 studies; two were controlled (Bennett and Holloway, 2012, Wales; Walley et al., 2013, Massachusetts) (p. 1179). The pooled survival figures have no comparison: they report survival after naloxone without the survival that would have occurred without it.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. The severity of the overdoses in which naloxone was used, and why bystanders used it in some overdoses and not others, are unknown in the pooled counts.

outcomes.instruments: Nine Bradford Hill criteria (strength of association, consistency, specificity, temporality, dose–response, biological plausibility, coherence, experimental evidence, analogy) and five WHO criteria (cost-effectiveness, absence of negative consequences, feasibility of implementation and coverage, unanticipated benefits, special populations), each judged narratively (Tables 1–2). Pooled counts: naloxone administrations, overdose reversals (administrations minus deaths, and for a lower estimate also minus unclear and unknown outcomes), deaths after naloxone, adverse reactions (Table 3). Study quality: an eight-item scale from Jinks et al. (an integrative review of obesity interventions for people with a learning disability), as modified by Clark et al., scored 4 to 7 (Table 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: The items of the quality scale are not listed, and the scores are not used in the synthesis.
outcomes.operationalization: Impact on mortality (aim 1) is proxied by the number of overdose reversals, because whether each overdose would have been fatal without naloxone cannot be known; the authors cite a ratio of one fatal overdose per 20 overdose events (p. 1179). Safety (aim 2) is the number of deaths and adverse reactions after naloxone.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis tests). Nine pooled proportions are reported (two reversal estimates, three fatality estimates, four adverse-reaction rates), and 14 criteria are judged.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; one reviewer judged eligibility, extracted data and appraised quality.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unweighted pooled counts across 17 non-duplicated studies: 2336 naloxone administrations; 2316 reversals counting only the 20 confirmed deaths after naloxone as failures; at least 2249 reversals (96.3%, 95% CI 95.5 to 97.1) when 4 deaths with unclear naloxone use and 63 unknown outcomes are also counted as failures (pp. 1179, 1181–1182). Deaths after naloxone: 20 per 2336 (0.9%, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2); 24 per 2336 (1.0%, 0.6 to 1.4) including the unclear cases; one per 123 in the nine studies with systematic follow-up (0.8%, printed 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2) (p. 1184). Adverse reactions, reported in six studies but divided by all 2336 administrations: withdrawal at least 65 (2.8%), vomiting 52 (2.2%), agitation 50 (2.1%), seizures 4 (0.1%) (p. 1184). Editors' calculations: 2249/2336 = 96.28% (Wald interval 95.5 to 97.0); the printed interval for one death in 123 equals one computed with n=2336 (0.45 to 1.18), whereas with n=123 the exact 95% interval is 0.02% to 4.4%; 1432 of the 2336 administrations (61%) come from studies whose adverse-reaction column reads not reported, and over the 904 administrations from studies that did report (including two reporting none) the rates are 7.2% withdrawal, 5.8% vomiting, 5.5% agitation and 0.4% seizures. All pooled intervals treat the 17 studies as one sample and ignore differences between them.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is reported in the article; the methods say the search followed PRISMA guidance and refer to a search protocol and list of excluded studies in Supporting Information Appendix S1, which was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract says all nine Bradford Hill criteria were met, while the results judge dose–response only partially fulfilled and give experimental evidence only preliminary support, both resting on one study (pp. 1177, 1183–1184). The abstract's split of the five WHO criteria (two met partially, three fully) is not traceable in the text. Pooled intervals are given for the favourable proportions without any assessment of between-study variation.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The fatality figure for studies with systematic follow-up rests on one death among 123 administrations.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 22 mostly uncontrolled programme evaluations, trained lay people reported 2336 naloxone administrations in 17 non-duplicated studies, after which 20 people were confirmed dead (0.9%) and at least 96.3% survived; adverse reactions, where recorded, were mainly withdrawal symptoms, vomiting and agitation, with four seizures. The only evidence on population death rates is one ecological interrupted time series (Walley et al., 2013), on which the dose–response and experimental-evidence criteria rest entirely; a Chicago programme description reports falling overdose deaths after naloxone distribution began in 2001, without a control group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that take-home naloxone programmes 'are found to reduce overdose mortality among programme participants and in the community' (p. 1177), and the discussion that alternative explanations are unlikely and that take-home naloxone should become standard care for preventing heroin overdose deaths (pp. 1185–1186). Gaps: (1) the strength-of-association criterion is judged from survival after naloxone, which has no comparison; at the ratio of one fatal overdose per 20 overdose events that the review itself cites (a ratio for overdoses in general, not for overdoses left without intervention), about 117 of 2336 overdoses would be expected to end in death (editors' calculation), so 2249 reversals are not 2249 lives saved and the number of deaths prevented is unknown; (2) the mortality conclusion rests, for participants, on self-reported reversals and, for the community, on one ecological study; (3) the abstract's one death in 123 (0.8%, CI 0.4 to 1.2) is a single death whose interval is miscalculated (exact interval about 0.02% to 4.4%); (4) the low adverse-event rate divides by administrations from studies that mostly did not report adverse events; (5) all nine criteria are said to be met although the results call two of them partial or preliminary. A headline version such as 'naloxone saves 96% of overdoses' overstates the review: 96% is the share of people who survived after a bystander gave naloxone, not the share whose death naloxone prevented.

timeline.event: Strang et al. make the case for take-home naloxone in the BMJ (ref. 4, as cited, p. 1177).

Take-home naloxone introduced in Chicago; a programme description (Maxwell et al., 2006) reports fatal overdoses falling 20% in 2001, 8% in 2002 and 6% in 2003 after a 135% rise from 1996 to 2000, with no control group (as summarized, p. 1182).
Walley et al.: interrupted time series in 19 Massachusetts communities, the review's only quasi-experimental and dose–response evidence (card sc_walley_2013, written from the BMJ print summary only).

WHO guideline on community management of opioid overdose recommends that people likely to witness an opioid overdose have access to naloxone; Clark et al.'s systematic review concludes only that programme participation is associated with overdose reversals (as cited, pp. 1177, 1185).
EMCDDA review states that education and training with take-home naloxone decrease overdose-related mortality (as cited, p. 1185).
This review: by the authors' account the first application of the Bradford Hill criteria to take-home naloxone.

replication.where_it_stands: A widely cited summary of the take-home naloxone literature to mid-2015 that agrees with the WHO 2014 guideline and the EMCDDA review it cites. Its pooled survival figures describe outcomes after lay naloxone use, not effects on mortality, and its causal conclusion leans on one ecological study (Walley et al., 2013). Later reviews, trials and population evaluations were not among this reader's files.

funding.funder: No funding statement for the review itself. J.S. is supported by the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centre for Mental Health at South London and Maudsley NHS Foundation Trust and King's College London (Declaration of interests, p. 1186).
funding.declared_conflicts: King's College London, employer of both authors, has registered intellectual property on a novel buccal naloxone formulation with which both authors are involved. J.S. has worked with governmental and non-governmental organizations and with pharmaceutical companies to seek new or improved treatments (including naloxone products), from whom he and King's College London have received research funding, honoraria, travel costs and/or consultancy payments, and he is named in a patent registration by a pharmaceutical company as inventor of a further naloxone formulation. R.M. declares no other interests (p. 1186).
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors at the National Addiction Centre, King's College London. J.S. is an author of two included studies (Dettmer et al., 2001; Strang et al., 2008) and of the 1996 paper that made the case for take-home naloxone (ref. 4), and supervised the first author's selection, extraction and appraisal, so the senior author's own work was appraised within his group. The declared naloxone-formulation interests concern the intervention under review. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cluster-randomized or stepped-wedge roll-out of naloxone distribution across communities with deaths from vital statistics as the outcome, or controlled interrupted time series in many regions; and, for individuals, cohorts linking programme participation to death records instead of self-reported reversals.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, intervention and outcomes are stated, but no comparator is specified and uncontrolled designs are admitted (p. 1179).
No registration and no statement that the methods were set before the review; the article refers only to a search protocol in Appendix S1 (not read).
Reliance on observational designs is explained: randomized trials of take-home naloxone would often be unethical and difficult because overdoses are infrequent and unpredictable (p. 1177).

Three databases (two of them overlapping) with one simple string and the reference lists of three reviews, but English only without justification (23 records excluded), no trial registries, no content experts, and grey literature only as a later check; the search ended in June 2015, within 24 months of publication.
The first author assessed eligibility, under the senior investigator's supervision (p. 1179).
The first author extracted the data (STROBE checklist) under supervision; no second extractor or consensus process is described (p. 1179).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the Methods say Appendix S1 gives the search protocol and the excluded studies (p. 1178), but the Supporting Information list names Appendix S1 only as the search protocol (p. 1187); the article itself gives only category counts in Figure 1 (case study 1, not relevant 8, population 2, qualitative 4, review article 4). The appendix was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 3 and 4 give location, sample size, kits distributed and used, deaths, reversal rate, unknown outcomes, adverse reactions, follow-up, design and quality score; participants' characteristics, programme content, naloxone formulation and follow-up timing are not tabulated.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: A summary score from an eight-item scale borrowed from an integrative review of obesity interventions (via Clark et al.); the items are not listed, no domain judgments are given, and the article does not show that confounding or selection bias were assessed (p. 1179; Table 4).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Meta-analysis was dismissed, yet counts were pooled unweighted across 17 studies as if from one sample, with 95% intervals that ignore between-study heterogeneity; the interval for one death in 123 was computed with the denominator 2336 (pp. 1179, 1184). If the pooled counts are not regarded as a meta-analysis, items 11, 12 and 15 become 'no meta-analysis' and the overall rating is unchanged.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Met narrowly: the fatality ratio was recomputed in the nine studies with systematic follow-up (one death per 123) and the discussion argues that reversals were reported regardless of follow-up type or data source (pp. 1184–1185). The quality scores were not used, and the subset's interval is miscalculated.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion names selection bias from unsystematic follow-up, reliance on self-report, wide variation in follow-up and the dependence of two criteria on one study (p. 1185), although the conclusions go further than this discussion supports.

Variability in size and quality is given as the reason for not doing a meta-analysis, but the pooled figures are presented without examining variation between studies (kit use 0% to 67%; follow-up 5% to 100%; unknown outcomes concentrated in four studies).
Only a grey-literature search judged by the authors as probably not exhaustive and broadly consistent; no graphical or statistical assessment of small-study effects (p. 1185).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Interests are declared in detail, including the employer's intellectual property and the senior author's patent registration on naloxone formulations; how they were managed is not described, and no specific funding for the review is stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional, because item 7 depends on Appendix S1, which was not read; no answer on item 7 could change the rating. AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item fails: items 2 (no protocol), 4 (English-only search without justification), 9 (no recognisable risk-of-bias assessment), 11 (naive pooling) and 15 (no assessment of publication bias) all fail, and even if the pooled counts are not treated as a meta-analysis, items 2, 4 and 9 still fail. This rates how far the review's synthesis can be trusted, not the importance of naloxone distribution: the review is transparent about its tables, names its main limitations and draws on a body of evidence that is itself mostly uncontrolled. Citable for: the counts of lay naloxone administrations (2336), confirmed deaths after them (20) and recorded adverse reactions in the included studies; the observation that the evidence on mortality at population level rested on one ecological study in 2015; and the authors' Bradford Hill judgments as their judgments. Not citable for: a proportion of overdose deaths prevented by naloxone, 'one death in 123' with the printed interval, adverse-event rates as true rates, or the statement that all nine Bradford Hill criteria were met without its qualifications.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 1397 records (Medline 150, PsycInfo 772, PubMed 475); after excluding 210 duplicates and 23 non-English records, 1164 were screened; 36 full papers were retrieved and 19 excluded (case study 1, not relevant 8, population 2, qualitative 4, review article 4); 5 studies were added by hand-searching; 22 were included. The search covered January 1946 to the third week of June 2015 with one string: (opioid OR opiate) AND overdose AND prevention.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Methods and Results (p. 1177); Methods › Identification of eligible studies, 1st paragraph (p. 1178) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1179); Figure 1 (p. 1178)
key_findings.note: Figure 1 (the PRISMA flowchart) is an image without a text layer; its counts (210 duplicates, 23 non-English, 1021 and 107 excluded on title and abstract, the 19 exclusions by reason) were read on the rendered page. Editors' check: 1397 − 210 − 23 = 1164; 1164 − 1021 − 107 = 36; 36 − 19 + 5 = 22.

key_findings.finding: Included studies: 22, all observational: one interrupted time series, 16 pre–post (nine with systematic follow-up), three case series and two cross-sectional; none randomized, two controlled; 15 in the USA, two in Canada, four in the UK and one in the UK and Germany; sample sizes 24 to 2912 (median printed as 203).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Identification of eligible studies, 5th paragraph (p. 1179); Table 4 (p. 1182)
key_findings.note: The printed median cannot be reproduced from the sample sizes in Tables 3 and 4 (editors' calculation: 244.5 with the two Dettmer samples combined, 239 with them separate).

key_findings.finding: Review methods: the first author extracted data (STROBE checklist), assessed eligibility and rated quality with an eight-item scale (Jinks et al., as applied by Clark et al.) under the senior investigator's supervision; meta-analysis was dismissed in favour of narrative synthesis because of variability in size and quality; summary statistics are pooled, unweighted estimates; for projects with more than one published study (Boston/Massachusetts, Los Angeles, New York, San Francisco) only the study with the largest sample was kept, unless the studies covered clearly distinct, non-overlapping periods, in which case all were kept.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Identification of eligible studies, 4th paragraph; Analysis, 1st and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 3 bears out the exception: both New York studies (Galea 2006, Markham Piper 2008) and all three San Francisco studies (Seal 2005, Enteen 2010, Rowe 2015) are in the pooled counts.

key_findings.finding: Reversals as a proxy for mortality: the number of overdose reversals was used as a proxy for the impact of take-home naloxone on overdose mortality, because whether each overdose would have been fatal without naloxone cannot be known; the authors cite a ratio of one fatal overdose per 20 overdose events (ref. 28).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Analysis, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: at the cited ratio (one fatal overdose per 20 overdose events, from ref. 28, which was not read), about 117 deaths would be expected among 2336 overdose events. The review gives the ratio for overdose events in general, not for overdoses left without any intervention, and overdoses in which naloxone was used may differ from them, so reversals are not deaths prevented and the number prevented is unknown.

key_findings.finding: Pooled naloxone use and survival: after excluding four studies with possibly duplicated samples, 2336 naloxone administrations in 17 studies; subtracting the 20 confirmed deaths gives 2316 reversals; counting also the 4 deaths where naloxone use was unclear and 63 administrations with unknown outcome as failures gives at least 2249 reversals (96.3%, 95% CI 95.5 to 97.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Strength of association, 1st paragraph (p. 1179, continued on pp. 1181–1182) and 2nd paragraph (p. 1182); Table 3 (p. 1181); footnotes 1 and 2
key_findings.note: The total of 2336 is reproduced only if the Strang 2008 row of Table 3, printed as 1 administration (5%), is 12 (editors' arithmetic; see reporting issues). 22 studies minus 4 leaves 18; the 17 appears to omit the one study with no administrations (Lopez-Gaston 2009).

key_findings.finding: Deaths after naloxone: 20 confirmed deaths per 2336 administrations, in five studies (0.9%, 95% CI 0.5 to 1.2); 24 per 2336 (1.0%, 0.6 to 1.4) including four deaths where naloxone use was unclear; in the nine studies with systematic follow-up, one confirmed death per 123 administrations (0.8%, printed 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2).
key_findings.locator: Results › Absence of negative consequences, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the printed interval for 1 in 123 matches one computed with n=2336 (0.45 to 1.18); with n=123 the exact 95% interval is 0.02% to 4.4%. The 123 includes Dwyer 2015, otherwise excluded from the pooled counts as a possible duplicate, and requires Strang 2008 to be 12 administrations.

key_findings.finding: Adverse reactions, reported in six of the 17 studies and expressed over all 2336 administrations: at least 65 withdrawal reactions (2.8%), 52 vomiting (2.2%), 50 agitation (2.1%) and 4 seizures (0.1%); the authors conclude that programmes have a low rate of adverse events, mostly symptoms of opioid withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Absence of negative consequences, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1184); Table 3, Adverse reactions column (p. 1181)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 3: 1432 of the 2336 administrations (61%) come from studies whose adverse-reaction column reads not reported; over the 904 administrations from studies that reported (including two reporting none), the rates are 7.2%, 5.8%, 5.5% and 0.4%. 4 of 2336 is 0.17%, printed as 0.1%.

key_findings.finding: Population evidence: only Walley et al. (2013) assessed death rates with vital statistics and by level of implementation; as summarized here, both low (1–100 enrolments per 100,000) and high (more than 100) implementation communities had significantly lower overdose death rates than communities without, with a significant implementation dose relationship. The review judges dose–response only partially fulfilled and the experimental-evidence criterion given preliminary support, both from this one study.
key_findings.locator: Results › Temporality, 2nd paragraph (p. 1182); Dose–response relationship, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Experimental evidence (p. 1183); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 1185)
key_findings.note: The trend test described here is not reported in the BMJ print summary of Walley et al. read for card sc_walley_2013.

key_findings.finding: Chicago, uncontrolled: after a 135% rise in local overdose deaths from 1996 to 2000, take-home naloxone was introduced in 2001 and fatal overdoses fell by 20% in 2001, 8% in 2002 and 6% in 2003 (against the previous year); the review says no definite conclusion can be drawn because there was no control group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Temporality, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Coherence: in Australia, overdose mortality fell between 2001 and 2002 with a shortage of imported heroin, before take-home naloxone was introduced there in 2011; the review judges this not to conflict with an effect of naloxone.
key_findings.locator: Results › Coherence

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: 10 of 19 pre–post and case-series studies relied on unsystematic follow-up; across them, by the authors' account, fewer than a quarter of recipients (22.9%; 1973 of 8602) returned for refills after naloxone use, so information on most participants was lost; people with good naloxone experiences may be more likely to return and be counted; follow-up ranged from 5% to 100%; 21 of 22 studies relied only on self-report for overdose outcomes; the vast majority of studies reported on heroin overdoses, so effectiveness for overdoses from long-acting opioids is unclear.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 6th paragraphs
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 1973 equals the summed naloxone uses of these 10 studies in Table 3, i.e. recorded uses.

key_findings.finding: Other reported outcomes: in San Francisco 25% of participants entered treatment within 6 months and in Los Angeles 53% reported less drug use at 3 months; 28% of recipients in an English study had trained a family member or peer within 3 months; the review finds no empirical support for the concern that programmes encourage heroin use (two studies reported less use, a more recent one no overall change).
key_findings.locator: Results › Unanticipated benefits (p. 1184); Discussion, 1st paragraph (pp. 1184–1185)

key_findings.finding: Feasibility: the text reports naloxone use rates between 5% and 63% across studies; San Francisco expanded from 24 kits in 2001 to 2962 kits in 2003–2009 and 2500 in 2010–2013; outside the included studies, use rates of 47% and 78% were reported in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
key_findings.locator: Results › Feasibility of implementation, expansion and coverage
key_findings.note: Table 3 shows use from 0% (Lopez-Gaston 2009) to 67% (Markham Piper 2008).

key_findings.finding: Grey literature (Scottish National Naloxone Programme): the share of opioid-related deaths occurring within 4 weeks of release from prison was 5.5% in 2012 and 4.7% in 2013, against a pooled 2006–10 baseline of 9.8%.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures from an official report (ref. 48), not appraised here.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints 1 naloxone administration (5%) for Strang 2008 (n=239). Editors' arithmetic: 1 of 239 is 0.4%, and the text's totals are reproduced only if the value is 12, giving 2336 administrations in the non-duplicated studies (2325 with the printed 1) and 123 in the nine studies with systematic follow-up (112 with the printed 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a typesetting error in the table; the totals and the percentage are consistent with 12, which should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: One death per 123 administrations is reported as 0.8% with 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2 in the abstract and results. Editors' calculation: that interval corresponds to a denominator of 2336; with one event in 123, the exact 95% interval is about 0.02% to 4.4%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's interval is about five times narrower than an exact interval for one death in 123 (width 0.8 against about 4.4 percentage points; exact interval 0.02% to 4.45%), and the systematic-follow-up subset is too small to show that its fatality ratio matches the overall one.

reporting_issues.issue: Adverse-reaction rates (2.8%, 2.2%, 2.1%, 0.1%) are divided by all 2336 administrations. Editors' arithmetic from Table 3: studies whose adverse-reaction column reads not reported contribute 1432 of them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed rates are lower bounds; among studies that reported adverse reactions they are about 2.5 times higher.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the summary of findings say all nine Bradford Hill criteria were met, while the results judge dose–response only partially fulfilled and give experimental evidence only preliminary support, both from one study.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should not repeat that all nine criteria were met without these qualifications.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion cites two studies (refs 14 and 20) as showing reduced deaths in the community from vital statistics, while the limitations paragraph on the same page says only Walley et al. (ref. 20) used vital statistics; ref. 14 (Seal et al., 2005) is a pilot study with 24 participants (Table 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The community-level mortality claim rests on one study.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives naloxone use rates of 5% to 63%, while Table 3 shows 0% (Lopez-Gaston 2009) to 67% (Markham Piper 2008), with 4% for Yokell 2011.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; use the table values.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says two of the five WHO criteria were met partially and three fully, but the text does not say which.
reporting_issues.consequence: The split cannot be checked from the article (it may be in Appendix S1, not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The median sample size printed as 203 cannot be reproduced from Tables 3 and 4, and the number of studies in the pooled counts is given as 17. Editors' calculation: the median is 244.5 with the two Dettmer samples combined (239 with them separate), and 22 included studies minus the 4 left out of the pooled counts is 18.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the 17 appears to omit the study with no naloxone administrations.

reporting_issues.issue: Two included studies, Leece 2013 (Toronto; 209 participants, 17 naloxone uses, no deaths) and Tobin 2009 (Baltimore; 250 participants, 22 uses, no deaths), are listed in Tables 3 and 4 and counted in the pooled totals, but have no entry in the reference list (refs 1–48); the consistency criterion also names Toronto and Baltimore without a citation.
reporting_issues.consequence: These two studies cannot be traced from the article, so their 39 of the 2336 pooled administrations cannot be checked against a source; the effect on the totals is small.
