design_detail: Community-level (ecological) panel analysis that the authors call an interrupted time series: yearly counts of opioid-related overdose deaths and of acute-care hospital use (inpatient and emergency-department discharges for non-fatal opioid overdose) in 19 Massachusetts cities and towns, 2002–2009, modelled with log-linear Poisson regression (counts with the census population as offset), community covariates, one linear time term common to all communities and a first-order autoregressive covariance structure chosen with quasi-likelihood information criteria (p. 3 of 13, Covariates; Statistical analysis). The exposure is cumulative enrolment in state-supported overdose education and nasal naloxone distribution (OEND), with enrolments counted from 18 September 2006: community-years with no implementation are the reference, against 1–100 and more than 100 cumulative enrolments per 100 000 (absolute model) or below and above that year's median (relative model) (p. 3; Table 4, p. 10). No community was without implementation in 2008–09, so the reference is all 19 communities in 2002–05 and those not yet implementing in 2006–07 (p. 4). There are no comparison communities outside the 19, and no community indicators or community-specific trends are described. Filed as retrospective-cohort, the nearest design in the schema (the units are communities followed over years), and appraised with ROBINS-I as a programme evaluation, as the round brief directs. Updated from the full article (13 pages, BMJ 2013;346:f174); the first version was written from the one-page print summary.
can_establish: Whether, in 19 high-burden Massachusetts communities in 2002–2009, community-years with OEND enrolment had lower opioid-overdose death rates, and different acute-care rates, than community-years without, after adjustment for community demographics, state-funded treatment, doctor-shopping prescriptions and one linear time trend.
cannot_establish: That OEND caused the lower adjusted death rates (implementation was not randomized; with no community-years without implementation in 2008–09, the contrast rests largely on later against earlier years and a linear time term, and the crude ratios are 0.93 and 0.82), how many deaths were prevented (no death or event counts are printed), a dose–response (seen in the absolute model only), or anything about the individuals trained or rescued (rescue attempts are bystanders' reports, not linked to death or hospital records).

sample.recruitment: Registry and programme data (no individual recruitment): the 19 of Massachusetts' 351 cities and towns with five or more opioid-related unintentional or undetermined-intent fatal poisonings in each year 2004–2006, the years just before OEND began (p. 2 of 13, Methods, 1st paragraph); together about 30% of the state population and almost half of its fatal opioid overdoses and acute-care uses for non-fatal opioid overdose (p. 4, Results, 1st paragraph). OEND programmes enrolled 2912 residents of these communities between 18 September 2006 and 31 December 2009 (4857 statewide), who reported 327 rescue attempts (545 statewide) (p. 4, Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Communities: five or more opioid-related unintentional or undetermined-intent fatal poisonings in each year 2004–2006. The article's wording (it included 'the 19 communities' meeting the criterion, p. 2) indicates that all communities meeting it were included. Enrolments and rescue attempts were assigned to communities by the enrolee's zip code of residence (p. 3).
sample.demographics: Communities (Table 1, p. 7 of 13): 2005 population 2 055 086 in all (mean 108 162, median 87 392, range 30 236–609 690); under 18 years 22.4%, male 48.0%, Hispanic 13.8%, white non-Hispanic 63.9%, black non-Hispanic 11.9%, other non-Hispanic 10.1%, below poverty level 16.4%; treatment events per 100 000 people in 2009: inpatient detoxification 630.0, methadone maintenance 161.8, state-funded buprenorphine maintenance 41.5 (printed 'Stated funded'); opioid prescriptions to doctor shoppers 10.9 (by the table's heading a percentage of opioid prescriptions dispensed; year not stated). No characteristics are given by implementation stratum. Enrolees (Table 2, p. 8): mean age 38.1 years (SD 12.1); 44.4% (1274/2870) female or male-to-female transgender; 69.5% white non-Hispanic, 16.2% Hispanic, 10.5% black or African American non-Hispanic.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (routine community data); no exclusions of community-years are reported. Deaths are in-state occurrent deaths of residents, so residents' deaths outside Massachusetts are not counted (p. 2 of 13); deaths during a hospital stay are excluded from acute care to avoid double counting (p. 3). Completeness of the zip codes used to assign enrolments is not reported; rescue-questionnaire items are incomplete (whether naloxone was successful is recorded for 153 of 327 attempts; Table 3, p. 9).
sample.selection_effects: Communities were chosen for high overdose mortality in 2004–2006, just before the programme began, and those years are part of the no-implementation reference, so regression toward the mean could favour a later decline. Where and how intensively OEND was implemented was not random (the Department of Public Health extended it to further agencies in 2007 and 2009, p. 2 of 13). All 19 communities had implementation in 2008–09 (p. 4), so community-years without implementation are all 19 communities in 2002–05, the 12 not yet implementing in 2006 and the 5 not yet implementing in 2007 (editors' count from p. 4: 93 of 152 community-years); the communities that started later may differ in ways the paper does not describe.

exposure.measurement: Programme records: cumulative OEND enrolments per 100 000 population in each community-year, assigned by the zip code of residence on the enrolment questionnaire (p. 3 of 13, Independent variables). Absolute model: none, 1–100 and more than 100 per 100 000; relative model: none, and below and above that year's median cumulative enrolment rate. The same paragraph says the models used cut points of 0, 1–75 and >75, with 0, 1–150 and >150 in sensitivity analyses, while the Results (p. 4) and Table 4 (p. 10) present 1–100 and >100 as the main categories and 75 and 150 as sensitivity analyses (reporting issue). Yearly medians among implementing communities: 3 (2006), 7 (2007), 55 (2008) and 142 (2009) enrolments per 100 000 (p. 4). Enrolment counts do not show kits in circulation, refills or where kits were carried; the authors say their measures were not validated in other populations (p. 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Programme as delivered (study conditions): 2912 residents of the 19 communities enrolled between 18 September 2006 and 31 December 2009, of whom 2007 reported active substance use, treatment or recovery and 905 were others, typically social-service staff, family and friends (p. 4 of 13; Table 2, p. 8). Trainers were non-medical public health workers who had completed a four-hour course, a knowledge test and two supervised trainings, working under a standing order; sessions took about 10 to 60 minutes and covered prevention, recognition and response (seeking help, rescue breathing, nasal naloxone, staying with the person); kits held two prefilled naloxone syringes and two mucosal atomization devices, and a refill was given when naloxone had been used (pp. 2–3). The number of kits distributed is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable at community level; not measured or addressed in the analysis (full article).

comparison.controls: Community-years without OEND implementation in the same 19 communities: all 19 in 2002–05, 12 in 2006 and 5 in 2007; none in 2008–09, when all 19 had implementation (p. 4 of 13, Results, 4th paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of the study, 1st paragraph). The introduction calls communities with low or no implementation concurrent controls (p. 2), but concurrent comparisons with no implementation exist only for 2006 and 2007. No comparison communities outside the 19.
comparison.matching: None. Regression adjustment (Covariates, p. 3 of 13; Table 4 and 5 footnotes, pp. 10–11): city or town population rates of age under 18, male sex, race or ethnicity (Hispanic, white, black, other) and below poverty level, linearly interpolated for each year from the 2000 and 2010 censuses; rates of medically supervised inpatient withdrawal, methadone treatment and buprenorphine treatment from the treatment database of the state Bureau of Substance Abuse Services, to which programmes licensed by and contracted with the Bureau must report (the tables say Bureau-funded buprenorphine); the proportion of schedule II opioid prescriptions dispensed to doctor shoppers (prescriptions from four or more prescribers filled at four or more pharmacies in 12 months; prescription monitoring programme data); and a linear time variable (1 for 2002, rising by one each year).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not in the model: other overdose-prevention activity in the period (the introduction names prescription monitoring, take-back days, prescribing guidelines and education, p. 2 of 13), office-based buprenorphine outside state funding (expanding during the study period, p. 3), drug supply and potency, policing and local services; community indicators, community-specific trends and any non-linear statewide trend are not described. The number of people who use opioids in each community was unknown (p. 5).

outcomes.instruments: Deaths (p. 2 of 13, Data collection and measures › Fatal opioid overdose rates): unintentional or undetermined-intent opioid-related poisonings by community of residence, from in-state occurrent deaths in the electronic database of the Massachusetts Registry of Vital Records and Statistics; ICD-10 X40–X44 or Y10–Y14 as underlying cause with T40.0–T40.4 and/or T40.6 in any multiple-cause field. Death certificates on fatal poisonings are completed through the single statewide office of the chief medical examiner, to which they must by law be reported; who assigned the ICD-10 codes, and what toxicology was done and in what share of deaths, are not reported. Acute care (pp. 2–3): inpatient and outpatient emergency-department discharges by city or town of residence from the Division of Health Care Finance and Policy databases, with ICD-9-CM 965 (.00, .01, .02, .09) or E850 (.0, .1, .2), excluding poisonings coded as intentional self-harm, assault, adverse effect in therapeutic use or legal intervention, and deaths during the hospital event; inpatient and emergency-department use are analysed as one outcome.
outcomes.operationalization: Rate ratios of yearly opioid-overdose deaths, and separately of acute-care discharges, per community-year in each implementation stratum against community-years without implementation, from Poisson models with population offsets (p. 3 of 13).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported: two outcomes (deaths; acute care), each in two exposure models with two strata (eight adjusted rate ratios), plus alternative cut points and two control-model outcomes; every test at α 0.05 (p. 3 of 13).
outcomes.validity_norms: T40.6 had a positive predictive value of 98% for an opioid-related death in an unpublished review of 2007 Massachusetts death certificate literals, and 96.7% of unintentional or undetermined-intent poisoning deaths in 2007 had at least one ICD-10 code in T36–T50.8 (p. 2 of 13). E codes are required by state regulation for discharges with a principal diagnosis of injury or poisoning (pp. 2–3); the authors call discharge codes a blunt measure but cite other studies that found no systematic directional misclassification (p. 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: Deaths (Table 4, p. 10 of 13), rate ratios against community-years with no implementation: absolute model, 1–100 enrolments per 100 000 crude 0.93, adjusted 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91), p<0.01; more than 100, crude 0.82, adjusted 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76), p<0.01; relative model, below the median crude 0.85, adjusted 0.71 (0.57 to 0.90), p<0.01; above the median crude 1.00, adjusted 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01), p=0.06. Acute care (Table 5, p. 11): absolute model crude 1.00 and 1.06, adjusted 0.93 (0.80 to 1.08), p=0.4, and 0.92 (0.75 to 1.13), p=0.4; relative model crude 0.96 and 1.10, adjusted 0.90 (0.76 to 1.07), p=0.2, and 1.00 (0.86 to 1.16), p=1.0. The crude column is headed only Rate ratio, without intervals or p values; crude is the editors' reading of it. Sensitivity analyses with cut points of 75 and 150 per 100 000 gave similar rate ratios for both outcomes, and the control model with the ratio of opioid-overdose deaths to cancer deaths showed significant associations in a similar pattern, all without numbers in the article (control models in supplementary tables 6 and 7, not among the files; no table is cited for the 75 and 150 cut-point analyses). Editors' note: the adjusted ratios lie much further from 1 than the crude ones, and Figure 1 (p. 12) shows unadjusted rates in implementing community-years that are not systematically lower than in earlier years without implementation, so the size of the association depends on the adjustment model, which includes one linear time term.
analysis.covariates: Community population rates of age under 18, male sex, race or ethnicity and poverty (interpolated between the 2000 and 2010 censuses); Bureau of Substance Abuse Services data on inpatient withdrawal, methadone and Bureau-funded buprenorphine treatment; proportion of schedule II opioid prescriptions dispensed to doctor shoppers; one linear time trend (p. 3 of 13; Tables 4–5, pp. 10–11).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration, protocol or analysis plan is mentioned in the full article; the original design is credited to three authors (Walley, Ozonoff, Hackman) and further model development to all authors (p. 5 of 13, Contributors).
analysis.selective_reporting: The full article reports both exposure models for both outcomes (Tables 4 and 5), but the abstract and the print summary give only the absolute model, which shows a gradient, and not the relative model, which does not; the alternative cut points (75 and 150) and the control models are reported only in words, without numbers, and the covariate coefficients are in supplementary tables 4a, 4b, 5a and 5b (not read); the Methods' description of the cut points contradicts the Results (p. 3 of 13 against p. 4). No death or event counts, no number of community-years per stratum and no test for trend are reported.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size or power considerations (19 communities over 8 years, 152 community-years by the editors' count).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 19 Massachusetts communities selected for high overdose mortality, community-years with OEND enrolment had lower adjusted opioid-overdose death rates than community-years without in the absolute model (adjusted rate ratios 0.73 with 1–100 and 0.54 with more than 100 enrolments per 100 000) and for below-median enrolment in the relative model (0.71), but not clearly for above-median enrolment (0.78, 0.60 to 1.01). Crude ratios were 0.93 and 0.82 (absolute) and 0.85 and 1.00 (relative), and unadjusted rates in implementing community-years (Figure 1) were not systematically lower than in 2002–06. Because every community was implementing by 2008, most of the contrast is between later and earlier years, adjusted with one linear time term. Acute-care use did not differ from community-years without implementation in any stratum (adjusted rate ratios 0.90 to 1.00, all intervals including 1).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that death rates were reduced where OEND was implemented and that the study gives observational evidence that OEND is 'an effective intervention' (p. 1 of 13); the Interpretation says implementation seemed to have a dose-related impact, the higher the cumulative implementation the greater the reduction in death rates (p. 5); the Implications call the study 'strong support' for public health agencies and community organizations to implement and expand OEND (p. 5); the box on what the study adds repeats effectiveness (p. 6). The authors also write that an observational study cannot prove definitively that OEND caused the reduction (p. 5). Gaps: (1) 'effective' and 'reduced' are causal readings of an association that appears only after adjustment and rests largely on comparing 2008–09 with earlier years through a linear time term, with concurrent communities without implementation only in 2006–07; (2) the dose-related impact holds in the absolute model only: in the relative model the above-median stratum had the weaker, non-significant association (0.78 against 0.71), as the authors themselves note among their strengths and limitations (p. 4), and no trend test is reported; (3) the authors explain the null acute-care result by bystanders calling emergency services, but emergency services were called or present in 33% (106/326) of reported rescue attempts (Table 3, p. 9); (4) the 327 rescue attempts and the 98% success (150 of the 153 attempts with that item recorded) are bystanders' reports. A headline such as 'naloxone distribution cut overdose deaths by up to 46%' overstates the study: 46% is one minus the adjusted rate ratio for one stratum of one of two exposure models, an association much weaker before adjustment, not a measured effect of the programme.

timeline.event: OEND enrolments in Massachusetts are counted from 18 September 2006 to 31 December 2009; two community public health agencies began providing OEND in 2006–07, and the Department of Public Health extended it to four more organizations in 2007 and two more in 2009 (full article, pp. 2 and 4).

Preliminary results presented at the American Public Health Association conference (1 November 2011), the Association of Medical Education and Research on Substance Abuse conference (5 November 2011) and the US Food and Drug Administration (12 April 2012) (full article, p. 5, acknowledgements).

This study, accepted on 31 December 2012 and published in full on bmj.com on 31 January 2013 (BMJ 2013;346:f174, the 13-page article read for this update), with a one-page print summary in the BMJ of 9 February 2013 (the version read for the first card).

McDonald and Strang's systematic review (searched to June 2015) treats this study as the only quasi-experimental evidence, the only evidence on dose–response and the only study using vital statistics among 22 studies of take-home naloxone; it records 2912 enrolments and 327 uses for it (card sc_mcdonald_2016, this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: The authors state that no controlled study of OEND and overdose rates had been completed before this one (p. 2 of 13, Introduction, 3rd paragraph). As of the June 2015 search of McDonald and Strang (2016), no other controlled population-level evaluation of naloxone distribution against death rates was available, and that review's judgments on dose–response and experimental evidence rest on this study alone. Later evaluations were not among this reader's files. The card was updated from the full article on 2026-11-12; the online supplementary tables (covariate coefficients, control models, map) remain unread.

funding.funder: Center for Disease Control and Prevention, grant 1R21CE001602 (principal investigator AYW), as printed in the full article (p. 5 of 13, Funding); the funder played no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit, and the researchers had independence from the funder. The print summary names the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, without a grant number.
funding.declared_conflicts: ICMJE forms completed; AYW, ZX, EQ, MDS, AS-A and AO had support from the Center for Disease Control and Prevention grant 1R21CE001602-01 for this study; no financial relationships with any organisations that might have an interest in the submitted work in the previous three years; no other relationships or activities that could appear to have influenced the submitted work (p. 5 of 13, Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Boston University Schools of Medicine and Public Health, the Massachusetts Department of Public Health and Children's Hospital Boston (p. 1 of 13). The first author is described as medical director of the Massachusetts opioid overdose prevention pilot (title block, p. 1), and the programme ran under a standing order from the OEND medical director (p. 2). Three authors (Walley, Hackman, Ruiz) list the Department of Public Health, which extended the programme and kept the programme database that supplied the enrolment and rescue data (pp. 2–3); an earlier paper by Doe-Simkins, Walley and colleagues is cited for the programme's start (reference 20, p. 2). The competing-interests statement does not mention these roles, so people connected with the evaluated programme and its supporting agency co-authored the evaluation. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount. Approved by the review boards of Boston University Medical Center (H-28736) and the Department of Public Health (249874-3); de-identified data, so no consent was required (p. 5).

what_would_settle_it: A stepped-wedge or cluster-randomized roll-out of naloxone distribution across many communities, or a controlled interrupted time series with pre-specified exposure categories, community-specific trends and comparison regions, reporting death counts and acute-care events alongside rate ratios.

domains.note: Implementation was not randomized. The model adjusts for interpolated demographics, Bureau of Substance Abuse Services treatment rates, the doctor-shopping proportion and one linear time term common to all communities, with no community indicators, community-specific or non-linear trends, comparison region, or measures of other prevention activity, privately funded buprenorphine or drug supply (pp. 2–3 of 13). All 19 communities were implementing in 2008–09, so those years are compared with the trend of earlier years; concurrent comparisons exist only for 2006 and 2007 (p. 4). Crude ratios (0.93 and 0.82; relative model 0.85 and 1.00) become 0.73, 0.54, 0.71 and 0.78 after adjustment, and the unadjusted rates in Figure 1 show no consistent reduction, so the result depends on the model. The control model with the ratio of opioid-overdose to cancer deaths addresses system-wide coding changes, not opioid-specific confounding (p. 4).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Communities were selected on five or more deaths in each of 2004–2006, the years just before implementation, which are part of the no-implementation reference; regression toward the mean could favour a later decline. The article indicates that all communities meeting the criterion were included (p. 2 of 13).

Exposure is cumulative enrolment per 100 000 assigned by the enrolee's zip code of residence (p. 3 of 13), not kits in circulation, refills or where kits were used; cumulative counts never fall, although enrolees move and kits are used up. The Methods' cut points (75 in the models, 150 in sensitivity analyses) contradict the 100 of the Results and Table 4 (pp. 3–4, 10), and the authors say the measures are their own and not validated elsewhere (p. 5). Enrolment records are independent of the outcome registries, so misclassification is likely non-differential.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: The full article describes delivery (a curriculum developed by the Harm Reduction Coalition and the Chicago Recovery Alliance and adapted for nasal naloxone, trainers certified by a four-hour course, a test and supervised trainings, a standing order, kits, refills after use; pp. 2–3 of 13), so the estimate is that of implementation as delivered. Fidelity by community, kit numbers and whether other overdose-prevention activities (named on p. 2) differed between implementation and non-implementation years are not reported.

Outcomes come from statewide registries with reporting required by law or regulation (death certificates through the chief medical examiner; mandatory E codes), and covariates were interpolated, so the main analysis has no reported missing outcome data (pp. 2–3 of 13). But residents' deaths outside Massachusetts are not counted (p. 2), completeness of the zip codes used to assign enrolments is not reported (p. 3), and the rescue questionnaires have missing items (naloxone success recorded for 153 of 327 attempts; Table 3, p. 9).

Deaths: ICD-10 codes including T40.6, whose positive predictive value of 98% comes from an unpublished review of one year (2007), certified through one statewide medical examiner office (p. 2 of 13); acute care: discharge codes, a blunt measure by the authors' account (p. 5). Coders were not part of the study and are unlikely to know implementation status, but coding or testing practice could change over 2002–09, which matters because the contrast is largely between years; the cancer-death and motor-vehicle control models address system-level coding effects only in part (p. 4).

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No protocol or registration is mentioned. Two exposure models, three sets of cut points and two control outcomes were analysed; the full article reports both main models, but the abstract and the print summary give only the absolute model (the one with a gradient), the alternative cut points and control models are reported without numbers, and the Methods' description of the cut points contradicts the Results (pp. 1, 3–4, 10 of 13).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Judged from the full article (13 pages); the online supplementary tables were not read. ROBINS-I is used because the exposure is a public-health programme compared across communities and years (METHODS §5.3). Serious overall because of confounding: implementation was not randomized, every community was implementing by 2008, the association appears only after adjustment with one linear time term, and there is no comparison region or control for community-specific trends. Citable for: in 19 high-burden Massachusetts communities, 2002–2009, adjusted opioid-overdose death rate ratios of 0.73 (1–100 enrolments per 100 000) and 0.54 (more than 100) against community-years without OEND, with crude ratios of 0.93 and 0.82; in the relative model 0.71 (below the median) and 0.78 (above the median, 0.60 to 1.01); no association with acute-care use (adjusted rate ratios 0.90 to 1.00); 2912 bystanders trained and 327 rescue attempts reported. Not citable for: a causal effect size of naloxone distribution, deaths prevented, a dose–response, effects outside high-burden communities, or the outcomes of the people rescued.

key_findings.finding: Between 18 September 2006 and 31 December 2009, OEND programmes enrolled 2912 residents of the 19 communities (4857 statewide); 212 of them reported 327 naloxone rescue attempts (545 statewide), 87% (286/327) of them by enrolees who reported active substance use, treatment or recovery.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Abstract › Results (p. 1); Table 2 (p. 8); Table 3 (p. 9)
key_findings.note: Rescue attempts are bystanders' reports to the programme, collected when a refill was requested; only attempts in which another person gave the naloxone were counted, and the authors expect under-reporting (pp. 3, 5). The abstract and the print summary call them rescues.

key_findings.finding: Design: the 19 of 351 Massachusetts cities and towns with at least five opioid-related unintentional or undetermined-intent fatal poisonings in each year 2004–2006; yearly opioid-overdose death and acute-care rates from 2002 to 2009, comparing community-years with high and low OEND implementation with community-years without, in Poisson models adjusted for community demographics, treatment, doctor shopping and a linear time trend.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Design and Setting (p. 1); Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Covariates and Statistical analysis (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Opioid-overdose death rate ratios against community-years with no implementation, absolute model: 1–100 cumulative enrolments per 100 000 population, crude 0.93, adjusted 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.91), p<0.01; more than 100 per 100 000, crude 0.82, adjusted 0.54 (0.39 to 0.76), p<0.01.
key_findings.locator: Table 4, absolute model; Results › Adjusted models: OEND implementation and fatal overdose rates (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The first column is headed only Rate ratio, as in the summary; the card reads it as crude (unadjusted) because the adjusted column beside it carries the adjustment footnote and the text calls the rates in Figures 1 and 2 unadjusted, but no part of the article labels the column. The crude ratios are printed without intervals or p values; the association is much stronger after adjustment.

key_findings.finding: Adjustment set: city or town population rates of age under 18, male sex, race or ethnicity (Hispanic, white, black, other) and below poverty level, linearly interpolated for each year from the 2000 and 2010 censuses; rates of medically supervised inpatient withdrawal, methadone treatment and Bureau of Substance Abuse Services funded buprenorphine treatment; the proportion of schedule II opioid prescriptions dispensed to doctor shoppers (4 or more prescribers, 4 or more pharmacies, 12 months); and a linear time variable for year (1 for 2002, rising by one each year).
key_findings.locator: Covariates, 1st–4th paragraphs (p. 3); Table 4 and Table 5 footnotes (pp. 10–11)

key_findings.finding: Acute-care use (inpatient and emergency-department discharges for non-fatal opioid overdose, analysed together) against community-years with no implementation: absolute model, 1–100 enrolments per 100 000 crude 1.00, adjusted 0.93 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.08), p=0.4; more than 100, crude 1.06, adjusted 0.92 (0.75 to 1.13), p=0.4; relative model, below the median crude 0.96, adjusted 0.90 (0.76 to 1.07), p=0.2; above the median crude 1.10, adjusted 1.00 (0.86 to 1.16), p=1.0.
key_findings.locator: Table 5; Results › Adjusted models: OEND implementation and opioid related non-fatal acute care hospital utilizations (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The print summary describes this as no significant difference in communities with low versus high implementation, and the article's Discussion (p. 4) says only that rates did not differ significantly in communities with low or high implementation; the comparisons tested are each stratum against no implementation, and no direct low-versus-high test is reported.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the observational design cannot prove definitively that OEND caused the reduction, and list as limitations, which they say they attempted to address: the number of people who use opioids in each community was unknown (to account for this they adjusted for demographics, use of addiction treatment and the proportion of prescriptions to doctor shoppers); deaths may have been misclassified, though one centralized medical examiner office processes every certificate; acute care rests on administrative discharge codes, a blunt measure, though systematic directional misclassification has not been found in other studies; overdoses may cluster; their implementation measures were not validated in other populations; and rescue attempts were likely under-reported.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations of the study, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: The print summary's statement that misclassification was unlikely to be directional is made in the article about the hospital discharge codes, not about deaths; the summary's paragraph on generalisability has no direct counterpart in the article, whose nearest statements are that the implementation measures were not validated in other populations and that tailoring OEND to different populations needs study (p. 5).

key_findings.finding: The programme: two community public health agencies began OEND in 2006–07, and the Massachusetts Department of Public Health extended it to four more organizations in 2007 and two more in 2009. Trained non-medical public health workers delivered it, under a standing order from the OEND medical director, to people who use opioids and are at risk of overdose and to social-service staff, family and friends, at syringe access programmes, HIV drop-in centres, addiction treatment programmes, emergency and primary care settings and community meetings; sessions took about 10 to 60 minutes, and kits held two prefilled naloxone syringes and two mucosal atomization devices.
key_findings.locator: The Massachusetts OEND program, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: None of the 19 communities had OEND implementation in 2002–05; 7 had some in 2006 (median 3 enrolments per 100 000), 14 in 2007 (median 7) and all 19 in 2008 and 2009 (medians 55 and 142). The no-implementation reference therefore comprises all 19 communities in 2002–05 and the communities not yet implementing in 2006–07, as the authors note; there are no community-years without implementation in 2008–09.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Discussion › Strengths and limitations of the study, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' count from these figures: 93 of the 152 community-years without implementation (76 of them in 2002–05) and 59 with; the article gives no number of community-years, deaths or events per stratum.

key_findings.finding: Deaths: unintentional or undetermined-intent opioid-related poisonings by community of residence, from in-state occurrent deaths in the Registry of Vital Records and Statistics database; ICD-10 X40–X44 or Y10–Y14 as underlying cause plus T40.0–T40.4 and/or T40.6 in any multiple-cause field; certificates for fatal poisonings completed through the single statewide office of the chief medical examiner. T40.6 had a positive predictive value of 98% for an opioid-related death in an unpublished review of 2007 certificates, and 96.7% of all unintentional or undetermined-intent poisoning deaths in Massachusetts in 2007 (not only opioid-related ones) had at least one ICD-10 code in T36–T50.8.
key_findings.locator: Data collection and measures › Fatal opioid overdose rates
key_findings.note: What toxicology was done, in what share of deaths, and who assigned the ICD-10 codes are not reported. Table 4 and Figure 1 call the deaths unintentional although the definition includes undetermined intent.

key_findings.finding: Acute care: inpatient and outpatient emergency-department discharges by city or town of residence from the Division of Health Care Finance and Policy databases, with ICD-9-CM 965 (.00, .01, .02, .09) or E850 (.0, .1, .2); poisonings coded as intentional self-harm, assault, adverse effect in therapeutic use or legal intervention, and deaths during the hospital event, were excluded.
key_findings.locator: Data collection and measures › Opioid overdose related acute care hospital utilization rates (p. 2, continuing on p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Exposure: cumulative enrolments per 100 000 population in each community-year, assigned by the zip code of residence on the enrolment questionnaire, in two ways: a relative model (no implementation; below and above that year's median cumulative enrolment rate) and an absolute model (no implementation; 1–100; more than 100 per 100 000). The same paragraph then says the models used cut points of 0, 1–75 and >75, and sensitivity analyses 0, 1–150 and >150.
key_findings.locator: Independent variables: OEND enrollment rates
key_findings.note: Contradicted by the Results (p. 4) and Table 4 (p. 10), which present 1–100 and more than 100 as the main categories and 75 and 150 as alternative cut points in sensitivity analyses; see the reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Analysis: annual counts by community of residence modelled as rates in a log-linear Poisson model with the census population as offset and the community covariates in the model; implementation coded per community-year; a linear time variable for year; a first-order autoregressive covariance structure for the repeated measures, chosen with quasi-likelihood information criteria; all tests at α 0.05; SAS 9.3.
key_findings.locator: Covariates, 4th paragraph and Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 3); end of Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: No community indicators (fixed effects), community-specific trends, level or slope change terms, handling of overdispersion or further detail of the estimation method are described.

key_findings.finding: Relative model for deaths (implementation below or above each year's median enrolment rate) against no implementation: below the median, crude 0.85, adjusted 0.71 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.90), p<0.01; above the median, crude 1.00, adjusted 0.78 (0.60 to 1.01), p=0.06. The authors note that in this model there did not seem to be a dose relation.
key_findings.locator: Table 4, relative model; Results › Adjusted models: OEND implementation and fatal overdose rates (p. 4); Discussion › Strengths and limitations of the study, 1st paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Not in the print summary or the abstract, which give only the absolute model.

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity and control analyses, reported without numbers: with cut points of 75 and 150 enrolments per 100 000, rate ratios for deaths and for acute care were similar; with the ratio of opioid-overdose deaths to cancer deaths as outcome, associations were statistically significant in a similar pattern to the main models; with the ratio of opioid-related acute care to non-fatal motor-vehicle injury care as outcome, there was no association.
key_findings.locator: Results › both Adjusted models subsections and Control models; Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph (pp. 3–4)
key_findings.note: The control-model estimates are in supplementary tables 6 (cancer deaths) and 7 (motor-vehicle injuries), which are not among the files and were not read; no table, printed or supplementary, is cited for the 75 and 150 cut-point analyses (p. 4; supplementary list, p. 1).

key_findings.finding: Of the rescue attempts with each item recorded: the person who overdosed was a friend in 69% (216/313), a partner or family member in 16% (49/313) and a stranger in 10% (32/313); 78% (249/317) were in private settings; naloxone was reported successful in 98% (150/153); 911 was called or emergency personnel were present in 33% (106/326); rescue breathing was given in 38% (123/327); and the rescuer stayed until the person was alert or help arrived in 89% (287/321). In the three attempts without success, the person received emergency care and survived (p. 4).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Bystanders' reports of rescues of a person who was unresponsive with signs of respiratory depression, as defined for the staff (p. 3); success was recorded for only 153 of the 327 attempts. The table also gives the number of naloxone doses used. Editors' calculation: 249/317 is 78.55% (printed 78%).

key_findings.finding: Enrolees in the 19 communities: 2007 reported active substance use, treatment or recovery and 905 did not; mean age 38.1 years (SD 12.1); 44.4% (1274/2870) female or male-to-female transgender. Those reporting use, treatment or recovery reported at enrolment detox in the past year 47.3% (950/2007), incarceration in the past year 27.1% (460/1695) and a lifetime history of overdose 54.0% (976/1808). Overdose ever witnessed, as reported at enrolment: 73.6% (2036/2767) of all enrolees; at least one rescue reported: 7.3% (212/2912).
key_findings.locator: Table 2

key_findings.finding: The 19 communities: 2005 population 2 055 086 (median 87 392, range 30 236 to 609 690), about 30% of the state population and almost half of Massachusetts' fatal opioid overdoses and acute-care uses for non-fatal opioid overdose; 16.4% below the poverty level; in 2009, 630.0 inpatient detoxification, 161.8 methadone maintenance and 41.5 state-funded buprenorphine maintenance treatment events per 100 000 people.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 7); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Figure 1 plots unadjusted opioid-overdose death rates by stratum and year without printing values. Editors' reading (approximate; axis in deaths per 100 000 population): the no-enrolment series runs from about 10 to 14 in 2002–06 and ends in 2007 at about 19, its highest point; the low-enrolment series is about 14 (2006), 11 (2007), 14 (2008) and 16 (2009), and the high-enrolment series about 12.5 (2007), 8.5 (2008) and 14.5 (2009).
key_findings.locator: Figure 1
key_findings.note: Read from the figure rendered at 300 dpi; values approximate. Implementing community-years are not systematically below the no-implementation years of 2002–06; the clearest contrast is with the 2007 no-implementation value, which by the counts on p. 4 comes from the five communities not yet implementing.

key_findings.finding: Figure 2 plots unadjusted acute-care rates by stratum and year without printing values. Editors' reading (approximate; axis in acute-care uses per 100 000 population): the no-enrolment series lies between about 83 and 96 in 2002–07; the low-enrolment series falls from about 90 (2006) to 78 (2007) and rises to about 96 (2009); the high-enrolment series is about 90 (2007), 86 (2008) and 98 (2009).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2
key_findings.note: Read from the figure rendered at 300 dpi; values approximate.

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that OEND may both reduce acute-care use, by preventing overdoses, and increase it, by encouraging bystanders to call emergency services as the curriculum teaches, and that this balance may explain why no association was found for acute care.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Interpretation
key_findings.note: Emergency services were called or present in 33% (106/326) of reported rescue attempts (Table 3, p. 9); the explanation is not tested.

key_findings.finding: The person who overdosed was the reporting enrolee themself in 5% of reported rescue attempts (16 of 313; enrolees who use drugs 16 of 276, others 0 of 37), besides a friend, a partner or family member, or a stranger.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, row Self

key_findings.finding: Among enrolees reporting use, treatment or recovery and a history of overdose, 60.0% (503 of 838) reported receiving naloxone at their last overdose, as they reported at enrolment.
key_findings.locator: Table 2

reporting_issues.issue: The full article prints no counts of deaths or acute-care events (overall, by year or by stratum) and no number of community-years per stratum; rates appear only as unadjusted plots without values (Figures 1 and 2). The covariate coefficients (supplementary tables 4a, 4b, 5a and 5b) and the control models (supplementary tables 6 and 7) are online supplementary material, listed on p. 1 with a map of the 19 communities, and are not among the files; no table, printed or supplementary, is cited for the 75 and 150 cut-point analyses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absolute effects (deaths or events averted) cannot be derived; the sensitivity and control analyses can be cited only as the authors' verbal summary; which covariates move the estimates cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The print summary describes acute-care use as not differing significantly in communities with low versus high implementation, and the article's Discussion (p. 4) says only that it did not differ significantly in communities with low or high implementation, but the Results and Table 5 compare each stratum with community-years without implementation (adjusted rate ratios 0.93 and 0.92 in the absolute model, 0.90 and 1.00 in the relative model; all intervals include 1); no direct low-versus-high test is reported. Emergency-department visits and admissions are analysed as one combined outcome.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the acute-care result as rate ratios against no implementation, not as a low-versus-high comparison; the summary's separate mention of emergency visits and admissions does not correspond to separate analyses.

reporting_issues.issue: The dose-related impact stated in the Results, the Interpretation and the print summary holds only in the absolute model, whose two strata have overlapping intervals (0.57 to 0.91 and 0.39 to 0.76) and no test for trend; in the relative model the above-median stratum had the weaker, non-significant association (0.78, 0.60 to 1.01, p=0.06, against 0.71 below the median), and the authors' own strengths-and-limitations paragraph says there did not seem to be a dose relation in that model.
reporting_issues.consequence: The data do not establish a gradient: point estimates fall with more enrolment in the absolute model (0.73 to 0.54, overlapping intervals, no trend test) but not in the relative model (0.71 below, 0.78 above the median); claims should not state a dose–response.

reporting_issues.issue: The rate ratios in the column headed only Rate ratio (0.93 and 0.82 in the absolute model, 0.85 and 1.00 in the relative model; read as crude because the adjusted column beside it carries the adjustment footnote and the text calls Figures 1 and 2 unadjusted rates, though no part of the article labels the column) are much closer to 1 than the adjusted ones and are printed without intervals; the article does not say which covariates moved the estimates (the coefficients are in supplementary tables 4a and 4b, not read).
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the association depends on the adjustment set, which includes one linear time term; claims should give the crude and adjusted ratios together and say that the article labels the first only as a rate ratio.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the models used enrolment cut points of 0, 1–75 and >75 and sensitivity analyses 0, 1–150 and >150, while the same paragraph defines the absolute model as 1–100 and >100, and the Results and Table 4 present 100 as the main cut point and 75 and 150 as sensitivity analyses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which categorization was planned first cannot be told; with the sensitivity estimates unreported, the reported categories may have been chosen after the results were seen.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction describes communities with low or no implementation as concurrent controls, and the abstract and print summary compare implementing community-years with communities with no implementation, but all 19 communities had implementation in 2008–09; the community-years without implementation are 2002–05 and the 12 and 5 communities not yet implementing in 2006 and 2007.
reporting_issues.consequence: For 2008–09 the comparison is with earlier years through one linear time term, not with concurrent communities without the programme; the design is closer to a staggered before–after comparison than to a controlled interrupted time series.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results give naloxone success as 98% (150/153) of rescue attempts without saying that the item was recorded for only 153 of the 327 attempts; and the authors' explanation of the null acute-care result, that bystanders are encouraged to call emergency services, sits beside a table in which emergency services were called or present in 33% (106/326) of attempts (26%, 75/285, among those reporting use, treatment or recovery).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 98% applies to fewer than half of the attempts and is bystander-reported; the explanation of the acute-care result is untested, and the study's own rescue data show emergency services involved in a third of attempts.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 and Figure 1 describe the death outcome as unintentional opioid-related overdose deaths, but the definition includes undetermined-intent poisonings (Y10–Y14).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the label understates the definition; claims should say unintentional or undetermined intent.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 heads its first column All enrollees (n=327) although 327 is the number of rescue attempts, reported by 212 enrolees (p. 4); three percentages do not match their fractions on rounding, by the editors' calculation: private settings 249/317 is 78.55%, printed 78%; public 68/317 is 21.45%, printed 22%; and in the column of enrolees reporting use, treatment or recovery, 129/272 is 47.43%, printed 48%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; no effect on the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: Statements of the one-page print summary (file Heroin/Walley_2013_NaloxoneDistributionDeaths.pdf, printed p. 13) that the full article qualifies: the reduction in death rates where OEND was implemented is relative to community-years, mostly earlier ones, and is much weaker before adjustment (rate ratios 0.93 and 0.82 in the unlabelled first column, printed without intervals); the dose-related impact holds in the absolute model only (the relative model, absent from the summary, shows none); acute care was compared with no implementation, not low with high, and as one combined outcome; misclassification unlikely to be directional refers in the article to discharge codes, not deaths; the 327 rescues are rescue attempts, with success recorded for 153; and the 'year' in the summary's adjustment footnote is one linear time term.
reporting_issues.page: Print summary p. 13; full article pp. 3–5, 10–11 of 13
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should cite the full article; the summary's wording is not a sufficient basis for any claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The data sharing statement says no additional data are available (p. 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: The death and event counts the article does not print are not offered by the authors.

reporting_issues.issue: The standing order for naloxone is attributed to the programme's medical director on p. 2 but described as issued by the health department on p. 5 (Implications, 2nd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Who issued the standing order is stated two ways.

disagreements.first_pass: Community-level (ecological) interrupted time series analysis, as the authors call it, of yearly rates of opioid-related overdose death and acute-care use in 19 Massachusetts cities and towns from 2002 to 2009, against the cumulative rate of enrolment in state-supported overdose education and nasal naloxone distribution (OEND) programmes, which trained potential bystanders from 2006. Community-years with no implementation are the reference; community-years with 1–100 and with more than 100 cumulative enrolments per 100,000 population are the exposure strata. Poisson regression adjusted for community demographics, treatment and doctor-shopping rates, and year. Filed as retrospective-cohort, the nearest design in the schema (the units are communities followed over years), and appraised with ROBINS-I as a programme evaluation, as the round brief directs. Written from the one-page print summary only (BMJ print edition, 9 February 2013, p. 13), which states that it summarizes a paper published on bmj.com; the full article (methods, model, death definitions and counts, acute-care estimates, sensitivity analyses) was not in the file and was not read, so the card is checked only for what the summary shows.

disagreements.resolution: Changed after reading Walley_2013_FullArticle.pdf, pp. 2–4 of 13 (Methods; Independent variables; Covariates; Statistical analysis; Results, 4th paragraph) and Table 4 (p. 10): design described from the full article; filing as retrospective-cohort with ROBINS-I kept.

design_detail: Letter (Correspondence, The Lancet 379:117) by six authors criticizing Marshall et al. (2011), the before–after study of overdose deaths near Vancouver's supervised injection facility (Insite). Data of its own: one figure of annual counts of overdose deaths, plotted without printed values, for all of British Columbia and for Vancouver (1997–2007) and for the Downtown Eastside (2001–2005), with one cited source, a British Columbia coroners' publication on illicit drug deaths (counts, not rates; areas not defined; no statistical test). The rest is argument from the study team's own earlier papers and an unnamed personal communication. An extended analysis is said to be online (a web document; not read).
can_establish: Which alternative explanations for the fall in overdose deaths near Insite were put in print within a year of publication (the choice of 2001 as start year, a fall in heroin supply, intensified policing, deaths not related to injection), and what evidence was offered for each.
cannot_establish: That policing or heroin supply, rather than the facility, explains the fall near Insite: the letter gives counts for larger areas than the study's, no rates, no reanalysis of the study's own area and comparison, and rests its central policing claim on a personal communication.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter). The figure plots public annual counts for British Columbia, Vancouver and the Downtown Eastside; the letter defines neither the areas nor the deaths counted.
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the letter's authors. According to the reply, the Downtown Eastside series covers the whole local health area of about 400 city blocks, which contains the study's 41 blocks within 500 m (Marshall et al., 2012, p. 118); the policing figures rest on an unnamed personal communication.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no individual data). The figure's single cited source is a British Columbia coroners' publication on illicit drug deaths, 1997–2007 (ref. 2); the letter does not say where the Downtown Eastside series comes from or which deaths it counts (see reporting issues).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, beyond the statement that 41% of British Columbia's overdose deaths are not injection-related (Milloy et al., 2010, as cited).

comparison.controls: Calls Vancouver and the Downtown Eastside the study's control areas (p. 117). By the companion card (sc_marshall_2011), the study compared the area within 500 m of the facility with the rest of the city, and the Downtown Eastside contains the study area.

outcomes.instruments: Annual counts of overdose deaths from public coroners' statistics (figure).
outcomes.operationalization: Overdose deaths as counted in the cited publication; not defined in the letter.

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics. The figure prints no values; editors' reading of the plotted lines at 300 dpi (approximate, about ±2 deaths): Vancouver about 141 deaths in 1997 and 189 in 1998, then about 89 in 2001, 50 in 2002, 49 in 2003, 67 in 2004 and 57 in 2005; Downtown Eastside about 31, 27, 29, 32 and 37 in 2001–2005; British Columbia about 243, 170, 190, 196 and 218 in 2001–2005. Second-hand figures: in a Vancouver cohort, non-fatal overdose in the previous 12 months 21% (1997), 12% (beginning of 2001), 5% (end of 2001) and 6% (2004) (Kerr et al., 2007, as cited); discarded needles 46% fewer in policed areas (Wood et al., 2004, as cited); 48–66 police added in 2003 in 12 city blocks (personal communication); 41% of British Columbia's overdose deaths not injection-related (Milloy et al., 2010, as cited).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only evidence against the study's conclusion is presented; the study's block-level and distance-gradient sensitivity analyses (companion card sc_marshall_2011) are not addressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Counts of overdose deaths for areas larger than the study's: from 2002 to 2005 they rose in the Downtown Eastside series (about 27 to 37) and, with a peak in 2004, in Vancouver (about 50 to 57; editors' reading), while the Vancouver count for 2005 was still lower than for 2001 (about 57 against 89). Three arguments come from the study team's earlier papers (a decline in heroin supply and in non-fatal overdose around 2001; police displacement of the drug market in 2003) and one from a personal communication.
interpretation_gap.claimed: That the study "contains serious errors"; that its decline depends on the anomalous year 2001; that its statements of no change in drug supply or policing are contradicted by its authors' earlier work; that the added policing around Insite is "clearly the most likely cause" of any real reduction nearby; and that the authors should have reported the share of non-injection deaths near Insite (p. 117). Gaps: (1) counts, not rates, so the population rise of 14% near the facility that the study reported is ignored (companion card sc_marshall_2011, from Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 1435–1436); (2) the areas plotted are larger than the study's and, for the Downtown Eastside, contain it, so the figure does not test the study's comparison of 500 m with the rest of the city; (3) the letter attributes to the study a claim that all overdose deaths in Vancouver declined, whereas the study reported a 35% fall within 500 m and a non-significant 9% fall elsewhere (companion card, p. 1433); (4) the policing conclusion rests on a personal communication and on needle counts, not on deaths in the policed blocks; (5) the non-fatal overdose and needle figures are second-hand. A headline version, that the study was shown to be wrong, would overstate the letter: it raises plausible confounders without testing them.

timeline.event: Insite opens on 21 September 2003 (p. 117); the letter says 48–66 police were added that year in 12 city blocks around it (personal communication).
Wood et al. (CMAJ), displacement of Vancouver's public drug market in response to a police crackdown, cited for discarded needle counts 46% lower in policed areas. Not read.
Kerr et al. (Drug Alcohol Depend), predictors of non-fatal overdose in a Vancouver cohort, cited for the fall from 21% (1997) to 5% (end of 2001). Not read.
Marshall et al.: the study criticized (appraised on its own card).

The authors' reply in the same issue: different area, death definition and measure (rates); daily heroin use stable; police operation ended within weeks of opening; 36% reduction among deaths with signs of injection.

replication.where_it_stands: The letter and the reply leave three facts in dispute: how long the added policing lasted (a personal communication against a police evaluation report whose web address names 2004), whether 2001 was an anomalous starting year, and the share of deaths not related to injection. Neither presents a reanalysis of the study's own area and comparison starting in 2002. A later interrupted time-series evaluation of the same facility (Myer & Belisle, 2017) is in the project's harm-reduction list but was not among this reader's files.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest (p. 117).
funding.affiliations_note: As printed: Drug Free Australia (G. Christian, corresponding author); Southern Cross Bioethics Institute (G. Pike); McCrae, Victoria (J. Santamaria, place only); Addiction Medicine Practice, Brisbane (S. Reece); Institute for Behaviour and Health, Rockville, Maryland (R. DuPont); Surrey, British Columbia (C. Mangham, place only). The extended analysis is hosted on the drugfree.org.au website. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the letter.

what_would_settle_it: A reanalysis of the study's coroner records as rates in the same 500 m area and comparison area, with the pre-opening period started in 2001 and in 2002, and with policing intensity and drug supply or purity measured over the same years; or an interrupted time series over several years before and after opening with more than one comparison area.

domains.note: No search; the authors chose the data and papers cited.
Uses the study team's earlier papers against it without appraising them; the central policing figure is an unnamed personal communication.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the letter's authors' own studies are cited.
Calls the policing change clearly the most likely cause of any real reduction, without data on deaths in the policed blocks.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the facility's effect (evidence for an effect under-represented)
domains.note: Only evidence against the study's conclusion is presented; its sensitivity analyses are not addressed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The letter names real confounders (start year, supply, policing) but does not test them. It may be cited as the published statement of these objections, with its figure described as counts for larger areas; it is not evidence that the facility had no effect.
