design_detail: Retrospective population-based before–after comparison with a concurrent comparison area (ecological; the authors call it a retrospective population-based study). All deaths in the City of Vancouver from 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2005 that the attending coroner ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses (British Columbia Coroners Service central registry) were geocoded by place of death. Rates per 100,000 person-years used census populations (2001 and 2006, interpolated linearly by dissemination block). The rate within 500 m of North America's first medically supervised safer injecting facility (SIF), a radius described as fixed a priori, was compared before (1 January 2001 to 20 September 2003) and after (21 September 2003 to 31 December 2005) its opening, against the same change in the rest of the city; rate differences were compared with the Breslow-Day test. Sensitivity analyses: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on block-level rate changes (census-based, and with the 2001 population held fixed), a census-tract analysis with an exponential distance model, and methadone-programme participation trends in a random sample of SIF clients (the SEOSI cohort). No adjusted analysis: the authors say area-level characteristics were suppressed by Statistics Canada. Filed as retrospective-cohort, the nearest design in the schema (areas followed over two periods), and appraised with ROBINS-I as a programme evaluation, as the round brief directs.
can_establish: Whether, in Vancouver in 2001–2005, the coroner-recorded fatal overdose rate fell more within 500 m of the SIF after it opened than in the rest of the city, by how much, and how sensitive this is to the population denominators.
cannot_establish: That the SIF caused the fall (no adjustment for other neighbourhood changes; only two periods with no earlier trend; the comparison area's rate was about 33 times lower), whether people who used the SIF were less likely to die (deaths are counted by place of death and not linked to SIF use or residence), or how many deaths were averted city-wide.

sample.recruitment: Registry: all deaths in the City of Vancouver from 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2005 ruled by the attending coroner to be accidental illicit drug overdoses, from the British Columbia Coroners Service central registry; complete case data for the period were obtained only in 2009 because coroners' investigations are lengthy (p. 1430).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Accidental overdose: a death whose proximate and primary medical cause was the self-administration of a psychoactive substance that is illegal or diverted from accepted use, as found by the coroner after an investigation whose file holds demographic data, police reports with witness statements, toxicology and other medical examinations and a summary of circumstances; the authors state the criteria stayed the same throughout (p. 1430).
sample.demographics: 229 of 290 decedents (79.0%) were men; median age at death 40 years (IQR 32–48). Within 500 m, median age at death was 39 (IQR 32–44) before the opening and 44 (36–50) after (p=0.050). Farther away, the share of women rose from 16 of 113 (14%) to 27 of 88 (31%) (p=0.005) and of First Nations decedents from 6 (5%) to 12 (14%) (p=0.040) (Table 1, p. 1431).
sample.attrition: None reported. Where the coroner could not assign a postal code, the postal code of the nearest building was used (p. 1430).
sample.selection_effects: The SIF was opened in the Downtown Eastside because of high overdose mortality in the 1990s (p. 1429), so the intervention area was chosen for high rates, which makes some later fall expected (regression toward the mean). Deaths are attributed to the place of death, not to residence or SIF use. Denominators are census residents (on average about 8,100 before and 8,800 after within 500 m; editors' calculation from person-years), not people who inject drugs.

exposure.measurement: Area and period only: place of death within 500 m of the SIF, the radius within which more than 70% of daily SIF clients in the SEOSI cohort lived, and date of death after the opening on 21 September 2003 (pp. 1429, 1431). No individual measure of SIF use.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: The intervention as described: supervised injection of pre-obtained drugs with sterile syringes, referrals and emergency care including oxygen and naloxone; no deaths recorded inside the facility; about 40% of injections there are heroin, 30% powder cocaine and 5% methamphetamine; 12 injection seats and over 500 supervised injections a day on average, in a neighbourhood with about 5000 people who inject drugs (pp. 1430, 1434).
exposure.polysubstance: Coroner-recorded contributory drugs: within 500 m, opioids in 27 of 56 deaths before and 18 of 33 after, cocaine in 34 and 20, alcohol in 6 and 3, more than one drug in 18 and 12; no significant change in the drugs implicated in either area (Table 1, p. 1431). About a third of deaths involved more than one drug.

comparison.controls: The rest of the City of Vancouver (deaths more than 500 m from the SIF) over the same two periods, and within the 500 m area the period before against the period after opening.
comparison.matching: None; no adjustment, because area-level characteristics were suppressed at the needed geographic level (p. 1435).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Area-level changes not measured: drug supply and purity (the authors report no evidence of change), supportive housing (population within 500 m rose 14% from 2001 to 2005, which the authors link to more supportive housing), other services and policing (no known change). Methadone participation was compared only within a sample of SIF clients, not in the wider population of people who inject drugs.

outcomes.instruments: Coroner-ruled accidental illicit drug overdose deaths, geocoded from six-digit postal codes; rates per 100,000 person-years from linearly interpolated census populations; rate differences and percentage reductions with 95% CIs; Breslow-Day test for interaction; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on block-level changes; exponential regression of census-tract rate differences on distance, weighted by overdose counts; Cochran-Armitage test for trends in methadone participation (pp. 1430–1432).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors call the coroners' registry the best available census of illicit drug overdose deaths in the province, and cite evidence that urban postal codes locate a place to within about one side of a city block (p. 1430).
outcomes.operationalization: Effect measured as the fall in the death rate within 500 m after opening, set against the change in the rest of the city.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome (overdose death rate) analysed several ways: rate differences in two areas, an interaction test, two block-level Wilcoxon tests and a census-tract model; the key p values lie between 0.039 and 0.049.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Coroners' rulings were made independently of the study; not otherwise applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Within 500 m: 56 deaths over 22,066 person-years before opening (253.8 per 100,000; 95% CI 187.3–320.3) and 33 over 19,991 after (165.1; 108.8–221.4); rate difference 88.7 (1.6–175.8), p=0.048; reduction 35.0% (0.0%–57.7%). Rest of the city: 113 over 1,479,792 person-years (7.6; 6.2–9.0) and 88 over 1,271,246 (6.9; 5.5–8.4); rate difference 0.7 (−1.3 to 2.7), p=0.490; reduction 9.3% (−19.8% to 31.4%). Breslow-Day test for interaction p=0.049 (Table 2, p. 1433). Block level: 15 of 22 blocks with recorded deaths showed decreases; Wilcoxon p=0.039, and p=0.039 with the 2001 population held fixed (pp. 1433–1434). With the population held at its 2001 level in the main comparison, the reduction was 30% and not significant; no interval or p value is given (p. 1435); editors' calculation: rate ratio 0.70 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.08; p about 0.11). Census tracts: RD(x)=0.40+212.4e^(−4.17x), r²=0.58, effect minimal beyond about 500 m and negligible beyond 1 km (p. 1434). Editors' calculations: the periods last 2.72 and 2.28 years, so deaths within 500 m fell from about 20.6 to 14.5 a year (about 30% fewer, or about 6 fewer a year) and elsewhere from about 41.6 to 38.6 a year; the rate ratio after against before is 0.65 within 500 m (95% CI 0.42 to 1.00) and 0.91 elsewhere (0.69 to 1.20), and a test of equal rate ratios gives p about 0.20, while a test of equal rate differences reproduces the printed p=0.049 (about 0.048); all printed rates and intervals reproduce from the counts and person-years.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration. The 500 m radius is described as specified a priori from SEOSI residence data (Summary; Methods, p. 1431), and the contributors' statement says three authors wrote the analytical protocol (p. 1436).
analysis.selective_reporting: The main comparison with the population held fixed (30%, not significant) is reported only in the limitations paragraph, without interval or p value, while the corresponding block-level test is reported with p=0.039 (pp. 1434–1435). Otherwise the planned sensitivity analyses are all reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. The main comparison rests on 56 and 33 deaths; the interval for the percentage reduction runs from 0.0% to 57.7%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Within 500 m of Vancouver's SIF, coroner-recorded overdose deaths fell from 56 in the 2.7 years before it opened to 33 in the 2.3 years after (253.8 to 165.1 per 100,000 person-years; 35% lower, 95% CI 0% to 58%, p=0.048), while the rest of the city changed little (7.6 to 6.9; 9% lower, not significant); the difference between the two areas' absolute falls was of borderline significance (p=0.049), while their relative falls do not differ significantly (rate ratios 0.65 and 0.91, p about 0.20, editors' calculation); with the population held at its 2001 level the fall near the SIF was 30% and not significant (rate ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.08, editors' calculation). Most deaths (201 of 290) occurred farther than 500 m away.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Summary's interpretation says SIFs should be considered where injection drug use is prevalent (p. 1429); the discussion says the findings indicate that such facilities are safe and effective public-health interventions (p. 1434); the research-in-context panel extends effectiveness to other cities internationally (p. 1435). The conclusion and the panel themselves say SIFs should be considered 'for assessment', a qualifier that the Summary and the discussion's first paragraph (which says they should therefore be considered where the burden of overdose is high) both drop (pp. 1429, 1434–1436), and the limitations concede that unmeasured confounding cannot be excluded and urge caution about the ecological fallacy (p. 1435). Gaps: (1) an unadjusted comparison of two periods in one small area, with key p values between 0.039 and 0.049, an interval reaching 0% and an interaction that is significant only for absolute rate differences (on the ratio scale p about 0.20, editors' calculation), supports an association, not an established effect; (2) the absence of evidence of supply, policing or treatment changes is treated as evidence of their absence, and the source cited for stable drug-use patterns and treatment (ref. 44) is titled as a study of changes in Canadian heroin supply coinciding with the Australian heroin shortage; (3) the 14% population growth near the SIF, which lowers the post-opening rate, is attributed to more supportive housing, itself a change that could affect deaths; (4) 'safe' rests on other studies (refs 38–39), not on these data; (5) no individual link between SIF use and survival was examined. A headline version such as 'the injection site cut overdose deaths by 35%' overstates the study: 35% is an unadjusted fall in a small area, about 6 fewer deaths a year (editors' calculation), with an interval reaching zero and a smaller, non-significant fall when the population is held constant.

timeline.event: The SIF opens in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside on 21 September 2003, with police referring people found injecting in public to it (pp. 1429, 1431).
A spike of overdoses from stolen powdered methadone, 15–30 August 2005: 10 overdoses, 4 within 500 m of the SIF (as reported here, p. 1435).

Milloy et al. (PLoS ONE), an estimate of overdose deaths averted by the same facility from the same research group, named by title in the project's harm-reduction list; not cited in this paper and not read.

The authors' search of PubMed and ISI Web of Knowledge to 31 December 2009 finds no peer-reviewed study of the real-world effect of SIFs on overdose mortality; two grey-literature reports (Germany; Sydney) describe reductions, the Sydney one coinciding with a heroin shortage (pp. 1434–1435).
This study, published with a Comment in the same issue (Lancet 377, p. 1385; not among the files, not read).

A published critique (Christian, 2012, The Lancet, doi 10.1016/s0140-6736(12)60054-3) and the authors' reply (Marshall et al., 2012, doi 10.1016/s0140-6736(12)60055-5), named in the project's harm-reduction list; not among this reader's files, not read.
Myer and Belisle, an interrupted time-series evaluation of the impact of the same facility (Journal of Drug Issues), named by title in the project's harm-reduction list; not read.
Kennedy et al. (PLOS Medicine), a cohort study of SIF use and all-cause mortality among people who inject drugs in Vancouver, named by title in the project's heroin list; not read.
Gareipy et al., a systematic review of supervised consumption sites and population-level overdose mortality, 2016–2024, with a published erratum, named in the project's harm-reduction list; not read.

replication.where_it_stands: By the authors' search to December 2009 this was the first peer-reviewed estimate of a SIF's effect on overdose mortality. Its published critique and reply, and later evaluations of the same facility and of supervised consumption sites elsewhere, are named in the project's lists but were not among this reader's files; the status 'not attempted' reflects this paper only and must be revised when they are read. Until then the finding is a single-site, unadjusted before–after association.

funding.funder: Vancouver Coastal Health, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) and the Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research (MSFHR) (Summary, p. 1429). The SIF assessment was originally funded by a contribution from Health Canada; the study is now supported by CIHR and Vancouver Coastal Health; TK holds a CIHR New Investigator Award and an MSFHR Scholar Award; BDLM and MJM hold CIHR Canada Graduate Scholarships, and BDLM an MSFHR Senior Graduate Trainee Award (Acknowledgments, p. 1436). The sponsors had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation or writing (Role of the funding source, p. 1432).
funding.declared_conflicts: JSGM has received educational grants from, serves as an ad hoc adviser to, or speaks at events sponsored by Abbott Laboratories, Agouron Pharmaceuticals, Boehringer Ingelheim Pharmaceuticals, Borean Pharma AS, Bristol-Myers Squibb, DuPont Pharma, Gilead Sciences, GlaxoSmithKline, Hoffmann-La Roche, Immune Response Corporation, Incyte, Janssen-Ortho Inc, Kucera Pharmaceutical Company, Merck Frosst Laboratories, Pfizer Canada, Sanofi Pasteur, Shire Biochem, Tibotec Pharmaceuticals and Trimeris. No other authors declared conflicts (p. 1436).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors at the British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS (with the University of British Columbia; BDLM also Columbia University). The authors' group conducted the facility's scientific evaluation (the SEOSI study used here; refs 18 and 24), whose assessment was originally funded by Health Canada, and wrote most of the earlier evaluation papers cited in the introduction; the introduction notes that the facility continued to be opposed by the federal government. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A controlled interrupted time series covering many years before and after opening, with several comparison neighbourhoods of similar drug-market intensity, adjustment for housing, treatment and supply changes, and individual-level linkage of deaths to residence and SIF use; or a stepped-wedge evaluation across cities that open facilities at different times.

domains.note: Unadjusted; only two periods with no pre-opening trend; the intervention area was chosen for its high mortality (regression toward the mean); concurrent changes near the SIF are argued away rather than measured (supply, policing), measured only among SIF clients (methadone) or acknowledged as growing (supportive housing, population up 14%); the comparison area's rate was about 33 times lower.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: All coroner-ruled accidental illicit drug overdose deaths in the city over the whole period were included, with the 500 m area fixed in advance.

Exposure is place of death within 500 m, a proxy for access: people living near the SIF who died elsewhere fall in the comparison area, and visitors who died near it count as exposed; SIF use is not measured.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: The SIF's capacity was small relative to the population (12 seats; about 5000 people who inject drugs nearby), and co-interventions in the same area (police referrals to the SIF, more supportive housing) are bundled with the opening.

Complete coroner data for the period were obtained in 2009; deaths without a postal code were placed at the nearest building. The methadone subanalysis omits 193 of 1084 SEOSI participants without explanation, but it is not the main analysis.

Deaths are well ascertained by coroners using constant criteria, but the rates depend on interpolated census populations that may not represent the population at risk; with the population held at its 2001 level the main reduction was 30% and not significant.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registered protocol; the fixed-population version of the main comparison is reported only in the discussion without statistics; several analyses give p values just under 0.05, against the a priori radius and the reporting of the other sensitivity analyses.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because the exposure is a public-health facility evaluated by comparing areas and periods (METHODS §5.3). Serious overall because of confounding: an unadjusted two-period comparison in an area chosen for its high mortality, with concurrent changes unmeasured or measured only among SIF clients. Within that, the outcome data are strong (all coroner-ruled deaths, fixed criteria, geocoded) and the radius was fixed in advance. The result is also statistically fragile: the interval for the 35% reduction reaches 0%, the interaction p is 0.049 for rate differences (on the ratio scale the relative falls do not differ significantly, p about 0.20, editors' calculation), and the reduction is not significant when the population is held constant. Citable for: in Vancouver in 2001–2005, coroner-recorded overdose deaths within 500 m of the SIF fell from 56 (253.8 per 100,000 person-years) in the 2.7 years before opening to 33 (165.1) in the 2.3 years after, a 35% reduction (95% CI 0% to 58%), against 9% (not significant) in the rest of the city. Not citable for: a causal effect of SIFs, a city-wide reduction in deaths, lower mortality among people who used the SIF, the size of an effect in other cities, or safety.

key_findings.finding: 290 accidental illicit drug overdose deaths in Vancouver from 1 January 2001 to 31 December 2005 (an average of 1.1 a week); 229 (79.0%) were men; median age 40 years (IQR 32–48); crude rate 10.4 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI 9.2–11.6); no evidence of seasonality was detected (the mean number of overdoses per 3-month period did not vary significantly, F=0.365, p=0.780); deaths concentrated in the Downtown Eastside, with 89 (30.7%) in city blocks within 500 m of the SIF.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 1432, continued on p. 1433); Figure 1 (p. 1432)

key_findings.finding: Within 500 m of the SIF: 56 deaths over 22,066 person-years before opening (253.8 per 100,000; 95% CI 187.3–320.3) and 33 over 19,991 person-years after (165.1; 108.8–221.4); rate difference 88.7 per 100,000 (1.6–175.8), p=0.048; reduction 35.0% (95% CI 0.0%–57.7%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: over periods of 2.72 and 2.28 years, deaths fell from about 20.6 to 14.5 a year; all printed rates and intervals reproduce from the counts and person-years.

key_findings.finding: Rest of the city: 113 deaths over 1,479,792 person-years before (7.6 per 100,000; 6.2–9.0) and 88 over 1,271,246 after (6.9; 5.5–8.4); rate difference 0.7 (−1.3 to 2.7), p=0.490; reduction 9.3% (−19.8% to 31.4%). Breslow-Day test for interaction of rate differences p=0.049, described in the results as indicating that heterogeneity might be present and in the Summary as a significant interaction.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Findings (p. 1429); Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2 (p. 1433)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 2: the rate ratio after against before is 0.65 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.00; p about 0.050) within 500 m and 0.91 (0.69 to 1.20) elsewhere; a test of equal rate ratios gives z about 1.27, p about 0.20. The printed p=0.049 matches a test of equal rate differences (recomputed p about 0.048), so the interaction is significant only on the absolute scale; because the pre-opening rate near the site was about 33 times that elsewhere, similar relative falls would still give very different absolute falls.

key_findings.finding: Block-level sensitivity analysis: of 22 blocks within 500 m with recorded deaths, 15 (68.2%) showed decreases; Wilcoxon signed-rank test p=0.039, and p=0.039 again with block populations held at the 2001 census level.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 1433, continued on p. 1434); Figure 2 (p. 1433)

key_findings.finding: With the population of the main comparison held at its 2001 level, the reduction within 500 m is 30% and not significant (no interval or p value given); the population of city blocks within 500 m rose 14% between 2001 and 2005, which the authors link to more supportive housing in the neighbourhood.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 1435, continued on p. 1436)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with the population fixed, the rate ratio equals the ratio of deaths per year, about 14.5 against 20.6 (periods of 2.28 and 2.72 years), giving 0.70 (95% CI 0.46 to 1.08; p about 0.11), which matches the authors' 30% and not significant.

key_findings.finding: Census-tract sensitivity analysis: reductions were larger in tracts close to the SIF; the exponential fit RD(x)=0.40+212.4e^(−4.17x), weighted by the number of overdoses, had r²=0.58 and suggested an effect that was minimal beyond about 500 m and negligible beyond 1 km.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Read from a 300-dpi crop of Figure 3 (approximate): only two census tracts lie within 0.5 km of the SIF (rate differences of about 55 and 115 per 100,000), and tracts at about 0.9 and 1.2 km show increases of about 30 per 100,000 (rate differences of about −30 and −28), which the paper does not discuss; the curve's value at zero distance (about 213) lies beyond the data.

key_findings.finding: Methadone check: of 1084 participants in the SEOSI cohort (a random sample of SIF clients), 93 of 398 (23.4%) living within 500 m and 118 of 493 (23.9%) living elsewhere were enrolled in methadone maintenance at baseline (p=0.843), with area of residence and enrolment as participants reported them; trends over three 6-month follow-ups did not vary significantly between the areas (Cochran-Armitage p=0.833).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, paragraph beginning Finally, we recognised (p. 1432); Results, 5th paragraph (p. 1434)
key_findings.note: 398 + 493 = 891; how the other 193 participants were handled is not stated (editors' arithmetic). The check concerns SIF clients, not all people who inject drugs in the city.

key_findings.finding: Decedents by area and period: within 500 m, median age at death 39 (IQR 32–44) before and 44 (36–50) after (p=0.050); farther away, women 16 of 113 (14%) before and 27 of 88 (31%) after (p=0.005), First Nations decedents 6 (5%) and 12 (14%) (p=0.040). Contributory drugs did not change significantly: within 500 m, opioids in 27 of 56 deaths before and 18 of 33 after, cocaine in 34 and 20, alcohol in 6 and 3, more than one drug in 18 and 12.
key_findings.locator: Table 1

key_findings.finding: Death data and definitions: files from the British Columbia Coroners Service central registry, each with demographic data, police reports including witness statements, toxicology and other medical examinations and a summary of circumstances; deaths deemed by the attending coroner to be accidental illicit drug overdoses were included (proximate and primary cause the self-administration of an illegal or diverted psychoactive substance, criteria constant over the study); complete data for 2001–2005 were obtained in 2009; place of death geocoded from six-digit postal codes, using the nearest building when no code was assigned.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedures, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The 500 m radius: SEOSI data showed that over 70% of daily SIF clients lived within four blocks (500 m) of the facility, so the authors defined the immediate vicinity as all dissemination blocks with a centroid within 500 m, specified a priori.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Methods (p. 1429); Methods › Statistical analysis, paragraph beginning 'To identify the set of city blocks' (4th paragraph, p. 1431)

key_findings.finding: Concurrent changes as the authors assess them: no evidence of significant changes in drug supply or purity; data from a neighbourhood cohort are said to suggest largely constant drug-use patterns (the share of people who inject drugs reporting daily heroin injecting 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting 17% and 15%); rates of methadone and other addiction treatment use are said to have remained stable (both from ref. 44); no known change in policing policy; one spike of deaths from stolen powdered methadone (10 overdoses between 15 and 30 August 2005, 4 within 500 m), after the opening; adjusted analyses were impossible because area characteristics were suppressed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 1434); 6th paragraph (p. 1435)

key_findings.finding: The facility: about 65 SIFs exist worldwide; at Vancouver's, people inject pre-obtained drugs under supervision, with sterile syringes, referrals and emergency care (oxygen, naloxone), and no deaths had been recorded inside it; about 40% of injections are heroin, 30% powder cocaine and 5% methamphetamine; it runs at capacity with 12 injection seats and over 500 supervised injections a day in a neighbourhood with about 5000 people who inject drugs; police referred people injecting in public to it.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (pp. 1429–1430); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 1434)

key_findings.finding: Authors' interpretation and limits: the Summary says SIFs should be considered where injection drug use is prevalent; the conclusion and the research-in-context panel say they should be considered for assessment; the authors state that confounding by unmeasured factors cannot be excluded, that the ecological design calls for caution, and that the census method assumes constant risk and may miss people at risk.
key_findings.locator: Summary, Interpretation (p. 1429); Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs and Panel: Research in context (p. 1435); Discussion, 7th paragraph (p. 1436)

reporting_issues.issue: The Summary calls the interaction of rate differences significant (p=0.049), while the results say only that heterogeneity might be present.
reporting_issues.consequence: Borderline; the difference between the two areas should be cited with its p value, not as clearly established, and as a difference in absolute falls: the relative falls do not differ significantly (p about 0.20, editors' calculation; see the note on key_findings[2]).

reporting_issues.issue: The fixed-population version of the main comparison (30% reduction, not significant) appears only in the limitations paragraph, without interval or p value, while the fixed-population block-level test is reported with p=0.039.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statistical significance of the main result depends on the census denominators; claims should say so.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 3's legend says that rate-difference values greater than one indicate a reduction; by the definition given (pre-opening minus post-opening rate), any value greater than zero does.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The methadone comparison reports 398 participants living within 500 m and 493 elsewhere, out of 1084 in the SEOSI cohort. Editors' arithmetic: 891 are compared and 193 are not accounted for.
reporting_issues.consequence: If residence was missing for them, the check may be biased; in any case it concerns SIF clients, not the wider population of people who inject drugs.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 44, cited for stable drug-use patterns and stable methadone and treatment use over 2001–2005, is titled as a study of changes in Canadian heroin supply coinciding with the Australian heroin shortage.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the cited source supports a stable drug market over the study period cannot be checked from this paper; it should be read before a claim repeats that no supply change occurred.

reporting_issues.issue: The Summary's interpretation (SIFs should be considered where injection drug use is prevalent) and the Discussion's first paragraph (they should therefore be considered in settings with a high burden of overdose) omit the qualifier for assessment used in the conclusion and the research-in-context panel.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper makes the recommendation both with and without the qualifier; claims should use the qualified wording of the conclusion.

reporting_issues.issue: In the reference list the item between 47 and 49 is numbered 58 (an HIV-burden paper); it is evidently reference 48, which the text cites with reference 47.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting error; no effect on content.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper cites Wood et al. (2006; its reference 44, p. 1437) twice on p. 1434 for drug use in the cohort staying constant over 2001 to 2005: daily heroin injection 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injection 17% and 15%, and stable methadone use. None of these figures is in Wood et al. (2006), whose data end in December 2004 (pp. 689, 691, 693).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures the study gives for stable drug use over its period cannot be traced to the source it cites; they cannot be used as evidence that drug use did not change.

design_detail: Authors' reply (Correspondence, The Lancet 379:118–119) by the five authors of Marshall et al. (2011), British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS, to the letter by Christian et al. (2012). Mostly argument and citation, with one new sensitivity analysis of the original coroner data: the reduction recalculated among deaths with indirect signs of injection (85% of the 89 deaths within 500 m of the facility). A map adapted from BC Stats shows the study's area inside the Downtown Eastside local health area (LHA 162). The reply occupies p. 118 and its references 3–5 the top of p. 119; the rest of p. 119 is unrelated correspondence.
can_establish: How the study's authors answered the published critique: the differences in area, death definition and measure between the study and the critique's data, their cited evidence on heroin use and policing, and one restricted reanalysis.
cannot_establish: That the fall near the facility was caused by it: the reply adds one unadjusted reanalysis without count, interval or comparison area, does not reanalyse from 2002, and does not address the non-fatal overdose trend the critique cited.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (reply). The restricted reanalysis uses the original study's coroner records: deaths with indirect signs of injection, 85% of the 89 deaths within 500 m (about 76 deaths, editors' calculation; the reply gives no count), with no figures given for the rest of the city.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Reanalysis: records in which injection drug use was indirectly suggested, for example by discarded injection equipment around the person who died; coroners' records do not state whether a death was injection-related (p. 118).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen to answer the critique; the evidence on heroin use comes from the authors' own research group (refs 3–4).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (no new individual data). Injection is inferred indirectly from the scene described in coroners' records (p. 118).

comparison.controls: As in the original study: 41 city blocks whose centroids lie within 500 m of the facility, before and after opening; the reply does not report the rest-of-city comparison for the restricted analysis (p. 118).

outcomes.instruments: Coroner-ruled accidental illicit drug overdose deaths, expressed as mortality rates (p. 118).
outcomes.operationalization: Deaths the coroner deemed caused by an accidental illicit drug overdose; rates rather than counts, to allow for changes in the population at risk (p. 118).

analysis.effect_sizes: Restricted reanalysis: reduction in overdose mortality within 500 m of 36%, slightly greater than the original 35%; no count, rates, confidence interval, p value or comparison-area change is given (p. 118). The original estimate was 35.0% (95% CI 0.0% to 57.7%), per the companion card (sc_marshall_2011, from Marshall et al., 2011, p. 1433).
analysis.selective_reporting: Answers the critique on area, death definition, measure, heroin use, policing and mode of use, but neither reanalyses the period from 2002, which was the critique's start-year argument, nor addresses the non-fatal overdose figures (21% falling to 5% by the end of 2001) that it cited.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Three definitional differences between the study and the critique's data (41 city blocks against about 400; coroner-ruled accidental illicit drug overdoses against, as the reply describes them, all drug-induced deaths; rates against counts); two disputed facts answered by citation (daily heroin use stable 2001–2005; the police crackdown ended within weeks of opening); and one unadjusted reanalysis among deaths with signs of injection (36%, no interval).
interpretation_gap.claimed: That the critique rests on several problematic assumptions; that the facility had a "localised yet significant effect" on overdose mortality; and that such facilities "can and should be" a central component of evidence-based responses where injection-related overdose is common (p. 118). Gaps: (1) the conclusion restates significance without the original estimate's uncertainty (35%, 95% CI 0% to 58%, p=0.048, per the companion card sc_marshall_2011); (2) stable daily heroin use is a different measure from the supply, purity and non-fatal overdose trends the critique raised; (3) the 36% has no interval and no comparison area; (4) the reply describes the critique's data source differently from the critique's own reference; (5) a recommendation for such facilities in general goes beyond a single-site, unadjusted before–after association. A headline version, that the critique was refuted, would overstate the reply: it shows that the critique's figure does not test the study's comparison, not that the alternative explanations are wrong.

timeline.event: Dandurand et al., evaluation of the Vancouver Police Department's city-wide enforcement team initiative (a web report; the reference prints no year, and the year here is taken from its web address), cited for the crackdown having ended within weeks of the facility's opening. Not read.
Marshall et al.: the original study (appraised on its own card).
Christian et al.: the letter this reply answers.

replication.where_it_stands: See sc_christian_2012: the duration of the added policing, the meaning of the 2001 peak and the share of deaths not related to injection remain disputed between the two letters, and neither side published a reanalysis of the study's comparison starting in 2002. Later evaluations of the same facility (for example Myer & Belisle, 2017, an interrupted time series in the project's harm-reduction list) were not among this reader's files.

what_would_settle_it: As for the critique (sc_christian_2012): the study's own records reanalysed as rates in the same areas with the pre-opening period starting in 2001 and in 2002, with intervals and the comparison area reported for every variant, and with policing and drug supply measured over the same years.

domains.note: No search; evidence chosen to answer the critique.
The police evaluation and the heroin-use reports are cited without appraisal; the restricted reanalysis is reported without its uncertainty.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Rests on the authors' own study, their own earlier publications on heroin use (refs 3–4) and a new analysis of their own data.
The conservative-bias argument is framed as probable, but the conclusion and the policy recommendation are stated without the original estimate's uncertainty.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the facility's effect (evidence against an effect under-represented)
domains.note: The critique's start-year argument and its non-fatal overdose trend are not answered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The reply makes valid points about area, death definition and rates, and adds one reanalysis; but it is the authors defending their own study, its reanalysis has no interval or comparison, and two of the critique's arguments go unanswered. Cite it for the authors' answers and for the 36% restricted estimate with its missing uncertainty stated, not as settling the confounding questions.

key_findings.note: The critique itself cites a coroners' publication on illicit drug deaths for its figure (Christian et al., 2012, p. 117, ref. 2).

design_detail: Prospective cohort analysis in VIDUS, a Vancouver cohort of people who inject drugs: 1587 participants recruited from May 1996 to May 2004 through self-referral and street outreach in the Downtown Eastside (DTES), interviewed at baseline and every 6 months. Outcome: a yes/no answer at each follow-up visit to whether the participant had experienced an overdose in the previous 6 months (overdose left undefined, any substance); a lifetime history was recorded at baseline. Analyses: (1) baseline comparison of participants with and without a lifetime non-fatal overdose (Table 1; chi-square and Wilcoxon tests); (2) repeated-measures logistic regression by generalized estimating equations (GEE, exchangeable correlation) relating overdose reports at each of 12,030 observations to self-reported characteristics in the same 6-month window, unadjusted and in a multivariate model containing every variable with p<0.10 (Table 2); (3) annual proportions of participants reporting an overdose, 1997–2004 (Fig. 1). Sensitivity analyses excluding people who died of a fatal overdose, restricted to people with at least two follow-up visits, and restricted to people with no more than two overdose reports are summarized without estimates.
can_establish: How often participants in this Vancouver cohort of people who inject drugs reported a self-defined non-fatal overdose between 1996 and 2004, how the annual proportion changed over those years, and which self-reported characteristics in the same 6-month windows went with reporting an overdose, adjusted for one another.
cannot_establish: That any characteristic caused or prevented overdose (exposure and outcome were reported for the same 6-month window, so their order is unknown, and confounding by correlated behaviours and calendar time is not addressed); why overdose reports fell after 2001 (the study collected no data on heroin supply, availability, price or purity, and says it could not consider purity); or how many overdoses occurred (a yes/no per 6 months counts repeat events once).

sample.recruitment: Community cohort: people who injected drugs, recruited since May 1996 through self-referral and street outreach from Vancouver's Downtown Eastside; interviewer-administered questionnaire and blood sample at baseline and every 6 months; Can$20 per visit; University of British Columbia ethics approval (p. 40).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Eligible: injected illicit drugs at least once in the previous month and lived in the greater Vancouver region. This analysis: all participants enrolled from 1 May 1996 to 30 May 2004; no exclusions are reported (p. 40).
sample.demographics: 1011 men (63.7%) and 576 women (36.3%); median age at baseline 33.4 years (IQR 25.7–40.1) (p. 40). From Table 1 (p. 41; totals are editors' calculation): 427 (26.9%) of Aboriginal ethnicity, 456 (28.7%) HIV-positive, 914 (57.6%) living in the DTES and 528 (33.3%) incarcerated in the 6 months before baseline.
sample.attrition: Not reported. 12,030 observations and a median of 9 follow-up visits (IQR 4–13) (p. 40); the numbers lost to follow-up, who died, who never returned after baseline or who missed visits are not given. A model excluding people who died of a fatal overdose during follow-up is said to be identical (data not shown, p. 41).
sample.selection_effects: Non-random community sample (authors' limitation, p. 43). Enrolment over 8 years means calendar time and time in the study are entangled in the annual proportions, and people who keep attending visits may differ from those who stop or die; people who overdose may be more likely to do both. The 32.7% figure uses all 1587 enrollees as denominator, although the number with any follow-up visit is not reported.

exposure.measurement: Interviewer-administered questionnaire at each visit; all drug-use and other behavioural variables refer to the previous 6 months and are yes/no: heroin, cocaine, morphine and speedball injection; crack smoking; benzodiazepine use; non-injection opiate use; alcohol use of more than four drinks a day; street (public) injecting; requiring help with injecting; binge injecting (periods in which drugs were injected more than usual); homelessness; incarceration; being denied drug treatment; and current methadone treatment, as opposed to illicitly obtained methadone (p. 40). Biological verification of drug use is not reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Frequency and amount were not modelled (yes/no for the previous 6 months), although the Discussion speaks of daily heroin and cocaine injection (p. 41). Routes: injection for heroin, cocaine, morphine and speedball; non-injection opiate use, crack smoking and benzodiazepine use were separate variables. Years of injecting at baseline: median 12 (IQR 5–23) in the lifetime-overdose column of Table 1 and 7 (2–16) in the other (p. 41).
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the design: all substances entered together in one model, with speedball injection (heroin with cocaine) alongside heroin and cocaine injection; the outcome covers overdose on any substance, and participants were not asked which drug was involved.

comparison.controls: Within the cohort: observations without an overdose report (the GEE compares visits within and between participants, Table 2); at baseline, participants without a lifetime overdose (Table 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric conditions (including depression and suicidal intent), whether overdoses were intentional, tolerance, the drugs involved in each event, and drug purity and supply (stated limitation, p. 44). HIV status, Aboriginal ethnicity and DTES residence were compared only at baseline and not entered in the GEE; calendar time was not modelled although the annual proportion fell from about 21% to about 6%.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Everyone injected drugs; each comparison is between observations with and without a given behaviour within a cohort where several drugs are commonly used together.

outcomes.instruments: One yes/no question at each follow-up visit: whether the participant had experienced an overdose in the past 6 months. No definition was given to participants, so any substance and any event they called an overdose counted; the question is said to have been piloted successfully during questionnaire development, without details (p. 40).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not validated against ambulance, emergency-department or hospital records; the authors acknowledge subjectivity, recall bias and the absence of a hard diagnosis (p. 44).
outcomes.operationalization: Non-fatal overdose = the participant's own yes for the previous 6 months. The 985 reports are visits with a yes, not overdose events. The annual rate is the proportion of participants followed at visits in that year who reported an overdose (p. 40); its denominators, and the handling of people seen twice in a year, are not given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One outcome tested against 18 candidate variables in the GEE (Table 2) and 7 baseline characteristics (Table 1); 25 counts these associations. With 12,030 observations, several adjusted odds ratios close to 1 reach p<0.05: age 0.99 per year (p=0.046), incarceration 1.14 (p=0.027), speedball injection 1.15 (p=0.047), non-injection opiate use 1.16 (p=0.014).

analysis.effect_sizes: GEE odds ratios with 95% CIs, adjusted (Table 2, p. 42): heroin injection 2.67 (2.30–3.10); cocaine injection 2.02 (1.76–2.31); benzodiazepine use 2.00 (1.77–2.26); requiring help injecting 1.58 (1.39–1.79); binge drug use 1.52 (1.36–1.70); denied treatment 1.46 (1.27–1.69); homelessness 1.38 (1.18–1.61); alcohol use 1.32 (1.09–1.60); public injecting 1.22 (1.06–1.41); non-injection opiate use 1.16 (1.03–1.31); speedball injection 1.15 (1.00–1.32); incarceration 1.14 (1.01–1.28); current methadone treatment 0.51 (0.44–0.59); age 0.99 per year older (0.98–0.99); not significant after adjustment: female sex 1.11 (0.96–1.28), morphine injection 1.01 (0.84–1.22). Unadjusted odds ratios were larger for most drug variables (heroin 4.45, cocaine 3.43, speedball 2.57, morphine 1.84). Baseline lifetime overdose (Table 1, p. 41): years injecting 1.04 per year (1.03–1.05), female sex 1.38 (1.12–1.69), incarceration 1.24 (1.00–1.55), HIV-positive 1.24 (0.99–1.55). No absolute risks by exposure are reported. Editors' calculation: 985 reports among 12,030 observations is about 8% of observations, so the odds ratios somewhat exceed the corresponding risk ratios.
analysis.covariates: Multivariate GEE with every variable significant at p<0.10 in bivariate GEE (a rule described as defined a priori): age, sex, homelessness, incarceration, heroin, cocaine, speedball and morphine injection, benzodiazepine use, non-injection opiate use, binge use, alcohol, requiring help injecting, public injecting, methadone and denied treatment; years injecting (p=0.516) and crack smoking (p=0.887) were not entered (p. 40; Table 2, p. 42). Calendar time, HIV status and ethnicity were not in the model.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The model-building rule is described as defined a priori (p. 40); there is no registration or published protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: The three sensitivity analyses are summarized without estimates (data not shown; details from the corresponding author, p. 41). The abstract, text and table give different values for some estimates and omit different variables (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not reported; with 12,030 observations precision is high for common behaviours, and odds ratios of 1.14–1.16 reach significance.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In a non-random Vancouver cohort of 1587 people who inject drugs followed from 1996 to 2004, 519 (32.7%) reported at least one self-defined overdose in a 6-month window during follow-up (985 reports over 12,030 observations). The annual proportion reporting one fell from about 21% (1997) to about 6% (2004), with the largest step between the 2001 (about 12%) and 2002 (about 5%) values. Within the same 6-month windows, overdose reports went with heroin injection (AOR 2.67), cocaine injection (2.02), benzodiazepine use (2.00), requiring help injecting (1.58) and several weaker factors, and less often with current methadone treatment (0.51); for age, Table 2 gives 0.99 per year older while the abstract and text describe younger age the other way, so the direction of the age result is unsettled.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports younger age as protective (p. 39), the reverse of Table 2 (p. 42). The summary states “Participation in methadone maintenance therapy had a strong protective effect against overdose” (p. 44), a causal reading the limitations disclaim, since temporal order could not be ascertained (p. 44). The Discussion's statement that about a third remained susceptible over several years and that the proportion may not change greatly with time (pp. 41–42) compares a cumulative proportion over up to 8 years with 12-month proportions from cross-sectional studies, and sits beside the authors' own fall from about 21% to 6% (Fig. 1). The decline is attributed tentatively to heroin supply, “global reductions in heroin supply may have played a role”, citing Wood et al. (2006), and to methadone expansion (p. 42), although the study collected no supply, availability, price or purity data and says it could not consider purity (p. 44). The discussion of morphine (pp. 42–43) explains an association that disappeared after adjustment (AOR 1.01).

timeline.event: Bennett & Higgins, accidental overdose among people who inject drugs in Dorset, UK (Addiction 94:1179–1189); cited with Warner-Smith et al. (2002) for about 30% reporting a non-fatal overdose in the previous 12 months; not appraised here
Warner-Smith, Darke & Day, morbidity associated with non-fatal heroin overdose (Addiction 97:963–967); cited for the same figure; not appraised here

Fischer et al., determinants of overdose among people who use illicit opioids in five Canadian cities (CMAJ 171:235–239); cited for 17% reporting a non-fatal overdose in the previous 6 months and for the association with homelessness; not appraised here

Wood, Stoltz, Li, Montaner & Kerr, changes in Canadian heroin supply coinciding with the Australian heroin shortage (Addiction 101:689–695); cited as reporting a reduction in heroin-related overdoses in the same period and as the basis for the heroin-supply explanation of the post-2001 decline; not among the files read

replication.where_it_stands: The paper describes its associations with opiates, benzodiazepines, alcohol, homelessness and methadone as consistent with earlier studies elsewhere (pp. 42–43); none has been appraised for this card. For the timing and cause of the post-2001 decline it relies on Wood et al. (2006), not on its own data; that paper was not among the files read.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health (R01 DA011591-04A1) and Canadian Institutes of Health Research (MOP-67262), described as further support (Acknowledgments, p. 44).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS (St. Paul's Hospital), the University of British Columbia Department of Medicine and Vancouver Coastal Health (p. 39). The Discussion calls for structural interventions and further investigation of naloxone distribution, notes that people who need help injecting are excluded from supervision in the newly opened supervised injection facility (p. 43), and cites the authors' own methodology for evaluating that facility (Wood et al., 2004a). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: For the predictors: a cohort in which overdoses are verified against ambulance, emergency-department and coroner records and exposures are recorded before each event (or a case-crossover design), with calendar time modelled. For the post-2001 decline: yearly series of heroin purity, price and seizures in Vancouver set against verified overdose counts and methadone enrolment over the same years.

domains.note: Adjustment by a data-driven rule (all variables with p<0.10); correlated drug behaviours adjusted for one another (speedball with heroin and cocaine), so each odds ratio is conditional on the others; no adjustment for calendar time although the outcome fell from about 21% to about 6%; HIV status and ethnicity not in the model; reverse causation (an overdose leading to treatment entry, refusal of treatment or homelessness) cannot be excluded within a shared 6-month window.
Self-reported yes/no behaviours for the previous 6 months, interviewer-administered; no biological verification; several items (requiring help injecting, public injecting) not defined.
Self-referral and street-outreach cohort; continued attendance may depend on drug use and overdose (death, incarceration, moving away).

Methadone provision expanded in British Columbia during follow-up and a supervised injection facility opened (pp. 42–43); such changes alter overdose risk over time but enter the model only through the methadone variable.
Loss to follow-up, deaths and missed visits are not reported; only a sensitivity analysis excluding fatal-overdose decedents, with no data shown.

Undefined, unverified self-reported overdose over 6 months, collected in the same interview as the exposures; repeat events collapse to one yes; what counts as an overdose may differ between people who mainly use opioids, stimulants or sedatives.
No registered protocol; sensitivity analyses not shown; values differ between abstract, text and table, and the abstract reverses the direction for age.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is used for the associations between self-reported characteristics and non-fatal overdose in a prospective cohort. High risk of bias overall from the outcome measure (undefined and unverified self-report, collected with the exposures) and from confounding (data-driven adjustment, correlated behaviours, no calendar-time term, unknown temporal order). Within that, the cohort is large (1587 people, 12,030 observations), the GEE accounts for repeated visits, and the strongest associations (heroin and cocaine injection, benzodiazepines, requiring help injecting) are large and, as summarized, survive the sensitivity analyses. Citable for: the share of this cohort reporting a self-defined non-fatal overdose (519 of 1587 during follow-up; annual proportions from about 21% in 1997 to about 6% in 2004) and the direction and size of the associations, as associations. Not citable for: causal effects such as methadone being protective; the direction for age stated in the abstract; or the cause of the post-2001 decline, including any claim about heroin availability or purity, which the study did not measure.

key_findings.finding: 1587 participants were enrolled between 1 May 1996 and 30 May 2004: 1011 men (63.7%) and 576 women (36.3%), median age at baseline 33.4 years (IQR 25.7–40.1). They contributed 12,030 observations, with a median of 9 follow-up visits (IQR 4–13).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: During follow-up, non-fatal overdose was the participant's yes to whether they had experienced an overdose in the past 6 months; the authors call this a broad definition, chosen because polysubstance injection is the norm locally and they were interested in overdoses involving various substances, and say it was piloted successfully during questionnaire development. They say this self-definition may introduce an element of subjectivity, and that the definitions used in previous studies also introduce limitations related to recall bias and do not provide a hard diagnosis of overdose.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 2nd paragraph (p. 40); Discussion, 8th paragraph (begins p. 43, continues on p. 44)

key_findings.finding: During follow-up, 519 of the 1587 participants (32.7%) reported a non-fatal overdose, in 985 reports; the median number of non-fatal overdoses during follow-up was 1.0 (IQR 1–2). Enrolment ran from May 1996 to May 2004 with semiannual visits; the end of follow-up is not stated.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 39); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 40)
key_findings.note: The 32.7% is a cumulative proportion over follow-up of variable length, with all 1587 enrollees as denominator; it is not an annual or 6-month rate. The median of 1 (IQR 1–2) can only refer to the 519 who reported any. Given the yes/no question, the 985 are visits at which an overdose in the previous 6 months was reported. Editors' calculation: 985 of 12,030 observations is 8.2%.

key_findings.finding: At baseline, 750 participants (47%) are reported in the abstract and text as ever having had a non-fatal overdose; Table 1, however, labels its columns non-fatal overdose n=837 and no overdose n=750.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 39); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 40); Table 1 column headings (p. 41)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 837 of 1587 is 52.7%. Table 1's percentages, odds ratios and the directions stated in the text fit the printed headings (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The proportion of participants reporting a non-fatal overdose fell from 21% in 1997 to 6% in 2004; the authors describe the largest decline as occurring during 2001, from 12% to 5%.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Approximate values read from Fig. 1 by pixel measurement on a 300-dpi crop (not printed values): 1997 about 21%, 1998 about 20%, 1999 about 14%, 2000 about 12.5%, 2001 about 12%, 2002 about 5%, 2003 about 7%, 2004 about 6%. The fall from about 12% to about 5% lies between the points labelled 2001 and 2002; how a year's proportion was computed (calendar year of the visit, with a 6-month recall window that can reach into the previous year) and its denominator are not stated.

key_findings.finding: The authors interpret the decline as consistent with other reports of a reduction in heroin-related overdoses during this period (Wood et al., 2006) and suggest that “global reductions in heroin supply may have played a role”; they add that the expansion of methadone treatment in British Columbia from 1995 to 2004 (Anderson & Warren, 2004) may also be involved. The study recorded no measure of heroin supply, availability, price or purity, and its limitations state that drug purity could not be considered. The only purity statement in the paper concerns cocaine (high local cocaine purity, cited to Kerr et al., 2003).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 41; the sentences on the decline are at the top of p. 42, left column); Discussion, 4th paragraph (begins p. 42; cocaine purity on p. 43, left column); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 44)

key_findings.finding: At baseline, participants in Table 1's non-fatal overdose column (n=837) had injected for longer (median 12 years, IQR 5–23, vs 7, 2–16; OR 1.04 per year, 1.03–1.05) and were more often women (39.78% vs 32.40%; OR 1.38, 1.12–1.69) and recently incarcerated (35.60% vs 30.67%; OR 1.24, 1.00–1.55); HIV-positive status was marginal (30.82% vs 26.40%; OR 1.24, 0.99–1.55); age, Aboriginal ethnicity and DTES residence did not differ (ORs 1.01, 1.08 and 1.01).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 40); Table 1 (p. 41)

key_findings.finding: In the multivariate GEE model over all observations, reporting a non-fatal overdose was associated with heroin injection (AOR 2.67, 95% CI 2.30–3.10), cocaine injection (2.02, 1.76–2.31), benzodiazepine use (2.00, 1.77–2.26), requiring help injecting (1.58, 1.39–1.79), binge drug use (1.52, 1.36–1.70), being denied treatment (1.46, 1.27–1.69), homelessness (1.38, 1.18–1.61), alcohol use (1.32, 1.09–1.60), public injecting (1.22, 1.06–1.41), non-injection opiate use (1.16, 1.03–1.31), speedball injection (1.15, 1.00–1.32, p=0.047) and incarceration (1.14, 1.01–1.28), and inversely with current methadone treatment (0.51, 0.44–0.59). Table 2 gives age as 0.99 per year older (0.98–0.99, p=0.046), an inverse association, whereas the abstract and text state the opposite direction (see reporting issues). Female sex (1.11, 0.96–1.28) and morphine injection (1.01, 0.84–1.22) were not associated after adjustment. The drug-use variables, incarceration and denial of treatment refer to the previous 6 months, the window of the outcome; methadone treatment is current, and no window is stated for homelessness.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, adjusted odds ratios

key_findings.finding: Unadjusted GEE odds ratios were larger for most drug variables: heroin injection 4.45 (3.89–5.09), cocaine injection 3.43 (3.03–3.88), speedball injection 2.57 (2.31–2.87), benzodiazepine use 2.50 (2.25–2.76), requiring help injecting 2.50 (2.24–2.78), binge drug use 2.42 (2.20–2.66), morphine injection 1.84 (1.56–2.17); methadone 0.57 (0.50–0.65). Crack smoking (0.99, 0.88–1.11) and years injecting (1.00, 0.99–1.01) were not associated and were not entered in the multivariate model.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, unadjusted odds ratios

key_findings.finding: The model is reported as identical when people who died of a fatal overdose during follow-up were excluded (data not shown) and largely unchanged when restricted to people with at least two follow-up visits. Restricted to people with no more than two overdose reports, heroin injection, benzodiazepine use, cocaine injection, requiring help injecting, binge use, alcohol use, homelessness and being denied treatment remained associated, non-injection opiate use became marginal (p=0.061) and methadone remained inversely associated; estimates are available only from the corresponding author.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (begins p. 40)

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations: VIDUS is not a random sample, so the findings may not generalize; overdose was self-defined; the exact temporal relationship between the outcome and the explanatory variables could not be ascertained, so the study does not allow a thorough investigation of causal relationships; and changing drug purity could not be considered.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph (begins p. 43) and 9th paragraph (p. 44)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that non-fatal overdose was common in this cohort, that it was associated with factors amenable to intervention (opiate and stimulant use, requiring help with injecting), that methadone maintenance had a strong protective effect, and that structural interventions are needed; the abstract states that younger age and methadone use were protective.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results and Conclusions (p. 39); Discussion, 10th paragraph (p. 44)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results give 750 (47%) participants with a lifetime non-fatal overdose at baseline, while Table 1's headings give 837 with and 750 without. Table 1's internal figures fit its headings: women make up 39.78% of the 837 column and 32.40% of the 750 column, giving the OR of 1.38 that the text describes as a positive association with overdose, and the 837 column has the longer injecting history (median 12 vs 7 years), as expected for a lifetime history.
reporting_issues.consequence: The baseline lifetime prevalence is either 47% (750/1587) or 52.7% (837/1587, editors' calculation). The table's consistency suggests the text figure is the one in error, but the paper does not allow this to be settled; the Discussion's approximately half fits either.

reporting_issues.issue: The direction of the age association is inconsistent. Table 2 labels the variable 'per year older', with odds ratios of 0.98 unadjusted (p<0.001) and 0.99 adjusted (p=0.046), meaning slightly lower odds of an overdose report with each year of age; the abstract (younger age, AOR 0.99, protective; p. 39), the Results (age among the factors positively associated in univariate analyses; p. 40) and the Discussion (age among the factors positively associated, methadone the only inversely associated variable; pp. 41, 43) all imply the opposite direction. Consequence: Two directions are printed, with the abstract and the text agreeing with each other against Table 2's label, so the paper does not allow the direction to be settled. The association is small (about 1% per year) and borderline after adjustment; neither the abstract's younger age being protective nor an inverse association with age should be cited as a finding.
reporting_issues.consequence: Taken at face value, Table 2 means younger participants reported overdose slightly more often, the reverse of the abstract. The effect is small (about 1% per year) and borderline after adjustment (p=0.046), but the abstract should not be cited for younger age being protective.

reporting_issues.issue: Several adjusted odds ratios differ between abstract, text and Table 2: cocaine injection 2.01 in the abstract against 2.02 in the text and table; binge drug use 1.46 (1.27–1.69) in the text against 1.52 (1.36–1.70) in the table and abstract; being denied treatment 1.43 (1.24–1.66) in the text against 1.46 (1.27–1.69) in the table. The text's value for binge use is the table's value for denied treatment. The abstract omits denied treatment (p<0.001 in Table 2), and the text's list omits speedball injection (1.15, p=0.047).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 2 is the most complete source; claims should cite its values (binge 1.52, denied treatment 1.46) and note that the abstract's list of independent factors is incomplete.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion explains the association between morphine and non-fatal overdose by the route of administration and tablet strength (pp. 42–43), but morphine injection was associated only before adjustment (OR 1.84); after adjustment the odds ratio was 1.01 (0.84–1.22), p=0.878 (Table 2, p. 42).
reporting_issues.consequence: The morphine discussion explains an association the adjusted model did not show; it should not be cited as a finding of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says longer years of injecting were associated with increased rates of non-fatal overdose (pp. 41–42), but in the longitudinal GEE years injecting showed no association (OR 1.00, 0.99–1.01, p=0.516; Table 2, where this continuous variable is labelled yes vs no). The association is only with lifetime overdose at baseline (OR 1.04 per year; Table 1), where more years of injecting give more time in which an overdose could have happened.
reporting_issues.consequence: The argument that risk persists throughout the injecting career is better supported by the null longitudinal association than by the baseline one, which is confounded by time at risk.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion refers to daily heroin and cocaine injection (p. 41), whereas the Methods list heroin and cocaine injection among behaviours in the previous 6 months without stating a frequency (p. 40; alcohol use, by contrast, has an explicit threshold of more than four drinks a day); the dagger and double-dagger markers in Tables 1 and 2 have no footnote text. Consequence: Whether the heroin and cocaine variables meant any or daily injection cannot be confirmed; claims should describe them as the Methods do (heroin or cocaine injection in the previous 6 months), without a frequency.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the heroin and cocaine variables meant any or daily injection cannot be confirmed; the Methods' definition (any, previous 6 months) is the safer reading.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results call the 985 events non-fatal overdoses (p. 40), but participants answered yes or no to any overdose in the previous 6 months, so 985 is the number of visits with a yes; repeated overdoses within one 6-month window count once. The abstract calls them reports (p. 39).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of overdoses is unknown, and the per-person frequency (median 1, IQR 1–2) counts reporting periods, not events.

reporting_issues.issue: The text places the steepest decline during 2001, from 12% to 5% (p. 40), but in Fig. 1 the value of about 12% is plotted at 2001 and the value of about 5% at 2002; neither the yearly denominators nor how a visit was assigned to a year is reported, and each answer covers the previous 6 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: The fall in reported overdose can be dated only to the interval between the 2001 and 2002 annual values (the recall window can reach back into the previous calendar year), and the series says nothing directly about heroin supply.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods describe an 85-month follow-up period (p. 40), whereas enrolment ran from May 1996 to May 2004 (about 97 months); the end of follow-up, the number of participants with any follow-up visit, losses and deaths are not reported, although the 32.7% uses all 1587 enrollees as denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cumulative proportion may be understated if some enrollees never returned, and the follow-up window behind Fig. 1 and the GEE is not fully defined.
