design_detail: Controlled before–after evaluation of a police operation, built from two independent cross-sections of a prospective cohort plus aggregate counts. Cohort part: participants in VIDUS (a Vancouver cohort of people who inject drugs) who attended a semiannual follow-up visit between 6 January and 7 July 2003 and had used heroin, cocaine or crack in the previous 6 months. Residents of the Downtown Eastside (DTES) interviewed in the 3 months before the crackdown began on 7 April 2003 (group 1, n=244) were compared with those interviewed in the 3 months after (group 2, n=142) on interviewer-administered yes/no items, with chi-square or Fisher tests and no adjustment; active participants living outside the DTES (107 before, 103 after) served as a comparison group whose results are summarized but not shown. Aggregate part: syringes distributed by the DTES needle exchange and the share not returned, and City of Vancouver monthly counts of used syringes found discarded in public in the core (within a 1-block radius of Main and Hastings) and in the rest of the DTES, and of syringes deposited in 6 outdoor safe-disposal boxes, January–March against April–June 2003 (t tests on monthly averages). Filed as cross-sectional (repeated cross-sections, not within-person change) and appraised with ROBINS-I because the exposure is an intervention (a police operation) evaluated by comparing periods.
can_establish: Whether active participants living in the DTES who were interviewed in the 3 months after the April 2003 crackdown reported police-related changes in where they used drugs, drug-market conditions, drug-use frequency, prices and service use more or less often than those interviewed in the 3 months before, and how the City's monthly counts of discarded syringes in the DTES changed between January–March and April–June 2003.
cannot_establish: That the crackdown caused the changes (two 3-month periods with no earlier series, seasonal and pre-existing trends visible in the syringe counts, and a comparison group whose data are not shown); displacement beyond the DTES (syringe counts exist only for the DTES); that use, prices or methadone enrolment were unaffected (the intervals allow changes of about 10 percentage points either way); effects on HIV risk, crime, sex work or starting to inject (not measured); or anything about heroin availability or purity before 2003.

sample.recruitment: Community cohort: VIDUS has recruited people who inject drugs in Vancouver since May 1996 through self-referral and street outreach (more than 1500 participants), with blood samples and an interviewer-administered questionnaire at baseline and every 6 months; the authors say the cohort appears to represent people who inject drugs in the Vancouver area, citing their own earlier paper (p. 1551). This analysis used the 774 participants who attended a follow-up visit between 6 January and 7 July 2003 (p. 1552).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: use of heroin, cocaine or crack during the 6 months before the interview (called active use); primary analyses restricted to DTES residents. Excluded from the study: 178 of 774 (23.0%) without such use; excluded from the primary analyses: 210 of 774 (27.1%) active participants living outside the DTES, used as the comparison group (pp. 1552–1553).
sample.demographics: DTES groups combined: mean age 39 years, 63% men, mean 13 years of injecting; the two groups did not differ significantly in age (p=0.25), sex (p=0.87), ethnic background (p=0.46), housing instability (p=0.57) or years of injecting (p=0.28). Group-specific values and the comparison group's characteristics are not printed (p. 1553).
sample.attrition: Not a follow-up of the same people: each group is whoever attended a visit in that window. Visits fell from about 446 in the 3 months before to about 328 in the 3 months after (editors' calculation from the exclusion counts and percentages, p. 1553); the authors attribute the fall to the study's visit cycle, citing a similar pattern in the same months of 2002 (data not shown, p. 1555). Whether anyone was interviewed in both windows is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Non-random cohort (authors' limitation, p. 1555). Attendance after the crackdown may itself have been affected by it (arrest, incarceration, moving away from the DTES), so group 2 may under-represent the people most affected; the explanation offered for the fall in visits rests on an unshown 2002 comparison. The proportion excluded for no recent use was similar in the two periods (21.3% vs 25.3%, p=0.19).

exposure.measurement: The intervention is assigned by date: cohort interviews from 7 April 2003 count as after the crackdown; the aggregate syringe data compare April–June with January–March 2003, split at 1 April because the data are monthly (p. 1552). The operation's size comes from secondary sources only: about 50 additional officers redeployed to the DTES (a newspaper report), an estimated additional cost of $2.3 million (a council report) and 236 additional trafficking charges against 162 people in its first several weeks (police board minutes) (pp. 1551–1552). Individual contact with police was not measured; participants were asked about perceived effects of police presence. Drug use was self-reported in the interviewer-administered questionnaire.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Drug use recorded as daily or more versus less than daily for heroin, cocaine and crack (Table 1, p. 1552); the abstract describes the heroin and cocaine items as injection (p. 1551). Active use means any use of heroin, cocaine or crack in the previous 6 months; the recall window of the frequency and police-effect items is not stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Everyone used heroin, cocaine or crack (inclusion criterion); daily use of each drug is reported separately, without analysis of combinations; alcohol, benzodiazepines and other drugs are not reported.

comparison.controls: Before–after: DTES residents interviewed in the 3 months before the crackdown (n=244) against those interviewed in the 3 months after (n=142). A concurrent comparison group of active participants living outside the DTES (107 before, 103 after) is described, but only as a summary of non-significant tests (data not shown, p. 1554). The syringe data have no comparison area and no earlier year.
comparison.matching: None; comparability checked with p-values on five characteristics (p. 1553).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Season (January–March against April–June), trends already under way before the crackdown (visible in Fig. 1), other events in the DTES in 2003, each participant's own contact with police, arrests and incarceration, and changes in syringe-collection effort are not measured or modelled.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison groups are the same kind of participants (active use of heroin, cocaine or crack).

outcomes.instruments: Interviewer-administered yes/no items whose wording is not given: perceived effects of police presence on the types of drugs available, access to drugs, drug quality, quantity used, buying and which drugs were used (Table 1); on where drugs were used, use inside or outside and the neighbourhood or alley of use (Table 2); injecting in public spaces (street, alley, doorway, public bathroom, park or parking lot); willingness to use a safer injecting site; contact with a street nurse; methadone maintenance; being denied drug treatment; median single-shot prices. Aggregate data: syringes distributed by the DTES needle exchange and the share not returned; City of Vancouver monthly counts of used syringes found discarded in public in the core and elsewhere in the DTES, and of syringes deposited in 6 outdoor safe-disposal boxes (4 in the core, 2 outside) (pp. 1552–1554).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation or source is given for the questionnaire items; how the City collected and counted discarded syringes (routes, frequency, effort) is not described, so a change in collection practice cannot be excluded.
outcomes.operationalization: Displacement was operationalized as more participants reporting police-related changes in place, outdoor use and neighbourhood of use, together with discarded-syringe counts falling in the core and rising in the rest of the DTES. Community levels of drug use were represented by syringes distributed at the exchange. Access to services: methadone maintenance, denial of treatment, street-nurse contact and willingness to use a safer injecting site. HIV risk behaviour (for example syringe borrowing) was not analysed, for lack of power (p. 1555).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; every test two-tailed at p<0.05 (p. 1552). The authors acknowledge that the number of comparisons was large (p. 1555). 26 counts the 18 survey items in Tables 1–2, 3 prices, needle-exchange distribution, 3 disposal series and the non-returned share; the comparison-group tests are not counted (not shown). Six of the 18 survey items are printed as significant, two of them at p=0.045–0.047. Only willingness to use a safer injecting site (p<0.001) and the non-returned share (p<0.001) clearly pass a Bonferroni threshold for 26 tests (0.0019); use outside and the outside-core disposal count (each printed p=0.002) sit at it (editors' calculation).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to self-report; interviewers and analysts knew the period.

analysis.effect_sizes: Odds ratios with 95% CIs from 2×2 tables, group 2 against group 1 (Tables 1–2, pp. 1552–1553): police affected where drugs were used 1.8 (1.1–2.8); use outside 6.1 (1.6–22.4); changed neighbourhood or alley 1.7 (1.0–2.7); injecting in public spaces 1.5 (1.0–2.3); willing to use a safer injecting site 0.3 (0.2–0.6); methadone maintenance 1.1 (0.8–1.7); daily heroin use 0.9 (0.6–1.5). Editors' calculation (Wald 95% intervals for differences in percentage points, after minus before): affected where used +11.3 (1.9 to 20.6); use outside +5.8 (1.4 to 10.2, approximate with 3 and 10 events); willing to use a safer injecting site −16.6 (−24.3 to −8.9); daily heroin −1.1 (−10.3 to 8.1); methadone +3.4 (−6.9 to 13.6). Aggregate data: monthly averages before and after with t-test p-values only, no intervals (p. 1554).
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted chi-square or Fisher tests for categorical items and Wilcoxon tests for continuous ones (p. 1552).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors say they followed a statistical protocol defined a priori (p. 1555); it is not published or registered, so the reported comparisons cannot be checked against it.
analysis.selective_reporting: Comparison-group results are summarized as non-significant without data (p. 1554); question wording and recall windows are not given; HIV-risk items such as syringe borrowing are mentioned but not analysed (p. 1555); the 2002 visit pattern used to explain the fall in visits is not shown (p. 1555).
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors say the sample was too small to evaluate HIV risk behaviour (p. 1555). The results read as no change are compatible with changes of up to about 10 percentage points either way (editors' calculation above), and each syringe comparison rests on three monthly values per period (4 degrees of freedom).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among active participants living in the DTES, those interviewed in the 3 months after the 7 April 2003 crackdown (n=142) more often than those interviewed in the 3 months before (n=244) said police presence had changed where they used drugs (33.8% vs 22.5%) or led them to use outside (7.0% vs 1.2%), and fewer said they would use a safer injecting site (11.3% vs 27.9%); reported daily use, prices, methadone treatment and denial of treatment did not differ detectably, with intervals compatible with changes of up to about 10 percentage points either way. Within the DTES, monthly counts of discarded syringes fell in the core and rose in the surrounding area between January–March and April–June 2003, partly continuing changes visible before the crackdown, and needle-exchange distribution was about 10% higher (not significant).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's interpretation says the crackdown did not alter drug prices or frequency of use nor encourage methadone enrolment (p. 1551), which restates an absence of detected difference over 3 months as an absence of effect. The abstract's results state “Needle-exchange data confirmed that the community levels of drug use were unchanged” (p. 1551), from a non-significant t test on three monthly totals per period with distribution 10% higher. The abstract speaks of displacement into adjacent areas of the city (p. 1551), but the syringe counts cover only the DTES, and the comparison participants living outside it showed no significant change (p. 1554). The summary says the results probably explain more sex-trade activity and crime outside the DTES (p. 1555), for which the paper has no data (newspaper reports and police board minutes are cited), and states “The crackdown also increased the rates of unsafe syringe disposal” (p. 1555), causal wording from an uncontrolled two-period comparison in which the count outside the core had already risen before the crackdown (Fig. 1, p. 1554). The fall in willingness to use a safer injection facility is attributed to police presence as a possibility (p. 1555). The limitations paragraph concedes the many comparisons and possible unmeasured confounding (p. 1555).

timeline.event: Maher & Dixon, policing and harm minimization in a street-level drug market (Br J Criminol); cited by the authors among studies of market adaptation and displacement under enforcement; not appraised here

Best, Strang, Beswick & Gossop, a concentrated high-profile police operation, titled as finding no discernible impact on drug availability, price or purity (Br J Criminol); cited as consistent; not appraised here
Aitken, Moore, Higgs, Kelsall & Kerger, the impact of a police crackdown on a street drug scene (Int J Drug Policy); cited as consistent; not appraised here

Wood et al., the same group's evaluation of the largest heroin seizure in Canadian history (CMAJ 168:165–169), summarized in this paper as detecting no measurable public-health benefit in terms of changes in heroin use; not appraised here

replication.where_it_stands: The paper places its findings among earlier studies of street-level enforcement that it describes as showing market adaptation and displacement (refs 22–26, pp. 1554–1555); none has been appraised for this card, and no replication of this Vancouver evaluation was among the files read. The paper contains no information on heroin availability or purity before 2003.

funding.funder: Status of Women Canada (financial support for this study); VIDUS: US National Institutes of Health grant R01 DA11591, and in part Canadian Institutes of Health Research grant 122258; personal support: Evan Wood, Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research and CIHR; Robert Hogg, Michael Smith Foundation for Health Research Career Investigator Award and CIHR Investigator Award; Martin Schechter, Tier I Canada Research Chair in HIV/AIDS and Urban Population Health (Acknowledgements, p. 1555).
funding.affiliations_note: All authors were at the British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS, St. Paul's Hospital, and several at the University of British Columbia (p. 1555). Several authors had published on safer injecting facilities (refs 33 and 38, their own papers, one of them on the rationale for evaluating North America's first such facility), and the conclusion recommends evaluating supervised injection centres (p. 1555). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: An interrupted time series with a comparison area: monthly discarded-syringe counts across the whole city (not only the DTES), needle-exchange distribution and returns, and cohort-reported place of use, for at least a year before and after an enforcement operation and for the same months of earlier years, with questionnaire recall windows starting at the operation's onset and each participant's police contact recorded.

domains.note: Two 3-month windows either side of the operation, no adjustment; season differs between January–March and April–June; Fig. 1 shows the outside-core count already rising and the core count already falling before 7 April; the comparison group outside the DTES is reported without data and with no test of the difference between areas.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Groups are whoever attended a visit in each window; visits fell by about a quarter after the crackdown, explained only by an unshown 2002 comparison; people arrested, incarcerated or displaced may have been less likely to attend.

Period assignment by interview date is clear, but if the items asked about the previous 6 months (stated only for active use), group 2's answers covered pre-crackdown months; the syringe data count 1–6 April as after. Both bias towards no difference (the authors note the second, p. 1555).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: The operation's intensity over the 3 months, and any co-interventions in the DTES, are not documented by the study; the secondary sources describe only its start.
Item non-response is not reported: four items total 243 in group 1 and the drug-quality item totals 108 of 142 in group 2 (Tables 1–2).

Self-reported perceptions of police effects, asked by interviewers who knew the period, in wording not given, after a publicized operation; the syringe counts depend on City collection practice, which is not described.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: 26 outcomes without correction under an unpublished protocol; comparison-group data not shown; two rows of Table 1 carry statistics that do not match their counts; the syringe p-values cannot be reproduced from Fig. 1.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I is used because the study evaluates a police operation, an intervention, by comparing periods (METHODS §5.3; compare sc_marshall_2011). Serious overall: the before–after design with 3-month windows cannot separate the operation from season and pre-existing trends, the outcomes are unblinded self-reported perceptions, and several reported results cannot be reproduced from the paper's own counts and figure. Within that, the larger self-reported differences (use outside, willingness to use a safer injecting site, police-related change of place) are internally consistent and unlikely to be due to chance alone. Citable for: what DTES participants reported in the 3 months before and after the April 2003 crackdown, with counts, and the DTES syringe counts for January–June 2003, as changes over time. Not citable for: the crackdown causing displacement beyond the DTES, increasing unsafe disposal or leaving drug use unchanged; or any statement about heroin availability or purity before 2003.

key_findings.finding: Of 774 VIDUS participants seen for follow-up between 6 January and 7 July 2003, 178 (23.0%) were excluded for no heroin, cocaine or crack use in the previous 6 months (21.3% [95] of those seen before the crackdown vs 25.3% [83] after; p=0.19) and 210 (27.1%) active participants living outside the DTES were analysed separately, leaving 244 DTES residents interviewed in the 3 months before 7 April 2003 (group 1) and 142 in the 3 months after (group 2).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (begins p. 1552, right column; continues on p. 1553)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed counts and percentages: about 446 visits in the 3 months before and 328 after (95/0.213 and 83/0.253); 446 − 95 − 107 = 244 and 328 − 83 − 103 = 142, consistent with the printed group sizes.

key_findings.finding: The two DTES groups did not differ significantly in age (p=0.25), sex (p=0.87), ethnic background (p=0.46), housing instability (p=0.57) or years of injecting (p=0.28); combined, participants had a mean age of 39 years, 63% were men and they had injected for 13 years on average.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (begins p. 1552)

key_findings.finding: The crackdown began on 7 April 2003 and reportedly redeployed 50 additional officers to the DTES; its stated goals involved disrupting the open drug market and interrupting the cycle of crime and drug use on the streets of the DTES. Its estimated additional cost was $2.3 million, and 236 additional trafficking charges against 162 people were reported in its first several weeks. These statements come from a newspaper report (the officers; ref 18), an administrative report by the Chief Constable to a Vancouver City Council committee dated 18 March 2003 (the goals and the cost; ref 10) and police board minutes (the charges; ref 11), not from the study.
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 2nd paragraph (p. 1551); Methods, 2nd paragraph (p. 1552)

key_findings.finding: Reported daily use did not differ between the 3 months before and after: daily heroin 68/244 (27.9%) vs 38/142 (26.8%), OR 0.9 (0.6–1.5), p=0.814; daily cocaine 70/244 (28.7%) vs 39/142 (27.5%), p=0.797; daily crack 145/244 (59.4%) vs 86/142 (60.6%), OR 1.1 (0.7–1.6), p=0.826.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows Heroin use, Cocaine use, Crack use (p. 1552); group sizes 244 and 142 from Results, 1st paragraph (p. 1553)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: difference in daily heroin use −1.1 percentage points (95% CI −10.3 to 8.1). The cocaine row's printed interval (0.6–1.2) does not match its counts (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Reported median single-shot prices did not change (all p>0.1): heroin $20 (IQR $20–$20) before and $20 ($16–$20) after the crackdown; cocaine $10 ($10–$10) in both periods; crack $10 ($8–$10) in both periods.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: After the crackdown more participants said police presence had affected the types of drugs available, 58/244 (23.8%) vs 47/142 (33.1%), OR 1.6 (1.0–2.5), p=0.047; had reduced their access to drugs, 73/244 (29.9%) vs 60/142 (42.3%), printed OR 1.5 (1.0–2.4), p=0.050; and had reduced drug quality, 73/244 (29.9%) vs 46/108 (42.6%; the row's group-2 counts, 62 and 46, sum to 108), printed OR 1.7 (1.1–2.6), p=0.014. There was no difference for reduced quantity used (15.2% vs 13.4%, p=0.631), being prevented from buying (14.8% vs 18.3%, p=0.368) or which drugs were used (9.0% vs 11.3%, p=0.474). The items concern drugs in general, not heroin specifically.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 1552); Results, 2nd paragraph (p. 1553)
key_findings.note: The access and quality rows are internally inconsistent: their group-1 counts are identical, the quality row's group-2 counts sum to 108 rather than 142, and the access counts reproduce the statistics printed for quality (editors' calculation: OR 1.71, 1.11–2.64, p=0.014), so the two rows' statistics may be interchanged (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: After the crackdown more participants said police presence had affected where they used drugs, 55/244 (22.5%) vs 48/142 (33.8%), OR 1.8 (1.1–2.8), p=0.016, and had led to use outside, 3/243 (1.2%) vs 10/142 (7.0%), OR 6.1 (1.6–22.4), p=0.002, but not use inside, 17/243 (7.0%) vs 14/142 (9.9%), p=0.319; more had changed the neighbourhood or alley of use because of police presence, 44/243 (18.1%) vs 38/142 (26.8%), OR 1.7 (1.0–2.7), p=0.045. Injecting in public spaces (street, alley, doorway, public bathroom, park or parking lot) was reported by 78/244 (32.0%) vs 59/142 (41.6%), OR 1.5 (1.0–2.3), p=0.058.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Denominators of 243 are the row totals printed in Table 2 (one group-1 answer missing on those items). Editors' calculation: Fisher's exact p for use outside is 0.006 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Fewer participants were willing to use a safer injecting site after the crackdown, 68/244 (27.9%) vs 16/142 (11.3%), OR 0.3 (0.2–0.6), p<0.001. Contact with a street nurse was 6/244 (2.5%) vs 0/142, p=0.060; methadone maintenance 100/244 (41.0%) vs 63/142 (44.4%), OR 1.1 (0.8–1.7), p=0.516; being denied drug treatment 17/244 (7.0%) vs 6/142 (4.2%), OR 0.6 (0.2–1.5), p=0.273.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: methadone difference +3.4 percentage points (95% CI −6.9 to 13.6); Fisher's exact p for street-nurse contact 0.089.

key_findings.finding: Among the 210 active participants living outside the DTES (107 seen before 7 April, 103 after), the authors report no significant increase in public injection (p=0.66) and no significant differences (all p>0.1) in the displacement measures or the other covariates; the data are not shown.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (begins p. 1553; the comparison-group sentence is at the top of p. 1554, left column)

key_findings.finding: The DTES needle exchange distributed 363,998 syringes in the 3 months before 1 April 2003 and 400,382 in the 3 months after (t test of monthly averages, p=0.516). The share of distributed syringes not returned to the exchange (including syringes from DTES needle sweeps) rose from 4.0% to 8.1% (p<0.001; the test and its unit are not described).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: distribution was 10.0% higher after.

key_findings.finding: City of Vancouver counts of used syringes found discarded in public, available only for the DTES: in the core the monthly average fell from 1082 (January–March 2003) to 585 (April–June) (t test p=0.003); outside the core it rose from 784 to 1253 (p=0.002); use of the 6 outdoor safe-disposal boxes (4 in the core, 2 outside) fell from 865 to 502 (p=0.018). Changes outside the DTES could not be assessed.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Fig. 1 (panels a–c)
key_findings.note: Approximate monthly totals read from the Fig. 1 bars by pixel measurement on 300-dpi crops (not printed values; the readings reproduce the printed averages within about 1%): core about 1300, 980 and 970 in January–March, then 690, 470 and 600; outside the core about 800, 560 and 990, then 1080, 1280 and 1400; disposal boxes about 770, 800 and 1020, then 360, 530 and 610. Outside the core the March count, before the crackdown, was already close to the April count.

key_findings.finding: The paper gives no data or statement on heroin availability or purity before 2003 or on any change around 2001. Its heroin-market data cover January–July 2003 only: median single-shot heroin price $20 before and after the crackdown, daily heroin use 27.9% vs 26.8%, and perceived police effects on the availability, access and quality of drugs in general. The introduction mentions the authors' earlier evaluation of the largest heroin seizure in Canadian history, which detected no measurable public-health benefit in terms of changes in heroin use; the seizure's date is not given in this paper (ref 9, Wood et al., CMAJ 2003).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 1st paragraph (p. 1551); Table 1 (p. 1552); Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 1553)

key_findings.finding: The authors list as limitations: VIDUS is not a random sample; the number of statistical comparisons was large despite an a priori protocol; the fall in visits between the periods (attributed to the study's cycle because of a similar pattern in 2002); possible unmeasured confounding; inclusion of 1–6 April in the post-crackdown period for the monthly syringe data, which would reduce differences; and too little power to evaluate HIV risk behaviour such as syringe borrowing.
key_findings.locator: Interpretation, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the crackdown did not alter drug prices or frequency of use or encourage methadone enrolment, that several measures indicated displacement of injection drug use into adjacent areas, that it increased unsafe syringe disposal and reduced returns to the city's largest needle exchange, and that it probably explains increases in drug-related sex-trade activity and crime outside the DTES (citing newspaper reports and police board minutes).
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Interpretation (p. 1551); Interpretation, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 1554–1555)

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the rows for reduced access to drugs and reduced drug quality do not match their own counts. Both rows have the same group-1 counts (171 no, 73 yes); the quality row's group-2 counts (62 and 46) sum to 108, not 142, without explanation; and the access counts (73/244 vs 60/142) give OR 1.71 (1.11–2.64), chi-square p=0.014 (editors' calculation), which is what is printed for quality, whereas access is printed as 1.5 (1.0–2.4), p=0.050. The quality counts give OR 1.74 (1.09–2.78), p=0.020 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's description of access as a marginal decrease and of quality as a significant change (p. 1553) follows the printed statistics, not the counts; which result is marginal, and how many participants answered the quality item, cannot be settled from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The cocaine row of Table 1 prints OR 0.9 (0.6–1.2); its counts (70/244 vs 39/142) give 0.94 (0.59–1.49) (editors' calculation), close to the heroin row's interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the upper limit appears misprinted; no conclusion changes.

reporting_issues.issue: The p-values for use outside (3/243 vs 10/142; printed 0.002) and street-nurse contact (6/244 vs 0/142; printed 0.060) match the uncorrected Pearson chi-square, although expected counts are below 5 and the Methods name Fisher's exact test (p. 1552); Fisher's exact test gives 0.006 and 0.089 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: use outside remains significant, but its p-value is three times the printed one, which matters with 26 uncorrected tests.

reporting_issues.issue: Item non-response is not reported: four items total 243 in group 1 (prevented from buying, use inside, use outside, changed neighbourhood) and the drug-quality item totals 108 of 142 in group 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 34 missing answers (24%) on the quality item in group 2 could change that comparison; no reason is given.

reporting_issues.issue: The t-test p-values for the disposal counts (core 0.003, outside the core 0.002, disposal boxes 0.018) cannot be reproduced from Fig. 1: two-sample t tests on the three monthly totals per period read from the bars give about 0.02, 0.04 and 0.03 (editors' calculation from approximate bar readings that reproduce the printed monthly averages within about 1%). The monthly values are not printed, and the test is described only as a t test of monthly averages.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction holds, but the evidence for a rise outside the core is weaker than printed (about p=0.04 with 4 degrees of freedom), before any allowance for 26 tests, season or trend. The needle-exchange p-value (0.516) cannot be checked either.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1 shows changes already under way before the crackdown: outside the core the count rose from about 560 in February to about 990 in March, close to the April value (about 1080); in the core it had fallen from about 1300 in January to about 980 in February and 970 in March (approximate readings). The comparison is January–March against April–June of a single year, with no earlier year shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: A difference between 3-month means cannot separate the operation from the pre-existing trend or from seasonal change in outdoor injecting and syringe discarding; the causal summary that the crackdown increased unsafe disposal (p. 1555) is not supported by this design.

reporting_issues.issue: Active use is defined over the 6 months before the interview (p. 1552), but the recall window of the drug-use frequency and police-effect items is not stated. If these too covered 6 months, group 2's answers (interviews within 3 months of the crackdown's start) would include pre-crackdown months.
reporting_issues.consequence: This would bias the comparisons toward no difference, which bears most on the conclusions that use, prices and methadone enrolment were unchanged; the paper does not allow it to be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison group outside the DTES is reported only as non-significant tests (p=0.66 for public injection; all others p>0.1; data not shown), and no test compares the change in the DTES with the change outside it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A significant change in one group and a non-significant one in the other is not evidence that the groups differ: the paper cannot show that the DTES changes exceeded background change, nor that displacement reached the areas where the comparison participants lived.

No supplement. The DOI printed in the left margin of p. 1551 reads 10.1053/cmaj.1031928, which differs from the Crossref DOI in the reference record (10.1503/cmaj.1031928).

These figures come from a newspaper report, a council report and police board minutes (refs 10, 11, 18), not from the study.

design_detail: Before–after comparison of calendar periods in four markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada, with no comparison place or series. The authors take the Australian heroin shortage to have begun in about January 2001 (citing an earlier review) and state as their primary hypothesis that Canadian markers would stay stable or rise after it. Three routine series are compared as yearly averages, with no statistical test: drug-induced deaths in the whole province of British Columbia from the provincial vital statistics agency (1998–2000 against 2001–03); ambulance responses that required naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside (fiscal years 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 2001–02 to 2002–03); and the weight of heroin destined for Canada that was seized, from a Royal Canadian Mounted Police report (1998–2000 against 2001–03). In VIDUS, a prospective cohort of people who inject drugs in Vancouver interviewed every 6 months, self-reported daily heroin injection at 13,609 observations (6-monthly interviews) of 1,587 participants (May 1996 to December 2004) is compared between 2001–04 and 1996–2000 by repeated-measures logistic regression (generalized estimating equations, GEE), adjusted for individual characteristics. Filed as prospective-cohort, the design of its only analysis with statistics; the other three series are aggregate counts. No figures for 2005, none for Vancouver's overdose deaths or for any area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and no mention of supervised injection.
can_establish: Whether four markers of heroin use and harm in western Canada (drug-induced deaths in British Columbia, naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, heroin seized for Canada, and self-reported daily heroin injection in a Vancouver cohort of people who inject drugs) were lower in 2001–03 (2001–04 for the cohort) than in the late 1990s, by how much, and, from the yearly figures, when each began to fall.
cannot_establish: That heroin supply, availability or purity fell, or why (none was measured; seizures may mark enforcement as well as supply, and the deaths include other drugs); that the falls began with the Australian shortage (deaths and naloxone use were already falling from 1998 and fiscal 1998–99); or anything about 2005, about Vancouver's overdose deaths, or about the area around the supervised injection site that opened in Vancouver in September 2003, which the paper does not mention.

sample.recruitment: Routine statistics: drug-induced deaths in British Columbia registered by the provincial vital statistics agency, 1998–2003 (ref. 19); ambulance responses that required naloxone in the Downtown Eastside, fiscal years 1997–98 to 2002–03 (the data's source is not named; the text cites two of the team's earlier papers for regular counting of naloxone use in the area, refs 2 and 20); heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2003 (a Royal Canadian Mounted Police report, ref. 22) (p. 690). Cohort: VIDUS, an ongoing prospective cohort of people who inject drugs in Vancouver since May 1996, described in earlier papers (refs 23–24); interviewer-administered questionnaire and blood sample at baseline and every 6 months; 1,587 participants gave 13,609 observations at which daily heroin use could be assessed, May 1996 to December 2004 (pp. 690–691).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not given for the cohort in this paper (earlier descriptions cited). Routine series as defined by each agency; the deaths are all drug-induced deaths, the drug not specified (p. 690).
sample.demographics: Not reported. Age, gender, Aboriginal ethnicity and Downtown Eastside residence enter the cohort model, but their distribution is not given (Table 2, p. 693).
sample.attrition: Not reported: interviews per period, loss to follow-up, deaths and enrolment after 2000 are not given.
sample.selection_effects: The cohort is a community cohort of people who inject drugs, recruited as described elsewhere and followed as it aged; who stayed in it and who joined later may differ between periods, which the paper does not report. The four markers describe different populations: the whole province (deaths), the Downtown Eastside (naloxone, chosen because most of the province's overdoses occur there and its naloxone data are counted regularly), all of Canada (seizures) and the cohort.

exposure.measurement: The exposure is calendar time: the period from January 2001, the authors' date for the start of the Australian heroin shortage (citing Degenhardt et al., 2005), stands for a fall in heroin supply that is not itself measured. Seizures are offered as a potential indicator of supply and, the authors note, could also mark supply-reduction (enforcement) activity (p. 690). The authors write that Canada has no standardized longitudinal measures of street heroin purity (p. 694); no price or availability data are used.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (comparison of periods). The cohort outcome, daily heroin injection, is self-reported at 6-monthly interviews.
exposure.polysubstance: The deaths are all drug-induced deaths, not attributed to a drug; the authors expect some not to involve heroin (p. 690). The cohort model adjusts for daily cocaine injection and daily crack use; the authors say other drugs did not fall similarly and methamphetamine use rose significantly over the period, with no data shown (p. 691).

comparison.controls: Earlier years of the same series (1998–2000; fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01; 1996–2000 in the cohort). No comparison place and no series unaffected by the supposed supply change; Australia appears only through other authors' reports.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Trends already under way before 2001 are not modelled: in Figure 1, deaths fall from 1998 and naloxone use from fiscal 1998–99 (p. 692). The routine series are counts without population denominators, and changes in treatment, policing, ambulance practice and the cohort's age and make-up are not measured. Canadian supply-reduction funding and activity are said to be unchanged since the mid-1990s on the strength of one citation (ref. 16), with no data shown.

outcomes.instruments: Provincial vital statistics counts of drug-induced deaths; ambulance counts of responses requiring naloxone; Royal Canadian Mounted Police figures for heroin seized; interviewer-administered questionnaire on daily drug use in VIDUS.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors say overdose statistics and seizure data may be poor proxies for heroin use and that the four measures were not counted at the same level; they cite other studies in which ambulance and overdose mortality statistics correlated strongly with street heroin purity (pp. 693–694). Self-reported daily heroin injection is not validated in this paper.
outcomes.operationalization: A fall in heroin supply is inferred from falls in the four markers. Heroin-related harm is drug-induced deaths (any drug) and naloxone-requiring ambulance responses; heroin use is self-reported daily heroin injection. The routine series are yearly counts, although the text calls them rates (pp. 690–691).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; only the cohort comparison has a statistical test.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (p. 691), yearly averages: drug-induced deaths 297 (1998–2000) against 192 (2001–03), a 35.4% reduction; naloxone-requiring responses 674 (fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01) against 370 (2001–02 to 2002–03), 45.1%; heroin seized 184 kg against 67 kg, 63.6%; no intervals or tests (the percentages reproduce from the averages, editors' calculation). Cohort (Table 2, p. 693): daily heroin injection in 2001–04 against 1996–2000, adjusted odds ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.61), P<0.001; shares reporting daily use 36.5% (1997/98), 32.6% (1999/00), 23.3% (2001/02) and 20.8% (2003/04), without counts or denominators (p. 691). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (p. 692) at 300 dpi, approximate (bar tops read inside the 0.96-point bar outlines against the axis ticks; the bar rectangles drawn in the PDF agree within 1): deaths about 399, 272, 218, 221, 169 and 186 (1998 to 2003); naloxone-requiring responses about 732, 840, 655, 464, 388 and 350 (fiscal 1997–98 to 2002–03); heroin seized about 234, 142, 177, 94, 46 and 60 kg (1998 to 2003). Means of these readings by period: 296 and 192 deaths, 673 and 369 responses, 184 and 67 kg, each within 1 of Table 1. Editors' calculations from the readings: deaths fell about 45% from 1998 to 2000 (about four-fifths of the fall from 1998 to the lowest year, 2002), were about the same in 2001 as in 2000, and the 2001–03 mean was about 12% below 2000; naloxone-requiring responses fell about 45% from fiscal 1998–99 to 2000–01 and about 20% from 2000–01 to the mean of the next two years; seizures fell about 47% from 2000 to 2001. Steps in the cohort's daily use: −3.9, −9.3 and −2.5 percentage points between successive two-year periods.
analysis.covariates: Cohort model: period, daily cocaine injection (adjusted odds ratio 2.32, 2.08 to 2.60), daily crack use (1.85, 1.65 to 2.06), sex-trade involvement (1.34, 1.20 to 1.52), current methadone use (0.43, 0.37 to 0.51), and age, Downtown Eastside residence, Aboriginal ethnicity and gender (no estimates shown; all P<0.05 in the final model); variables entered if P ≤ 0.05 in univariate GEE; behaviours time-updated (p. 691; Table 2, p. 693). Routine series: none.
analysis.preregistration_detail: An a priori statistical protocol is mentioned (p. 691); it is not published or registered.
analysis.selective_reporting: Trends for methamphetamine and other drugs are summarized with 'data not shown' (p. 691); the cohort is reported only as one odds ratio and four two-year shares, and the visual inspection said to confirm its trend is not shown; period boundaries follow the date of the Australian shortage and differ between series (calendar years, fiscal years, 1996–2000 against 2001–04).
analysis.power: Not reported. The cohort estimate is precise (interval 0.50 to 0.61); the routine series have no statistical comparison.

interpretation_gap.results_show: All four markers were lower after 2000 than in the late 1990s. The yearly figures show deaths and naloxone use falling from 1998 and fiscal 1998–99, with most of the fall in deaths before 2001 (about 399 in 1998, 218 in 2000, 221 in 2001, and 169 and 186 in 2002 and 2003; editors' reading); seizures were lower in each year from 2001 (about 94, 46 and 60 kg) than in any earlier year (about 234, 142 and 177 kg), and the cohort's largest step in daily heroin injection came between 1999/00 and 2001/02. Nothing measures heroin purity, price or availability, the deaths include other drugs, and the data end in 2003 (2004 for the cohort).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and summary describe massive decreases in independent markers of heroin use coinciding with the Australian shortage despite no increase in Canadian enforcement funding, and conclude that external global heroin supply forces deserve greater investigation and credence (pp. 689, 694); the discussion finds the Canadian shortage “so clearly evident in these crude data” (p. 693). Gaps: (1) the paper does not mention that its own Figure 1 shows deaths and naloxone use falling about two years before 2001, so the period comparison partly measures an earlier trend; (2) deaths and naloxone responses are markers of overdose, not of use, and are not independent of each other; (3) the fall in seizures, which the authors say could also mark enforcement activity, is read as a fall in supply, while unchanged Canadian enforcement rests on one citation (ref. 16) with no data; (4) the statement that reduced heroin availability on Vancouver's streets was widely reported in the media cites a study of HIV viral rebound (ref. 17); (5) no measure of purity, price or availability is used; the authors acknowledge only the lack of standardized measures of street heroin purity (p. 694).

timeline.event: Same cohort (VIDUS) and four of the same authors: the share reporting a non-fatal overdose in the previous 6 months fell from 21% in 1997 to 6% in 2004, the largest decline placed during 2001; the authors cite this paper and suggest reduced heroin supply may have played a role (not an independent replication)

Evaluation of the Vancouver supervised injection site, with three of this paper's authors, cites it (ref. 44, p. 1434) for drug use largely constant from 2001 to 2005, daily heroin injecting 24% in 2001 and 25% in 2005, daily cocaine injecting 17% and 15%, and stable methadone use; none of these figures is in this paper, whose data end in 2004
A published letter on that evaluation cites this paper, dated 2004 there, for higher heroin availability until 2001 that declined by 2002 and stayed low (its ref. 3)
The evaluators' reply cites a different 2006 paper by the same five authors (Addiction 101, 623–625) and a 2009 web report for daily heroin use stable from 2001 to 2005; neither is on file

replication.where_it_stands: The only source on file for yearly drug-induced deaths in British Columbia, naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside and Canadian heroin seizures around 2001. Its finding that these markers were lower after 2000 fits the same cohort's fall in reported non-fatal overdoses (Kerr et al., 2007; same team, not independent). Whether heroin supply fell, and why, is not measured in these papers. Both sides of the dispute over the Vancouver supervised injection site cite it: the critics for higher availability until 2001, the evaluators for stable drug use from 2001 to 2005, figures it does not contain.

funding.funder: VIDUS is supported by the US National Institutes of Health (R01 DA011591–04A1) and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (MOP-67262) (Acknowledgements, p. 694); no other funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors at the British Columbia Centre for Excellence in HIV/AIDS, St Paul's Hospital, Vancouver; three also at the Department of Medicine, University of British Columbia (p. 689). Three of them (Wood, Montaner, Kerr) are also authors of the 2011 evaluation of the Vancouver supervised injection site that cites this paper. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Yearly measures of heroin purity, price and availability in Vancouver (for example, laboratory analysis of street samples) from the late 1990s to 2005, with overdose deaths by drug and by area, analysed as an interrupted time series that models the trend before 2001 and compares a market with no change in supply.

domains.note: Two-period averages with no adjustment and no comparison series; trends already under way in the paper's own figure (deaths from 1998, naloxone use from fiscal 1998–99) are not modelled; changes in population, treatment, policing and ambulance practice are not measured for the routine series. The cohort model adjusts for individual characteristics, age among them (Table 2 footnote, p. 693), but has no term for time in the cohort or turnover, so its period term carries every other change between the late 1990s and 2001–04.

The exposure that matters, a fall in heroin supply, is not measured: it is assumed from the date given for the Australian shortage. Seizures, the only supply marker, may also mark enforcement. The naloxone fiscal years place some months of 2001 in the before period (4 months, by the authors' account).
The routine series are complete counts at their level; the cohort is a community cohort whose make-up across periods (who stayed, who joined) is not reported.

Methadone use is adjusted for in the cohort only; other changes during 2001–04, such as the Downtown Eastside police crackdown of April 2003 and the supervised injection site of September 2003 (both described in other papers on file), are not considered.
For the cohort, interviews per period, loss to follow-up and missing answers are not reported.
Deaths are drug-induced deaths from any drug; naloxone use depends on ambulance practice; daily heroin injection is self-reported. Counts without population denominators.
Period boundaries are set by the date of the Australian shortage and differ between series; other drug trends are not shown; the cohort is reported only as one odds ratio and four two-year shares.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E is used because the paper relates calendar periods, standing for a change in heroin supply, to markers of heroin use and harm (METHODS §5.3). High overall, from confounding by trends already under way, visible in the paper's own figure, and from an exposure that is assumed, not measured; for any inference that heroin supply fell from 2001, a stricter reading would give very high. Within that, the counts come from routine sources and the cohort analysis is large and adjusted for individual characteristics. Citable for: the yearly averages of Table 1; the yearly values of Figure 1 as the editors' approximate readings, including that deaths fell mostly before 2001 and that 2001 was about level with 2000 and above 2002 and 2003; and the cohort's self-reported daily heroin injection (adjusted odds ratio 0.55 for 2001–04 against 1996–2000; 36.5%, 32.6%, 23.3% and 20.8% for 1997/98 to 2003/04). Not citable for: a measured fall in heroin supply, availability, purity or price; a fall beginning in 2001; any figure for 2005, for Vancouver's overdose deaths or for the area around the supervised injection site.

key_findings.finding: The authors take the Australian heroin shortage to have begun in about January 2001 and hypothesize that, because western Canada receives heroin from similar source countries and (citing one paper, ref. 16) had not changed its supply-reduction funding or strategies, Canadian markers of heroin-related harm would stay stable or rise after it.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Aims (p. 689); Introduction, 3rd paragraph, and Methods › Assumptions and hypothesis, 1st paragraph (p. 690)

key_findings.finding: Data sources: overdose deaths (the paper's term; its source, ref. 19, is titled drug-induced deaths) for the whole of British Columbia, 1998–2003, from the provincial vital statistics agency (the drugs responsible were not available, and the authors expect some deaths not to involve heroin); ambulance responses requiring naloxone in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside, by fiscal year, 1997–98 to 2002–03; heroin destined for Canada that was seized, 1998–2003, as a potential indicator of supply that could also mark supply-reduction activity. Periods compared: 1998–2000 against 2001–03; for naloxone, four fiscal years (1997–98 to 2000–01) against two (2001–02 to 2002–03).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (right column)

key_findings.finding: Cohort analysis: VIDUS questionnaire data from May 1996 to December 2004; daily heroin use at each 6-monthly interview related to the period (1996–2000 against 2001–04) by GEE logistic regression, with age, gender, ethnicity, daily cocaine injection, daily crack use, sex-trade involvement, methadone use and Downtown Eastside residence considered as confounders, under an a priori protocol entering variables with P ≤ 0.05 in univariate analyses.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources, 4th paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Yearly averages (Table 1): overdose deaths in British Columbia 297 in 1998–2000 against 192 in 2001–03 (35.4% reduction); naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside 674 a year in fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01 against 370 in 2001–02 to 2002–03 (45.1%); heroin destined for Canada seized 184 kg a year against 67 kg (63.6%). No intervals or statistical tests.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Timing, from the Figure 1 readings (editors' calculations): deaths fell about 45% from 1998 to 2000, were about the same in 2001 as in 2000 and lower in 2002 and 2003; naloxone-requiring responses peaked in fiscal 1998–99 and fell every year after, fiscal 2000–01 already about 45% below the peak; seizures, after a fall from 1998 to 1999 and a rise in 2000, fell about 47% from 2000 to 2001 and again to 2002, with 2003 a little higher, so that every year from 2001 was below every earlier year. The paper does not comment on the falls before 2001.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1, panels A to C

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 1,587 participants gave 13,609 observations (May 1996 to December 2004); daily heroin injection was less likely in 2001–04 than in 1996–2000, adjusted odds ratio 0.55 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.61), P<0.001; in the same model current methadone use 0.43 (0.37 to 0.51), daily cocaine injection 2.32 (2.08 to 2.60), daily crack use 1.85 (1.65 to 2.06) and sex-trade involvement 1.34 (1.20 to 1.52); age, Downtown Eastside residence, Aboriginal ethnicity and gender also in the model, estimates not shown.
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (p. 691); Table 2 (p. 693)

key_findings.finding: Shares of the cohort reporting daily use, by two-year period (the text's breakdown of 1997–2004 by quarter): 36.5% (1997/98), 32.6% (1999/00), 23.3% (2001/02) and 20.8% (2003/04); no counts, denominators or yearly values, so 2001 is not shown apart from 2002. Other drugs did not fall similarly, and methamphetamine use rose significantly (data not shown).
key_findings.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Coverage: the routine series end in 2003 (fiscal 2002–03 for naloxone) and the cohort in December 2004; no figure is given for 2005, for Vancouver's overdose deaths or for any area smaller than the Downtown Eastside, and the text does not discuss supervised injection: it appears only in the title of reference 24 (p. 695), a 2005 paper on safer injection facility use cited with reference 23 for the cohort's description (p. 691).
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data sources (pp. 690–691); Results (p. 691); Figure 1 (p. 692); whole paper searched

key_findings.finding: Limitations as the authors state them: overdose statistics and seizure data may be poor proxies for heroin use, and the measures were not counted at the same level; fiscal years put 4 months of post-shortage data in the before period for naloxone; Canada has no standardized longitudinal measures of street heroin purity; other studies (cited) found ambulance and overdose mortality statistics to correlate strongly with street purity.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 693, right column, continued on p. 694)

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: deaths and naloxone use fell markedly in western Canada at about the time of the Australian shortage, corroborated by the cohort's fall in heroin use; seizures fell by more than 60%; that Canada saw a similar reduction without increasing supply-reduction efforts, they write, suggests that external global heroin supply forces deserve much greater investigation and credence as a potential explanation of the Australian shortage. They acknowledge that supply may instead have been diverted elsewhere or production switched to other drugs such as methamphetamine.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 692, continued on p. 693) and 6th paragraph (p. 694)

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the after period for seizures as 2000–03 (Results, 3rd paragraph), while Table 1 and the abstract give 2001–03.
reporting_issues.consequence: A misprint in the text: the Figure 1 readings for 2001–03 average about 67 kg, as in Table 1; with 2000 included the mean would be about 94 kg (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 1 footnote dates the naloxone before period from fiscal '199–98' (the Methods and Results say 1997–98), and the table's column heads (1998–2000, 2001–03) do not describe the naloxone row, which compares four fiscal years with two.
reporting_issues.consequence: The naloxone comparison covers different years from the other two rows; it has to be read with the footnote.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract places the naloxone series in British Columbia; the Methods, Table 1 and Figure 1 give it for Vancouver's Downtown Eastside only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The naloxone figures describe one neighbourhood, not the province.

reporting_issues.issue: The routine series are called rates (the annual total event rate, the annual overdose mortality rate, the annual rate of naloxone use) but are yearly counts with no population denominator.
reporting_issues.consequence: Population change over 1998–2003 is not taken into account; the falls are falls in counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Two references do not match the statements they support: reduced heroin availability on Vancouver's streets, said to be widely reported in the media, cites a study of HIV viral rebound on antiretroviral drugs (ref. 17); the interest of drug policy-makers in the Australian supply-reduction efforts cites a study of self-perceived HIV risk and seroconversion (ref. 18).
reporting_issues.consequence: No source is given for media reports of reduced heroin availability in Vancouver; the statement rests on the authors' word.

reporting_issues.issue: The cohort's breakdown of 1997–2004 by quarter is four two-year periods, given as shares without counts or a stated denominator (people or interviews); the outcome is named inconsistently: daily heroin use in the abstract's Methods, the Methods and the Results sentences on data points and shares, and daily injection of heroin, injection of heroin or daily heroin injection in the abstract's Results, the Results sentence on the odds ratio and Table 2 (pp. 689, 691, 693).
reporting_issues.consequence: The yearly course of daily heroin injection, including 2001 on its own, cannot be recovered from the paper.
